Profile pages, polls, threads, pins, forums, task boards, photos channels (their albums, captions and reactions; the pictures and videos are files in `uploads/`), events, roles, groups (their encrypted messages), webhooks (only a hash of each secret), outgoing webhooks (with their signing secrets), built-in bots and push subscriptions are all in `iskra.db` too, so copying the folder takes everything along.

On Linux and macOS the server creates the folder (and `certs/`) readable by its own user only, writes secrets as `0600`, and tightens older secret files to `0600` when it starts.

Uploads that nothing uses (no message, direct message, avatar, emoji, sticker, sound, webhook, event cover, profile page or running watch party) are deleted after a day.

**Security log and retention:** the owner reads the server's security log in **Server settings → Sign-ins & security** (failed sign-ins, new members and devices, key changes, account deletions, backups, moves, data downloads; IP addresses only if you turn that on) and sets how long messages, files, the audit log and the security log are kept. Deleting happens every hour and can't be undone. Members download what the server keeps about them in **Settings → Privacy & data**; if someone asks you instead, use **Someone's data** in Server settings → Sign-ins & security.

**Backups and moving:** see [Backups, moving and importing](#backups-moving-and-importing). Copying the stopped server's folder works too; it holds secrets (`server.key`, `vapid.json`, `livekit.key`, `certs/`, `backups/`), so keep copies private. **Updating:** see [Updating](#updating). Automatic updates keep their state in `.update/` next to `iskra-server`, not in the world folder.

## Logs

The server writes its log itself, into `logs/` in its folder: one file per day (`2026-10-17.log`, UTC days), the same
lines it prints on its console (or to `journalctl` under systemd). Each line is one event:

```
2026-10-17T13:41:30.112Z INFO  srv   sess   closed      SES-120 conn=k3f acct=4be1d9 close=1000 why=kicked dur=6.9s
```

time (UTC), level, who wrote it (`srv` the server, `lk` voice, `p2p` the tunnel, `hook` webhooks), area, event, a code
for problems, then details. Voice rooms log people joining and leaving with the count left (`count=`) and why a room
closed; the tunnel logs its announce (with the NAT type: `open`, `consistent` or `randomized`), friends connected (a
count), voice carried through it (flows and packets, every 5 minutes while in use) and restarts (`TUN-130`). Codes and what to do about each: [log-codes.md](log-codes.md). The line format in full:
[development.md, Logs](development.md#logs).

**What's never in it:** names (people's, channels', webhooks', files'), message text, keys, tokens, invite or p2p
secrets, claim codes, IP addresses and file paths. People appear as `acct=` (a short code that only matches up inside
this server's log) and each connection as `conn=`, an id the member's app is told too. So you can share a log with
someone helping you.

**How long it's kept:** files stay plain for 60 days, are gzipped (`.log.gz`) until 180 days, then deleted; and all of
`logs/` together stays under 200 MB, the oldest files going first. Set `Logs` in `server.json` to change that. Trimming
runs at start and once a day. The startup lines list the version, ports, voice, p2p and these settings.

**The desktop app's own log.** The desktop app keeps a log of its own in the same format, in its data folder:
`%APPDATA%\iskra-desktop\logs` on Windows, `~/Library/Application Support/iskra-desktop/logs` on macOS and
`~/.config/iskra-desktop/logs` on Linux (one `YYYY-MM-DD.log` per UTC day). It has the app's start and stop, its windows
and tray, sleep and wake, a page or helper process that stopped (`DSK-110`), the servers it hosts starting and stopping
(by port, with their exit code: `DSK-120`), update checks (`upd`), the tunnel (`p2p`: how each connection to a server
got through, its NAT type, how long it took, failures with HyperDHT's reason), and the app page's own lines (`app`:
connections to each server with its `srv=` and `conn=` ids, the direct address tried first, voice joins and why they
ended, voice's route and a quality sample every 30 s, errors). Same rules: no names, message text,
keys, tokens, addresses or paths. It's kept like the server's (plain 60 days, gzipped until 180, then deleted) and under
50 MB in all. A server hosted in the app writes its own log in `logs/` in its server folder. **Report a bug** in the
desktop app adds the last 30 minutes of this log to the report, so a host can match a member's report with the server's
log by `srv=` and `conn=`.

## Public page

Opening the server's address in a browser shows its public page (Server settings → Overview → Public page). Off by default it shows nothing about your server, only that it's an Iskra server and where to get the app; turned on, you pick what it shows: name, picture, banner, a short description, the start of the rules, a rounded member count and a Join button for an invite you choose. The apps still read the same JSON at `/`, which includes the server's name and icon for invite previews.

## Server icon and banner

**Server settings → Overview → Icon and banner** (the owner and admins; a server can give or take that power per built-in role under **Roles**). The **icon** is square (at least 128×128 pixels, up to 1 MB) and shows in everyone's server list, the server's header and menu, and on invite links before people join. The **banner** is wide (2.5 to 4 times as wide as it is high, for example 960×360, up to 3 MB) and shows above the channel list. PNG, JPEG or WebP, still pictures only. The app lets you crop either before it uploads; everyone sees the change at once.

The server checks every picture itself and takes out its metadata (EXIF with GPS positions, text, comments, thumbnails) before anyone sees it. Invite pages only ever get the icon, from `/icon` on your server: no banner, no names, no channels. Both are in your backups with the other uploads. The server's name still comes from `Name` in `server.json`.

## Roles and moderation

Everyone has a **built-in role**: `Guest < Member < Trusted < Admin < Owner`. Each channel has a built-in role needed to see it and one needed to post (or speak, in voice). Admins can kick and ban people ranked below them and hand out built-in roles below their own; the owner can do everything. Invite links can carry a built-in role and expire after 1 hour to 30 days, optionally single use. What each built-in role may do is adjustable under **Server settings → Roles** (for example, members may by default use emoji and stickers from their other servers here: their app copies the picture into your server, which keeps up to 300 such emoji and 100 stickers, the same picture once; turn that off per role if you don't want it).

On top of the built-in roles, admins can make **custom roles** (Server settings → Roles) with a name, colour and icon, and give them permissions such as managing messages, timing people out, kicking, banning, managing channels or roles, muting and moving people in voice, or mentioning everyone. Roles can also change what a channel allows (**per-channel overrides**), and roles can be made mentionable. Moderators have **timeouts**, **slowmode** per channel, **server mute** and **move** in voice, and an **audit log** of moderation actions (kept 90 days).

**Letting people in:** an invite can be made with *Approve each person who joins*: whoever opens it waits outside (they see only the server's name and icon) until a moderator lets them in or turns them away under **Server settings → Reports**; moderators see the name, which invite and since when, never an address. Admins can **pause invites** (Server settings → AutoMod → Joining, or the banner in the invite dialog) so every link stops letting people in until resumed, and set a **newcomer slowmode**: members younger than N hours wait at least X seconds between messages in every channel. AutoMod's **Join flood** rule pauses invites by itself when more than N people join within M minutes and posts an alert; resuming is always by hand. All of it lands in the audit log.

**A picture per server:** next to the server nickname (server menu → *Server nickname…*, or a member's sheet), anyone can set a picture shown instead of their profile picture on that server only, with the same crop and limits as the profile picture (1 MB; the server stores a copy without metadata). Admins can change it for members below them. It goes when the member leaves.

**Moderators' tools:** *Select messages…* in a message's menu ticks up to 100 messages in a channel and deletes them in one go (one audit log entry); in an encrypted channel only the stored copies go. Banning offers *Also delete their messages from the last 24 hours / 7 days*. A member's sheet has a **Warning** (the person sees it at once), private **Moderator notes** and their **Moderation history**; **People who left** at the bottom of Server settings → Members lists recent leaves, kicks and bans so a report about someone who's gone can still end in a ban, and keeps their notes and history; entries are kept 90 days (the audit log's horizon), the name removed earlier if the account is deleted.

**Roles members pick themselves:** tick *Members can pick this role themselves* on a role (for platforms, interests, ping lists; such a role can never carry permissions or count as rank), then write the questions under **Server settings → Onboarding**: a title, an optional question, one or several answers, and the roles to pick from. New members answer right after agreeing to the rules; everyone can change their picks later from **Pick your roles** in the server menu or with `/roles`. Give one of these roles *view* on a channel to make an opt-in channel. Templates carry them as `selfAssign` and `roleGroups` ([templates](templates.md)).

---

Source: https://iskra.foo/docs/home-server

# An Iskra box at home

> **Your server, your choice.** Iskra gets nothing from any of this; this is just a guide.

A small computer that's always on is a great home for your group's Iskra server: an old PC or laptop, a mini PC, or
a Raspberry Pi. It costs a few euros of electricity a year, everything stays in your home, and nobody has to keep
their gaming PC running so friends can chat.

This guide covers picking the box, installing Iskra, starting it with the computer, letting friends in from the
internet, updates, backups and keeping the power bill small. The full reference is [hosting.md](hosting.md).

## 1. Pick a box

Anything from the last ten years or so works for a friend group. What matters is that it's **64-bit** and can stay on.

| Box | Iskra package | Good to know |
|---|---|---|
| Old PC or laptop with Windows | `iskra-server-<version>-win-x64.zip`, or the desktop app | Easiest if it already runs Windows. A laptop has a built-in battery for short power cuts |
| Old PC, laptop or mini PC with Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora…) | `iskra-server-<version>-linux-x64.tar.gz` | The best fit: [automatic updates](#5-updates) work here. Mini PCs (Intel N100 and similar) are quiet and frugal |
| Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 | `iskra-server-<version>-linux-arm64.tar.gz` | Needs the **64-bit** Raspberry Pi OS (or Ubuntu for Pi). A good microSD card works fine; an SSD is the upgrade: see [below](#a-raspberry-pi-microsd-card-or-ssd). A Pi 3 runs the 64-bit system too, but slowly |
| Other 64-bit ARM boards | `iskra-server-<version>-linux-arm64.tar.gz` | Any 64-bit Linux (`uname -m` says `aarch64`) |
| Mac (Apple silicon or Intel) | `iskra-server-<version>-osx-arm64.tar.gz` / `osx-x64` | Works, but Macs like to sleep: see [power tips](#7-power-use) |

**Not supported:** 32-bit systems (Raspberry Pi OS 32-bit, `armv7l`, old 32-bit Windows). On a Raspberry Pi, check
with `uname -m`: it must say `aarch64`; if it says `armv7l`, install the 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS.

**How big?** 1 GB of memory is enough for a group of friends (the cheapest cloud servers Iskra runs on have 1 GB);
2 GB or more is comfortable. Disk space is mostly the files people share, plus about 100 MB if someone uses live
captions. A wired network cable is better than Wi-Fi for voice.

Voice (LiveKit) is in every package: nothing else to install.

### A Raspberry Pi: microSD card or SSD

Both work. Pick what you have:

- **A good microSD card works fine.** Use one from a known brand marked **A2** (32–64 GB is plenty). In
  [Raspberry Pi Imager](https://www.raspberrypi.com/software/) choose your Pi, **Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit)** (no
  desktop needed) and the card. Let Imager set a host name, your user and password, and turn on SSH. Put the card in
  the Pi and start it.
- **An SSD is the upgrade** if you want it to last for years or run faster: an NVMe SSD on an M.2 HAT for a **Pi 5**
  (the official M.2 HAT+ or a similar board, with the official 27 W power supply), or a USB 3 SSD in a **blue** USB 3
  port on a Pi 4 or 5. Steps below.

Either way, do [Make it last](#make-it-last) and set up [encrypted backup copies on a USB stick or another
computer](#6-backups): then even a dead card is a 5-minute fix.

**Putting the system on an SSD** (Raspberry Pi's own guides: [boot from NVMe](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/accessories/m2-hat-plus.html#boot-from-nvme),
[boot order](https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/raspberry-pi.html#BOOT_ORDER)):

1. **Write the system to the SSD** with Imager, as for a card. A USB SSD can be written from your PC. An NVMe SSD sits
   in the Pi, so start the Pi once from a microSD card with Raspberry Pi OS, then run Imager on the Pi and pick the
   NVMe drive.
2. **Update the bootloader** (on the Pi running from the card): `sudo rpi-eeprom-update` shows its date. For NVMe it
   must be December 6, 2023 or later; if it's older, run `sudo raspi-config` → **Advanced Options** →
   **Bootloader Version** → **Latest**, then `sudo rpi-eeprom-update -a` and `sudo reboot`.
3. **Boot from the SSD:** `sudo raspi-config` → **Advanced Options** → **Boot Order** → the option with **NVMe/USB**
   first → **Finish**, and reboot. Then take the card out: the Pi starts from the SSD.
4. **Pi 5 with a USB SSD on a power supply that isn't the official 27 W one:** the Pi 5 won't boot from USB with a
   3 A supply. Use the official supply, or add `usb_max_current_enable=1` to `/boot/firmware/config.txt` if you know
   your supply and SSD are fine with it.

`findmnt /` then says `/dev/nvme0n1p2` (NVMe) or `/dev/sda2` (USB) instead of `/dev/mmcblk0p2` (the card). If a USB
SSD doesn't start, try the other blue port or another USB case; some cheap adapters misbehave.

### Make it last

A few small settings mean far fewer writes. They help on an SSD and matter most on a microSD card:

- **Keep the system log small:** create `/etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/iskra.conf` with
  ```ini
  [Journal]
  SystemMaxUse=50M
  ```
  and run `sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald`. On a card you can use `Storage=volatile` instead, which keeps the
  log in memory only (it's gone after a restart, along with any clues about what went wrong).
- **`noatime`:** the disk doesn't note every time a file is read. Raspberry Pi OS already does this; `findmnt -no OPTIONS /`
  should show `noatime`. If not, add `noatime` to the options of `/` in `/etc/fstab`.
- **Swap:** leave Raspberry Pi OS's own setting alone (current versions mostly swap into compressed memory). Iskra
  needs about 1 GB, so a Pi with 2 GB or more rarely swaps. Don't add a big swap file on a card.
- **Keep the Iskra folder on the system disk** (the card or the SSD), as in the steps below. Don't run it from a USB
  stick or a network share; those are for [backup copies](#6-backups).

## 2. Install

Download the package for your box from the [releases page](https://github.com/quikmn/iskra-voice/releases) and
unpack it into a folder of its own, then start it with a folder for the server (it's made on the first run):

```sh
# Linux and Raspberry Pi
mkdir -p ~/iskra && tar -xzf iskra-server-*-linux-*.tar.gz -C ~/iskra
~/iskra/iskra-server ~/iskra/world
```

```powershell
# Windows: unpack the zip into, say, C:\Iskra, then in a terminal:
C:\Iskra\iskra-server.exe C:\Iskra\world
```

The first time, the server prints a **one-time owner link** (also saved in `world/owner-invite.txt`). Open it in the
Iskra app, or at [app.iskra.foo](https://app.iskra.foo), and you're the owner. Then press Ctrl+C to stop it: the next
step makes it start on its own.

Windows asks once whether Iskra may use the network: choose **Allow** (private networks are enough at home).

**With a screen and a desktop app instead?** On a Windows, Mac or Linux PC you can also use the Iskra desktop app:
**Create a server**, then tick **Keep my server running**. Iskra then starts with the computer, hidden in the tray,
and updates together with the app. The rest of this guide is about the standalone server, which needs no screen.

## 3. Start with the computer

### Linux and Raspberry Pi: a system service (recommended)

A system service starts at boot, before anyone logs in, and is what [automatic updates](#5-updates) need. Install
Iskra in `/opt/iskra` for its own user:

```sh
sudo useradd --system --create-home --home-dir /opt/iskra iskra
sudo tar -xzf iskra-server-*-linux-*.tar.gz -C /opt/iskra
sudo mv ~/iskra/world /opt/iskra/world        # if you already made the server in step 2
sudo chown -R iskra:iskra /opt/iskra
```

Then create `/etc/systemd/system/iskra.service` with the unit from
[hosting.md](hosting.md#on-a-linux-vps-with-systemd) (it's the same at home and on a rented server) and turn it on:

```sh
sudo systemctl enable --now iskra
sudo journalctl -u iskra -f          # its output; shows the owner link on a new server
```

### Or: one command, as your own user (Windows, macOS, Linux)

```sh
iskra-server install-autostart ~/iskra/world      # Windows: iskra-server.exe install-autostart C:\Iskra\world
```

It prints how to start it right away. What it sets up:

- **Windows:** a scheduled task that starts when you log in, without a window. Run the command from an
  **administrator** terminal and it starts with the computer instead, before anyone logs in (still as you, never with
  administrator rights).
- **Linux:** a systemd user service that starts when you log in. `loginctl enable-linger $USER` makes it start at
  boot. Automatic updates need the system service above.
- **macOS:** a launchd agent that starts when you log in.

`iskra-server remove-autostart <folder>` undoes it.

## 4. Let friends in from the internet

At home, friends on your own network can join right away. For everyone else:

### The easy way: Let friends anywhere join

As the owner, open **Server settings → Internet access** in the app and turn on **Let friends anywhere join**. Iskra
asks your router to open the ports (UPnP or NAT-PMP), gives the server a free address like `203-0-113-7.sslip.io`,
gets an HTTPS certificate for it, and keeps all of that up to date. A checklist shows how each step went. Details:
[hosting.md](hosting.md#one-switch-let-friends-anywhere-join).

Give the box a **fixed address on your network** (in the router: "DHCP reservation" or "static lease" for the box),
so the router keeps sending friends to the right computer.

### If the router won't open ports

Many routers have UPnP turned off. Either turn it on in the router's settings, or forward these ports to the box by
hand (**Server settings → Internet access → Forward the ports yourself** lists them with your addresses, and can write
a question for an AI assistant with your router's model filled in):

| Outside port | To the box | What |
|---|---|---|
| `80/tcp` and `443/tcp` | the server's port, `47070` by default | The app, invites, HTTPS and its certificate |
| `7881/tcp` and `7882/udp` | the same ports | Voice and video |

If the box has its own firewall (ufw on Ubuntu, firewalld on Fedora), allow `47070/tcp`, `7881/tcp` and `7882/udp`
there too.

### If your connection is shared (CGNAT)

Some providers share one public address between many homes (carrier-grade NAT, common on mobile broadband and some
fiber). Then no port forwarding can work, and **What Iskra found out** in Server settings → Internet access says so.
Your options:

1. **Ask your provider for a public IPv4 address.** Often free and done once; then everything above works.
2. **[Tailscale](hosting.md#use-tailscale-free)** (free for small groups): you and each friend install it once, and
   friends reach your box as if it were on their own network. Iskra notices Tailscale on the box by itself and offers
   **Invite friends → Over Tailscale**. Friends join with the Iskra app (browsers need HTTPS, which this route doesn't
   have).
3. **Connect without port forwarding** (experimental): turn it on in Server settings → Internet access. It works with
   the desktop app's **Keep my server running** and with the standalone server, Raspberry Pi included (the
   `iskra-p2p` program in the download does it; see [hosting.md](hosting.md#let-friends-connect-without-port-forwarding-experimental)).
4. **Rent a small server instead.** If home hosting doesn't work out, the app can set one up for about $6 a month
   ([Rent a small server](hosting.md#rent-a-small-server)), and your server can [move there](hosting.md#moving-a-server-to-another-computer)
   with everyone and everything in it.

## 5. Updates

As the owner, open **Server settings → Server updates**:

- **Install automatically** (Linux with the system service from step 3): the server checks every 6 hours, downloads
  new versions from GitHub, checks them (checksums and the signed build attestation), installs them at night once
  nobody is in voice, and puts the old version back by itself if the new one doesn't start.
- **Tell me** (the default, and everywhere else): you get a notice in the app. To update by hand, stop the server,
  unpack the new package over the old files (the `world` folder isn't in the package and stays as it is), and start
  it again.

The operating system needs updates too. On Ubuntu and Debian, security updates install themselves with
`unattended-upgrades` (`sudo apt install unattended-upgrades`); on Raspberry Pi OS, run
`sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade` now and then, or install `unattended-upgrades` too.

## 6. Backups

- **Daily backups** are on by default: every day the server keeps a copy of its database, settings and keys in
  `world/backups/` (the last 7). They help with mistakes, not with a dead disk.
- **Copy them to another disk, encrypted:** in **Server settings → Backup & move → Also copy them to**, enter a
  folder on a USB stick, a second disk or a network share mounted on the box (another computer's shared folder works
  too), such as `/mnt/usb/iskra`, and choose a passphrase. After each daily backup the server encrypts it with that
  passphrase (the same format as a downloaded backup) and writes it there as `auto-YYYY-MM-DD.iskrabackup`, keeping the
  same number of days. Keep the passphrase somewhere safe, like a password manager: you need it to restore a copy. The
  folder must exist and the server's user must be able to write to it
  (`sudo mkdir -p /mnt/usb/iskra && sudo chown iskra:iskra /mnt/usb/iskra`); if the stick isn't mounted, Server
  settings says so and the next try is an hour later. For a stick that's always plugged in, mount it at boot with a
  line in `/etc/fstab` using its `UUID` (from `lsblk -f`) and `nofail`, so the Pi still starts without it. Details:
  [hosting.md](hosting.md#backups).
- **Download a backup now and then:** **Server settings → Backup & move → Make backup** gives you one encrypted file
  with everything (keep the passphrase somewhere else). Put it on another computer or a USB stick.
- From a script, for example a weekly job that writes to a NAS. It works while the server runs; run it as the
  server's user (the folder is readable by that user only), into a folder that user can write to:

  ```sh
  echo "$PASSPHRASE" | sudo -u iskra /opt/iskra/iskra-server backup /opt/iskra/world /mnt/nas/iskra/iskra-$(date +%F).iskrabackup --passphrase-stdin
  ```

**If the card or disk dies:** get a new card (or SSD), install the system and Iskra again ([1](#a-raspberry-pi-microsd-card-or-ssd),
[2](#2-install), [3](#3-start-with-the-computer)), then restore the newest backup into an empty world folder instead of
starting a new server, before you start the service:

```sh
sudo -u iskra /opt/iskra/iskra-server restore /mnt/usb/iskra/auto-2026-10-14.iskrabackup /opt/iskra/world   # asks for the passphrase
```

A downloaded `.iskrabackup` file restores the same way. Everything comes back, with the
server's own key, so friends' apps simply reconnect: no new invites. See [Restoring](hosting.md#restoring); to hand the server
to another computer, [Move this server](hosting.md#moving-a-server-to-another-computer).

## 7. Power use

An always-on box runs about 8,760 hours a year, so every watt is about 9 kWh a year.

| Box | Typical power while idle | A year, roughly |
|---|---|---|
| Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 | 3–5 W | 25–45 kWh |
| Mini PC (Intel N100 and similar) | 6–10 W | 50–90 kWh |
| Old laptop, lid closed | 8–15 W | 70–130 kWh |
| Old desktop PC | 30–60 W | 260–525 kWh |

Iskra itself uses next to nothing while nobody talks; voice calls add a little.

- **Keep it awake, let the screen sleep.** Turn off sleep and hibernation (Windows: Settings → System → Power;
  macOS: System Settings → Energy, "Prevent automatic sleeping"; Linux desktops: the power settings). Turning off the
  display is fine.
- **No screen at all?** On Linux, a server or "Lite" install without a desktop saves memory and power.
- **Back after a power cut:** in the PC's BIOS/UEFI settings, set "Restore on AC power loss" (or similar) to
  **Power On**. A Raspberry Pi starts by itself when power comes back. The service from step 3 starts Iskra.
- **Laptops:** close the lid with "do nothing" as the lid action, and keep it plugged in. Many laptops can limit
  charging to about 80 %, which is kinder to the battery.
- **Old desktops** use the most. If you have one, a mini PC or a Pi usually pays for itself in electricity within a
  few years.
- Use a wired connection for voice, and a small UPS if power cuts are common where you live.

## Help

- Something's off? **Server settings → Internet access** explains what it found. The server's log is in
  `logs/` in the server folder (one file per day), and also in `journalctl -u iskra` (system service) or
  `journalctl --user -u iskra-…` (user service). The desktop app keeps its own log too, in `logs/` in its data folder
  (Windows: `%APPDATA%\iskra-desktop\logs`; see [hosting.md, Logs](hosting.md#logs)).
- The full reference, every setting and every file: [hosting.md](hosting.md).

---

Source: https://iskra.foo/docs/templates

# Server templates

A template sets up a new Iskra server in one go: channels of every kind, who can see and use each one, roles, what the
built-in roles can do, rules, the AFK channel and server settings, and even some starting content: channel topics,
welcome messages and docs pages. It's a small JSON file you can read and edit.

- **In the desktop app:** **Create a server**, then pick a starting point: *Gaming group*, *Friends hangout*, *Board
  games and tabletop*, *Empty*, or **From a template file…**. You see everything a template sets up before anything is
  created.
- **Save your own:** **Server settings → Overview → Save as template** (admins). The file has your channels (with their
  topics and disappearing-message timers), who can see and use them, roles, rules and settings. It never has members,
  messages, docs pages, files, invites or keys. Channels you can't
  see yourself are left out. Encrypted channels are saved as ordinary channels, because a template can't hold keys:
  turn encryption on again after creating the server.
- **Standalone server:** `iskra-server my-server --template gaming`, `--template ./book-club.json`, or
  `"Template": "./book-club.json"` in `server.json` before the first start. A relative file is looked for in the
  server's folder first.
- **Check a file:** `iskra-server templates ./book-club.json` prints what it would set up, or exactly what's wrong.
  `iskra-server templates` lists the built-in ones.

A template is applied **once**, on the first start of a new server (nobody has joined, nothing set up yet). On a server
that's already in use it's ignored, so a leftover setting never adds channels to it. A bad template stops the server
from starting, with a message saying what to fix. Applying one is written to the security log.

## Adding a template to a server in use

```
iskra-server templates apply <world-folder> <template.json>           # shows what it would add
iskra-server templates apply <world-folder> <template.json> --apply   # adds it
```

Stop the server first (the command refuses while it runs). This only **adds**: roles and categories the server doesn't
have (by name), channels it doesn't have (by name and kind, anywhere on the server), and settings that are still at
their defaults (a colour or permissions for a built-in role nobody changed, rules if there are none, the AFK channel if none
is set, the default notifications, limits, built-in bots, the bug inbox, translation). A channel it already has gets
the template's starting content only where it has none yet: a topic if it has none, the template's messages if the
template never posted there, docs pages whose titles it doesn't have, and a disappearing-messages timer if none was ever
set. It never deletes, renames or changes channels, roles, members or messages that are there. Running it twice adds
nothing the second time.

The bug inbox is left off (the command says so) if the server's channel of that name can be read by more people than
the template says: reports can hold email addresses. It is also left off, with a message, on a server that doesn't take
bug reports (`BugInbox.Accept` in server.json is off, which is the default: only the server that receives Iskra's
bug reports turns it on).

## The format

```jsonc
{
  "version": 4,                                // 4 for this format; 3, 2 and 1 (no version) still work
  "name": "Book club",                         // 1–60 characters
  "description": "Reading together.",          // optional, up to 300
  "channels": [                                // optional: outside any category, listed first
    { "name": "welcome", "writeRole": "admin", "topic": "Start here",
      "messages": [{ "text": "# Welcome!\nGrab a book and say hi in **#now-reading**.", "pin": true }] }
  ],
  "categories": [                              // optional, up to 50
    {
      "name": "Books",                         // 1–32 characters
      "channels": [
        { "name": "now-reading", "slowmode": 30 },
        { "name": "announcements", "writeRole": "admin",
          "overrides": [{ "role": "Moderator", "allow": ["send"] }] },
        { "name": "mod-room", "readRole": "admin",
          "overrides": [{ "role": "Moderator", "allow": ["view", "send"] }] },
        { "name": "reviews", "kind": "forum", "tags": [{ "name": "Fiction", "emoji": "📖" }, { "name": "Non-fiction" }] },
        { "name": "reading-list", "kind": "docs",
          "pages": [{ "title": "How we pick books", "text": "We vote every month…", "startHere": true }] },
        { "name": "spoilers", "disappear": 86400 }
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "Voice",
      "channels": [
        { "name": "Reading room", "kind": "voice", "userLimit": 8 },
        { "name": "Listening party", "kind": "voice", "hifi": true },
        { "name": "Author talk", "kind": "stage" },
        { "name": "AFK", "kind": "voice" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "roles": [                                   // optional, up to 100, highest first
    { "name": "Moderator", "color": "#3fa66b", "icon": "📚", "hoist": true, "mentionable": false,
      "permissions": ["manageMessages", "timeoutMembers", "kickMembers", "muteMembers", "moveMembers", "viewAuditLog"] },
    { "name": "Fiction", "selfAssign": true },  // members pick it themselves (no permissions allowed)
    { "name": "Non-fiction", "selfAssign": true }
  ],
  "roleGroups": [                              // optional, up to 20: what new members are asked to pick
    { "title": "Shelf", "question": "What do you mostly read?", "multi": true, "roles": ["Fiction", "Non-fiction"] }
  ],
  "builtinRoles": {                            // optional: owner, admin, trusted, member, guest
    "owner": { "color": "#c27ce0" },
    "admin": { "color": "#e5534b" },
    "member": { "abilities": ["invite", "events", "pin"] }   // the whole set; left out: the defaults
  },
  "rules": { "text": "Be kind.", "welcome": "Welcome!", "required": false },
  "afk": { "channel": "AFK", "minutes": 30, "canTalk": ["owner", "admin", "Moderator"] },
  "settings": {
    "notifyDefault": "auto",                   // "auto" (all messages under 15 people), "all" or "mentions"
    "limits": { "maxUploadMb": 512, "guestMbPerDay": 1024, "emojiMaxKb": 1024 },
    "builtinBots": ["dice", "polls", "reminders"],
    "bugInbox": "mod-room",                    // a text channel of the template: bug reports land there
    "translation": true                        // offer message translation to members
  }
}
```

Comments and trailing commas are fine. Unknown fields are an error, so typos don't go unnoticed; a file made by a newer
version of Iskra says so. Files can be up to 256 KB, with up to 500 channels.

### Channels

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | 1–32 characters |
| `kind` | `text` (default), `voice`, `forum`, `stage`, `docs`, `whiteboard`, `media`, `tasks` (a task board) or `photos` (photo albums) |
| `readRole` | the lowest built-in role that can see it: `guest`, `member` (default), `trusted`, `admin` or `owner` |
| `writeRole` | the lowest built-in role that can post (text, forums), speak (voice), ask to speak (stage), edit (docs), draw (whiteboards), change tasks (task boards) or add photos (photos channels). Default: the same as `readRole`; for docs `trusted` |
| `overrides` | for the template's own roles: `{ "role": "Moderator", "allow": [...], "deny": [...] }` with `view`, `send`, `connect`, `speak`. Denies apply first, then allows |
| `userLimit` | voice only: 0 (no limit) to 99 |
| `hifi` | voice only: hi-fi audio allowed |
| `slowmode` | seconds between messages per person: 0 (off), 5, 10, 15, 30, 60, 120, 300, 600, 900, 1800, 3600, 7200 or 21600. Not for docs or whiteboards |
| `tags` | forums only: up to 20, `{ "name": "Bug", "emoji": "🐛" }` |
| `topic` | one line saying what the channel is for, shown at its top: up to 300 characters |
| `messages` | text channels only: up to 10 messages, `{ "text": "...", "pin": true }`, posted once under the server's name. Markdown as in the app, up to 4000 characters each; mentions never ping |
| `pages` | docs channels only: up to 20 pages, `{ "title": "...", "text": "...", "startHere": true }`. Markdown as in docs, up to 100 KB each. One page in the whole template can be the server's **Start here** page |
| `disappear` | text and voice channels: messages disappear after this many seconds: 0 (off), 300, 3600, 28800, 86400, 604800 or 2419200. Not together with `messages` |

The server's starting `#general` becomes the template's first text channel. A template has at most 100 messages and 50
pages in all. Messages and pages are plain text in the app's Markdown: they're shown like any message or page, never
run as code.

### Roles

`roles` are custom roles. Names can't be `everyone` or a built-in role's. Permissions: `manageMessages`,
`timeoutMembers`, `kickMembers`, `banMembers`, `manageChannels`, `manageRoles`, `viewAuditLog`, `manageExpressions`,
`manageWebhooks`, `mentionEveryone`, `moveMembers`, `muteMembers`, `manageAutoMod`. A role with `"selfAssign": true`
is one members give themselves (Pick your roles); it can't have permissions.

`roleGroups` are the questions new members answer after agreeing to the rules (and from "Pick your roles" later):
`title` (1–60 characters), an optional `question` (up to 200), `multi` (several answers at once; otherwise picking one
drops the others) and `roles`, 1–25 of the template's `selfAssign` roles in the order shown. Up to 20 groups. Opt-in
channels come from `overrides` on those roles (allow `view` for "PlayStation" on `#playstation`).

`builtinRoles` sets a built-in role's `color` (`#rrggbb`, or `""` for none) and, optionally, what it can do:
`abilities` and `permissions`, each the whole set (left out: the defaults, the same as in **Server settings → Roles**).
Abilities: `invite`, `events`, `pin`, `mentionEveryone`, `uploadSounds`, `giveBaseRoles`, `bots`, `organize`, `rules`,
`stickers`, `gifs`, `stageModerators`, `forumTags`, `profilePages`, `resolveDisputes`, `serverImages`. The same safety rules apply as in
the app: the owner's permissions never change, `runServer` and `transferOwnership` stay the owner's, and guests and members
only get everyday permissions (`invite`, `events`, `pin`, `mentionEveryone`, `uploadSounds`, and the permission
`mentionEveryone`).

### Rules and the AFK channel

- `rules`: `text` up to 6000 characters, `welcome` up to 500; `required` makes members agree before they can write
  (needs `text`).
- `afk`: `channel` names one of the template's voice channels; people idle in voice for `minutes` (5, 15, 30 or 60;
  0 = never move anyone; default 30) are moved there. Everyone in it is muted and deafened by the server except the
  built-in roles and template roles (by name) in `canTalk` (default `["owner", "admin"]`).

### Settings

- `notifyDefault`: what people who chose nothing get: `auto`, `all` or `mentions`. Admins can change it later in
  their notification settings for the server.
- `limits`: any of `maxUploadMb` (1 or more), `memberMbPerDay`, `guestMbPerDay`, `soundMaxSeconds`, `soundMaxMb`,
  `emojiMaxKb`, `stickerMaxKb` (0 = no limit). Left out: the server's defaults.
- `builtinBots`: built-in bots to turn on: `dice`, `polls`, `reminders`.
- `bugInbox`: a text channel of the template where bug reports from Iskra apps land (normally only useful on the
  server that runs the bug inbox). Applied only when that server's `server.json` has `"BugInbox": { "Accept": true }`;
  on any other server it is skipped with a message, and a saved template leaves it out.
- `translation`: `true` offers message translation to members (Server settings → Translation): the server fetches each
  language's model from Mozilla the first time a member needs it.

## The built-in templates

- **Gaming group:** announcements (admins and moderators post), general, clips, looking-for-group (slowmode), a
  moderators' channel, Lobby, Squad and Raid voice channels with limits, a Tournament stage and an AFK channel;
  Moderator and Raid lead roles; Dice and Polls on.
- **Friends hangout:** general, photos, memes, a *plans* forum with tags, voice channels and an AFK channel; members can
  pin; Polls and Reminders on.
- **Board games and tabletop:** campaign notes as a docs channel (game masters edit), a private GM screen, tables with
  limits and a hi-fi music room; Moderator and Game master roles; Dice on.
- **Empty:** #general and one voice channel.

---

Source: https://iskra.foo/docs/security

# How Iskra keeps you safe

Iskra is built so that **nobody has to trust a company**, and so you only have to trust the people you actually rely on.

## Your account is a key

There's no email and no password. On first launch the app creates a key pair on your device; the public half *is* your account. Each device gets its own key, certified by your account key.

- Joining a server means signing a fresh challenge from that server. Nobody can join as you without your device, and a login meant for one server can't be replayed against another.
- Names aren't unique, keys are. If you want to be sure who someone is, compare **safety numbers** (open a direct message, click *Verify*).
- Your **recovery key** (Settings → Recovery key) restores your account on a new device. It's the only copy outside your devices, so keep it somewhere safe, like a password manager. Anyone who has it can use your account, until you replace your account key (below).

## Replacing your account key

If your recovery key leaked, or someone may have copied one of your devices, **replace your account key** (Settings → Recovery key → Replace account key).

- Your device makes a new key and your old key signs it over, and the new key signs too, so nobody can point your account at a key they don't hold. Your servers check both signatures, then move your membership, role, profile, messages, reactions and direct messages to the new key, and keep a record of the change.
- You choose which of your devices to keep. Each one gets a new certificate and the new key, sealed to that device (libsodium `crypto_box_seal`); it only accepts a key that matches the signed hand-over, so a server can't slip in one of its own. Devices you untick are signed out for good.
- Your old key and old recovery key stop working on every server that has the change. You get a new recovery key straight away. Servers you weren't connected to get the change the next time you connect.
- Your friends' apps check the signatures themselves, keep your conversation and its history, and show **"safety number changed"**, so they can verify you again.

**What if someone else has your old key?** They could try to replace it too, and a server can't tell which of you is the real one. Iskra's rule:

1. The first valid replacement wins on each server.
2. Every device of the old account is told. A device that wasn't given the new key says "Your account key was replaced" and offers **That wasn't me**: it claims the account for a new key of yours.
3. A second, different claim within 30 days doesn't win, but marks the account as **disputed**: its role drops to member (so a thief can't keep admin or owner rights) and admins are asked to decide. An admin who knows you keeps the right key, which restores your role. After 30 days the old key is simply dead.

So act fast: on servers where you replace the key first, you win outright. On a server where a thief got there first and nobody else is an admin, the account stays disputed. Your friends' apps warn them while an account is disputed.

## Your devices

- **Linking a device** (Settings → Devices → Link a device) moves your account to a phone or another computer without typing the recovery key: scan the QR code or type the code. The code holds a one-time secret that never reaches the server; both devices prove they know it, then the new device shows a six-digit number that you type into the signed-in one before anything is sent (a wrong number cancels the link). Your account is encrypted from one device straight to the other (libsodium `crypto_box`), so the server that relays it can't read it or slip in a device of its own. Codes expire after five minutes and work once.
- **Removing a device** (Settings → Devices) signs a revocation with your account key and hands it to every server you're on. Servers then refuse that device, sign it out, stop listing it and stop sending it push notifications, and senders stop encrypting messages for it.
- Every linked device keeps your account key in the app's storage (that's what lets it link and remove devices too). **Removing a device stops that device's own key**: it can't connect or get new messages. It does **not** stop someone who copied the device's storage: with the account key they can certify a new device as you. For a copied device, [replace your account key](#replacing-your-account-key) and leave that device out. Servers let one connection remove at most 10 devices an hour, so a thief can't use up the account's 100 removals at once.

## Your keys on your device

Your keys, your devices' short-lived direct message keys and your decrypted direct messages are stored **encrypted** (XChaCha20-Poly1305), with a key that is itself protected by:

- **the desktop app:** your operating system's keychain (Windows DPAPI, macOS Keychain, or GNOME Keyring / KWallet on Linux). A copy of Iskra's data folder is useless on another computer or user account. On Linux without a keyring, the app says so and uses the browser method below.
- **the browser:** a key the browser keeps for Iskra and never reveals to the page (a non-extractable WebCrypto key). That keeps your keys out of copies, exports and casual snooping of the stored data. It does *not* stop someone who can use your browser profile or run code in the app.
- **the phone apps (iPhone, Android):** the browser method above, inside the app's web view, in the app's private storage; there's no extra Android Keystore or iOS Keychain wrapping. Android keeps it out of cloud backups and device transfers (backups are off for the app). On iPhone the app's storage isn't excluded from iPhone backups (iCloud or a computer) yet. The app's page can read the app's own files (that's how shared files reach it), so as in a browser, code running in the page could read the stored data; React-only rendering and the CSP are what stop that. With an app lock, a copy of the storage (a backup, say) is useless without your passphrase or passkey.
- **an app lock (optional, My settings → App lock):** a passphrase, stretched with Argon2id, that Iskra asks for at every start. Without it, nobody can read your keys or messages from the device's storage, even with a full copy. Forget it and you'll need your recovery key.
- **passkeys (optional, My settings → App lock):** unlock with your fingerprint, face, device PIN or a security key (Windows Hello, Touch ID and Face ID, Android, iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, security keys). This isn't just a screen in front of the app: Iskra asks the passkey for its PRF secret (the WebAuthn PRF extension, which only that passkey can produce, after it has checked it's you) and derives the key that unlocks your data from it (HKDF). Without the passkey or your passphrase, the stored keys stay encrypted. Passkeys that can't do PRF are refused with an explanation, and the passphrase is always there instead. You can add several (a laptop's Windows Hello and a security key, say), rename and remove them; your recovery key works as before.

Data stored before this existed is encrypted the first time the app starts. Linking devices and recovery keys work as before.

### Where passkeys work

| Where | Passkeys for the app lock |
|---|---|
| Chrome, Edge (Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS) | Yes, with passkeys that support PRF: Google Password Manager, security keys with `hmac-secret`, phones (scan a QR code), and Windows Hello or iCloud Keychain where the system offers PRF |
| Safari 18 and later (macOS, iPhone, iPad) | Yes, with iCloud Keychain passkeys and security keys |
| Firefox | Recent versions, with security keys and passkeys that support PRF |
| Chrome on Android | Yes, with Google Password Manager passkeys and security keys |
| Android app | Not yet. The app runs in Android's System WebView, and it doesn't turn WebView's passkey support on yet, so the app lock offers no passkey there (or says passkeys aren't supported) and you use a passphrase |
| Desktop app on Windows | Yes: Windows Hello, security keys and phones. The app's own page can't use WebAuthn, so it opens a small window on `app.iskra.foo` for the passkey prompt |
| Desktop app on macOS and Linux | Security keys. Touch ID and iCloud Keychain are only offered to browsers, so on a Mac use a security key, a passphrase, or Iskra in Safari |
| iPhone app | Prepared (`webcredentials:app.iskra.foo`), not yet confirmed on devices; if iOS refuses, the app says so and you use a passphrase |

## Key transparency

A server can't forge anyone's signature, but it does decide which key it shows you as "Alice". Key transparency makes it hard for a server to show different people different keys, or to rewrite what it showed, without being caught.

- **Each server keeps a key log**: every account key it has shown (with a salted hash of the name it showed; the name itself is kept beside it and erased when the account is deleted), every key replacement and every dispute, in order. Each entry is linked to the one before it by a hash, and the server signs the newest one with its own key. Entries are only ever added.
- **Your app checks it every time it connects**: the log must carry on from the point your app saw last (never shorter, never different), every member the server shows must be in it, and every key replacement it announces too.
- **Your servers are compared with each other**: if two servers say someone's old key moved to different new keys, you're told.
- **Your friends' apps compare notes with yours**: now and then a direct message carries a small signed summary (inside the end-to-end encryption) of the logs you both see and the key replacements you know. If a server signed one log for you and a different one for your friend, the two signatures prove it, and both apps say so. It also shows when a server lists a device for a friend that their own app doesn't know.
- **Someone using a friend's name** with a different key, on a server your friend isn't on, gets a gentle warning.
- You see what was found in My settings → Recovery key, above the chat when it's serious, and in the direct message with the person concerned. Anyone can read a server's whole log in the app (My settings → Recovery key → View log), checked from the first entry: the view an owner or auditor uses. Problems an app finds are also reported to the server's owner, in its security log, and so is a log that was changed in the database.

**What it catches:** a server that shows you a key its own log doesn't have; a server that shows two people different histories (a "split view"), as soon as two people who use that server talk to each other by direct message; a server that rewrites or rolls back its log; servers that disagree about where someone's account went.

**What it doesn't:** it detects, it doesn't prevent. A server that shows *everyone* the same fake person is consistent: names aren't identities, so if the first time you ever meet someone is on a server you don't trust, nothing but comparing safety numbers tells you it's really them. A split view stays hidden from someone who shares no friend with the people they're checking and never compares safety numbers. A server can refuse to answer (the app then shows it as unchecked, not as fine). The log tells members which keys joined when, under which names, which they could see in the member list anyway. Restoring a server from an older backup rolls its log back too, so members' apps will flag it: tell your members when you do.

**Compared to the big systems:**

| | Iskra | CONIKS | Keybase | WhatsApp key transparency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Directory | One small log per server, read in full by every member's app | A Merkle prefix tree per provider, one signed root per epoch | Per-user signature chains plus one global Merkle tree | An auditable key directory (append-only Merkle tree), one published root per epoch |
| Catching a split view | Signed heads gossiped between friends inside E2EE direct messages, plus comparing servers | Clients and auditors gossip signed roots | The root was anchored in a public blockchain | A third-party auditor checks that each root only extends the last one |
| Checking your own key | Your app sees the whole log and every replacement of your key | Clients check their own entry every epoch | You sign your own chain | Your app checks your own entry |
| Privacy of the directory | Members see the log (as they see the member list) | Hidden names (VRFs) | Public | Hidden (VRFs) |
| Who could still fool you | A server you only use with people you never send direct messages to, on first contact | A provider nobody gossips with | The service, until someone checks the anchored root | The provider and the auditor together |

Iskra's version is deliberately light: servers are small and many, so a full log costs little, and there's no company to run auditors. It adds most where several servers or friends overlap.

## Who can read what

| What | Protected by | Who can read it |
|---|---|---|
| Everything on the wire | HTTPS / WSS (when the server has HTTPS) | You and the server |
| Server channels, voice channels, files, profiles | The server's permissions | Members allowed in that channel, and whoever runs the server |
| Direct messages, with their pictures, files and voice messages | **End-to-end encryption** | Only the two of you |
| Group chats, with their files | **End-to-end encryption** | Only the people in the group |
| **Encrypted channels** (an option for small private text, voice, whiteboard and photos channels), with their files, threads, voice, boards and photos | **End-to-end encryption** | Only the people who can see the channel, on their own devices |
| Calls in direct messages and group calls (voice and video) | **End-to-end encryption** | Only the people in the call |

Server channels trust the server, because a server is run by you or your friend; the app always tells you which server you're on. Direct messages, group chats, calls and encrypted channels don't trust anyone: servers only pass encrypted envelopes and encrypted media along.

### Direct messages in detail

- Encrypted with XChaCha20-Poly1305; the key is wrapped for each of the recipient's devices and your own.
- **Forward secrecy.** Each device has a short-lived encryption key (a *prekey*), signed by the device, replaced every week and deleted 30 days after that. Each message's key is sealed to the recipient devices' current prekeys with a fresh one-time key (libsodium `crypto_box_seal`, around a `crypto_box` from the sender's device that proves who sent it). Once a prekey is deleted, messages sealed to it can't be decrypted again, even by someone who later steals your devices' long-term keys and every encrypted message a server ever stored. Your app keeps the messages it has already decrypted on the device, so your history stays readable.
- Why not a ratchet like Signal's: a conversation here travels over whichever server you share, across several devices each, which are often offline for days. Weekly prekeys give forward secrecy without per-device session state that can get out of step. There's no "healing" after a break-in, though: a stolen device can read new messages until you remove it.
- The sender, recipient, time and message id are bound into the encryption, so a message can't be altered, replayed or moved to another conversation.
- Device keys come with certificates signed by the account, so a server can't slip in a device of its own.
- There's no unencrypted fallback: if a message can't be encrypted, it isn't sent.
- **Read receipts** (off unless you turn them on, in DMs and group chats) are encrypted the same way as a message. They are mutual: only someone who sends them is shown other people's. The server keeps the newest one per conversation, so it can tell that you read a conversation and when, not which message. Whether you have them on is a setting only your devices can read.
- **Private names** you give people are a setting only your devices can read. Servers, and the people you renamed, never get them.

### Pictures, files and voice messages in DMs and group chats

- Each file is encrypted on your device with its own random key (libsodium `crypto_secretstream`, in 64 KB chunks, so a changed, reordered or cut-off file is caught). The key, the name and the type travel inside the encrypted message; the server only stores ciphertext.
- Files can be as big as the server allows for any upload (512 MB by default). Your app encrypts a big file a piece at a time while it uploads it, and decrypts it a piece at a time while it downloads, so it never holds the whole file in memory. In the desktop app and in Chrome or Edge, saving writes straight to disk; the file only appears under its name once every chunk, the end marker and the hash of the whole file have checked out, and a file that fails any check is deleted. Other browsers and phones decrypt into memory first, with the same checks before you can save it.
- The server hands a file only to the people in the conversation (for a group: its members when the file was shared), through short-lived signed links, and never shows it as a web page or image.
- Your app decides how to show a file from its **decrypted bytes**, with the same rules as channel uploads: only real pictures, video and audio play inline; anything else is a download.
- The server sees how many files you send, when, to whom and roughly how big they are; not what's in them, their names or whether one is a voice message.

### Group chats in detail

- Group messages are encrypted like direct messages, with forward secrecy, for every device of every member.
- **Who is in a group is a chain of signed changes**: every add, removal or leave is signed by the member who made it and linked to the change before it. Your app checks every link itself, so a server can't add anyone to a group, reorder its history or slip in a member list of its own. Someone who replaced their account key stays the same member.
- A message names the exact member list it was encrypted for, so it can't be passed off as sent to different people. New members only read what's sent after they joined.
- Group calls work like direct message calls: a fresh key per call sent inside the encrypted group chat, and a new one when the group changes during the call.
- The server knows who is in which group and when people write; it doesn't know the group's name or anything said in it. Notifications only say "New message from X".

### Encrypted channels in detail

When an admin creates a text or voice channel they can tick **End-to-end encrypted**. It's meant for small private channels (up to 50 people) and can't be turned off later. A lock marks it everywhere.

- **Who's in it follows the channel's permissions**, but the permissions don't decide alone. Membership is a chain of signed changes, like a group chat's: every add, removal or new key is signed by the member who made it and linked to the one before. When roles or channel settings change, the server says who should be added or removed, and the first member whose app is online signs that change. Your app checks every link itself, so **the server can't add anyone on its own**: it needs a member's signature (members' apps sign the adds the channel's permissions call for, see Limitations below), and while you're still in a channel's chain your app never accepts a different chain in its place (unless you choose to start over, see below). The server also refuses changes that don't match the permissions, and only ever delivers the channel's (encrypted) messages to people who can read it right now.
- **Every change brings a new key.** Each change starts a new *epoch* with a fresh random key, made on the device of the member who signed the change and sealed to every device of every member (the same forward-secret envelopes as direct messages). Someone who loses access never gets the next key: what's written after they're removed is unreadable to them even if they kept a copy of everything the server stores. Keys of different epochs are unrelated, so an old key says nothing about a new one.
- **Messages** are encrypted with the epoch's key (XChaCha20-Poly1305) and **signed by the sender's device**, because everyone in the channel shares the key: without the signature one member could write as another. The channel, the thread, the exact member list and the sender are bound into each message (and into each edit, the message it edits), so the server can't move a message into another channel or thread, or pass an edit off as a different message. Your app remembers which versions of a message it has shown, so a replayed message or an older version after an edit is refused on that device. A message that claims to come from someone more than 10 minutes after they lost access is shown with a warning and never notifies. Messages sent by apps from before this protection show as "Older format".
- **New members** read from when they were added. Older messages stay unreadable to them, as in Signal; there's no way (yet) for an admin to share older history.
- **Your devices:** a device linked later gets the key automatically (it asks for a new one if nobody included it), and when you remove a device, one of your other devices hands out a new key in each encrypted channel you're in.
- **Files, voice notes and threads** are encrypted the same way. **Voice** in an encrypted voice channel uses LiveKit's end-to-end encryption with a key derived from the channel's current key, and switches when it changes.
- **It stays encrypted on your device.** Once your app has seen a channel encrypted, it remembers that (with the channel's keys, so also after a restart) and doesn't take the server's word that it isn't any more: the lock stays, the channel shows "The server says this channel isn't encrypted any more", nothing can be sent in it (no messages in the clear, no voice without the key, nothing on its board), and a message that arrives there without encryption is never shown as a member's ("Not encrypted, so it can't be from a member"). Threads keep the channel they were in. This ends only when the channel is really gone from the device: deleted and replaced by another channel, or not seen for 30 days.
- **Safety:** the encryption panel (the lock in the channel's header) lists exactly who holds the key, with each person's safety number and any key-transparency warnings about them.
- **Starting over:** if everyone in a channel's chain loses access (they all lose the permission to see it, or leave), nobody is left to add the people who can see it, so the first of them whose app is online starts a new chain. Its messages are new; the old ones stay readable only on devices that already had their keys. Someone who was in the old chain and gets access back is the hard case: from inside the chain, a new one looks exactly like a server trying to hand the channel to an account it controls, so **their app never switches by itself**. It keeps the chain it checked, turns sending off, and says *"The people in this channel started its encryption over. Check their safety numbers before trusting new messages."* The encryption panel then shows who signed the new chain (who started it, who added you, who handed out keys; each change signs the whole chain before it) and how well you know each key: **same key as before** (they were in the old chain with you), **someone you know** (a friend or someone you've messaged), or **new to you**. Starting over is a button, never automatic. If none of the signers is a key you knew, or a new key carries the name of someone from your old chain, you must tick that you compared safety numbers first; a serious key-transparency warning about a signer, or a chain that doesn't list you yet, blocks it. Afterwards the old chain and its keys stay on your device for old messages, your app signs a new key in the new chain (so the others see you joined, and anyone starting over later sees a key they knew), the channel shows "You started encryption over on …", and a chain you left is never accepted again.
- **What doesn't work there**, because the server would have to read or write the text: webhooks (incoming and outgoing), bots reading or posting in the channel, built-in bots, polls, scheduled messages, forwarding, clips, stickers, GIFs, AutoMod and link previews. Commands for bots that take interactions still work, privately: the app warns first that the command goes to the bot unencrypted, and only you see the answer (see Limitations). Search runs on your device, over the messages it has decrypted. Notifications only say "New message in #channel". A report can include what the message says, but only if the reporter shares it, and moderators are told the server can't check it.

**What the server still sees** in an encrypted channel: who is in it and when that changes; who writes, when, how often and how big each message is; who replied to which message, reactions (which emoji on which message), pins, deletions and edits (that one happened, not what changed); thread structure (threads have no name); who joins its voice channel and when; the channel's name and settings. It can delay or withhold messages and membership changes, but not read, forge or reorder them.

### Calls in detail

- The caller's app makes a fresh random key for each call and sends it inside a normal end-to-end encrypted direct message (with forward secrecy), so the server never has it.
- Both apps hand that key to LiveKit's end-to-end encryption: every audio and video frame is encrypted with AES-GCM before it leaves your device. The voice server only forwards ciphertext.
- A browser that can't encrypt media can't join the call. There's no unencrypted fallback.
- The server decides who may join a call's room: only the two people in the call get a ticket for it, and anyone else who shows up is removed.

## What servers do to protect members

- Identity comes only from the signed handshake; every request and every broadcast is checked against your role *at that moment*.
- Private channels never leak, not even their existence. Search only looks in channels you can read right now.
- **Deleted means gone, everywhere.** Ids of channels, threads, categories, docs pages, events and forum tags are never handed out again, so nothing of a deleted channel (its messages, search entries, pins, settings, voice room, tokens or anything an app kept) can turn up in a later one. Deleting a channel removes everything in it on the server, including scheduled messages waiting for it and its place in webhooks and AutoMod settings, and apps drop what they kept for it (messages, threads, drafts, read state, decrypted messages) as soon as it's deleted or you lose access to it. An app can't tell those two apart, so for an **encrypted channel** it keeps only the channel's signed history and keys (never message text) for up to 30 days: if you get access back to the same channel, it carries on with the history it checked (the server still can't slip in a different one); if another channel turns up under that id, or 30 days pass, they're wiped.
- Uploads are checked by content, never by name. Only real images, video and audio display inline; everything else is a download, served with headers that stop it from running as part of the site.
- **Server icon and banner:** the server keeps only an allowlist of what's needed to draw them, so their metadata (EXIF with GPS positions, XMP, text, comments, embedded thumbnails, unknown chunks or segments) goes before anyone sees them, and it deletes the original upload once the change has gone through. The ICC colour profile is kept, so colours stay right (it describes the picture's colours, not where or when it was taken). Invite pages, which anyone with a link can open, only get the icon from `/icon`: nothing else about the server.
- **Photos channels:** every photo and video is cleaned before it is stored, by the app before it uploads and again by the server (so an app that didn't clean can't leave anything). Nothing is re-encoded: pixels, sound and quality are the uploader's. What stays in a picture: what is needed to draw it, its ICC colour profile, which way up it is, and the date and time taken with its time zone offset if the uploader keeps the date (a switch when adding; on by default). What goes: GPS position, camera and phone make, model and serial numbers, lens, software, owner and copyright fields, maker notes, XMP and IPTC, comments and embedded thumbnails. In a video (MP4, MOV), the location, make, model and software boxes, XMP, handler names and every track that isn't video, audio or a timecode (GPS and other timed metadata, subtitles) are overwritten with zeros in place; creation times stay only with the date. A GIF keeps its frames, their timing and its looping and loses comments and every other block. A HEIC or AVIF (what phones take by default) is changed in place: its Exif item is overwritten with the same minimal block (orientation, and the date if kept), its XMP item and any other non-picture item with zeros, and the coded picture is untouched, so the original keeps its full quality. Because Chromium (Windows, Linux, Android) can't draw HEIC, the uploader's app also stores a JPEG it made on the device for display (libheif, compiled to WebAssembly, where the system has no decoder; loaded only when a HEIC is picked); the original stays as the download. WebM files aren't taken. The server stores the date taken (if kept) and the picture's size next to the file, for sorting. In an **end-to-end encrypted photos channel** the app cleans, makes the thumbnail and encrypts each file with its own key; the server gets ciphertext and one sealed envelope per photo and album, can't check the cleaning, and can't build the zip (the app does). It still sees who added how many files when, how big each is, which album a photo is in, reactions, and that comments exist.
- Link previews are fetched by the server so your IP isn't sent to every site, and the fetcher refuses private and internal addresses (also through redirects), and never goes through a proxy set on the machine (the address check would see the proxy, not the site).
- Limits per address count an IPv6 address by its /64 (one home network), so switching addresses inside it doesn't buy fresh limits.
- Rate limits, size limits and strict input validation on everything. Uploads, calls and new threads are limited per account, and each account has a daily upload allowance.
- On Linux and macOS, the server's keys and other secrets are readable only by the user that runs it.
- Who's in a voice channel or call comes only from the voice service's signed reports, never from what a client claims.
- **Roles:** custom roles only add the permissions given to them; someone who manages roles can only change roles below their own highest one and can't hand out permissions they don't have. Channel overrides are checked on the server for every message, upload, voice join and broadcast. Only people with the right permission can mention a role that isn't open to mentions.
- **Stages:** who may speak is enforced by the voice service itself. Everyone joins a stage listen-only, and the server tells the voice service to allow (or stop) someone's microphone, camera and screen share when a moderator brings them up (or back down). If it can't, it fails closed.
- **Blocking someone** stops direct messages and calls between you on every server you share (the list goes with you, but never to anyone else), ends a call with them, and stops their messages, mentions and group call rings from notifying you. Their messages in shared channels and groups are still there, collapsed in your app.
- **Timeouts and slowmode** are enforced by the server: a timed-out member can't write, react, use voice or make posts and events until it ends. The server keeps a short list of what a timed-out member (or one who hasn't agreed to the rules yet) may still do, mostly reading and looking after their own account; everything else, including every new feature, is refused by default. Moderation actions are written to an audit log admins can read (moderators see each member's own slice of it as that member's history); message text, moderators' private notes and invite codes never are.
- **Backups** are encrypted with a passphrase you choose (Argon2id, then XChaCha20-Poly1305 in chunks, so a changed or cut-off file is caught). The passphrase is sealed to the server's key before it leaves your app, so it never crosses the network in the clear, even without HTTPS. The automatic daily backups in the server folder aren't encrypted: they sit next to the keys already, so keep that folder private.
- **Backup buddies:** daily backups sent to a friend's server are encrypted on your server first, with a recovery code only you get (the same format as downloaded backups). Your friend's server stores opaque blobs: it never gets the code and never opens what it holds. Pairing uses a single-use code that names your friend's server key, so a pasted code can only pair with that server; after that every request between the two servers is signed with the sender's server key (with a timestamp, a nonce and a hash of the body), and only your server or the holder of the recovery code can list or download the copies. Pairing also proves your server holds the restore key it registers, and no key can be registered twice. A friend's server keeps your newest copies within the space it gave you, at most 3 a day, always keeps one older copy besides the newest (the newest one at least 2 days old, or else the oldest), and keeps them for a grace period after either side stops (at least a day when your side stops). Your server only ever connects to the address in the code (a server, never a path on it), follows no redirects, uses plain http only on local networks, and never reaches its own machine unless it's a localhost-only test server. A code that points at a local network address contacts nothing until you've seen the address and said yes, and every way of not getting an answer reads the same, so a code can't be used to map your network. Your friend's server checks each request's signature before it reads the body. When you restore, the date sealed inside the copy is shown, with a warning if it's well before the newest copy your friend's server lists (it can't change a copy, but it could hand you an older one). This is the one place where an Iskra server talks to another one.
- **Discord imports** only read the uploaded export: files referenced inside it are matched by name inside the archive, never fetched from Discord or read from anywhere else on disk.

### Security log, retention and your data

- **Security log** (Server settings → Sign-ins & security, the owner only): failed sign-ins, rate-limit hits, new members and devices (and people waiting to be let in, let in or turned away, invites paused or resumed), account key changes, account deletions, removed devices, backups and restores, moves, retention changes and data downloads, with the account key and time. Never message text, invite codes, passphrases or keys. IP addresses only if the owner turns that on (off by default). Bursts of the same event are capped, so a flood can't fill the disk. Moderators' actions stay in the audit log.
- **Disappearing messages:** a timer per channel, direct message and group chat (5 minutes to 4 weeks). Each message's expiry is fixed when it's sent; in direct messages, group chats and encrypted channels it is also in the encrypted message's authenticated header (signed, in channels), so a server can't stretch it: apps delete at the sooner of the two. The server deletes expired messages with their files every few seconds (overwritten on disk, checkpointed out of the write-ahead log). **Backups never contain them**: they're taken out of every backup as it is made, so a backup can't keep a message past its time. Apps delete their own copies on time, even after being offline. People can still screenshot or copy them, and apps from before disappearing messages can't open the encrypted ones at all.
- **The server's own log** (`logs/` in its folder, for whoever runs it): what the server did and what went wrong, one line per event with a code. Never names (people's, channels', webhooks', files'), message text, keys, tokens, invite or p2p secrets, IP addresses or file paths; LiveKit's own lines are cut down to their level and fixed wording. People appear only as a short code that matches up inside that one server's log (`acct=`), connections as `conn=` (an id your app is told too, so a bug report and the log can be matched). Kept 180 days at most and 200 MB at most ([hosting.md](hosting.md#logs)).
- **Retention:** the owner chooses how long the server keeps messages (and encrypted direct message and group envelopes), files in messages and direct messages, the audit log (90 days by default) and the security log (365 days). 0 keeps forever; older data is deleted every hour.
- **Download my data** (Settings → Privacy & data): a zip of everything a server keeps about you, through a link that works for 10 minutes; the owner can make one for a member who asks. The content of your direct messages and group chats is only on your devices, so **Download data on this device** exports it from there (without your keys).
- **HTTP:** every response refuses MIME sniffing, referrers and framing by other sites; HTTPS uses TLS 1.2 or 1.3 and HSTS for domain names. The voice service's own API only listens on the server itself.

### Profile pages

A profile page is HTML someone else wrote, so it's locked in a strict sandbox. It only loads when you click *Open profile page*. The promise: **a page can't make your device contact anyone, so its author can't learn your IP address or anything else about you.** It can use HTML, CSS, JavaScript, canvas and animations, with pictures and sound from `data:` URLs. Everywhere:

- it runs on an empty, throwaway origin: no cookies, no storage, no access to the app, your keys or the server;
- it has no network: it can't fetch anything, load outside images, fonts, styles, audio or video, open pop-ups, submit forms or navigate anywhere;
- it gets no camera, microphone, autoplay or other device access.

How each app keeps that promise:

- **Desktop app: scripts run for everyone.** Pages (and the editor's preview) run in a separate, in-memory browser session used only for pages, inside a view the app checks before it opens. In that session no request reaches the network except the page itself, which the app fetches for it from its server; WebRTC can't use UDP, and everything else, including WebRTC over TCP, goes to a proxy on a closed local port with no direct fallback. The page view has no Node.js or preload, no permissions, no pop-ups, no downloads, and can't navigate.
- **Browsers and the phone apps: other people's pages show without scripts.** Browsers can't fully block WebRTC: a page script can create a child frame with its own script, and that frame's WebRTC can reach any address. With scripts off, plain HTML and CSS can't reach anything (we test 41 ways, from images and fonts to preconnect hints and speculation rules). The app says interactive pages run in the desktop app. Your own page and the editor's preview keep their scripts, since they're your own code.

We test this: the tests point a page at a fake attacker on the same machine with 70 different ways to reach it, check that a page without the wall *does* reach it, and require zero connections from a page in each app. Admins can turn pages off for their server or remove a member's page.

### The server's public page

Opening a server's address in a browser shows a small page made by the server itself. While the owner hasn't turned it on (the default), it says only that this is an Iskra server, with links to get Iskra: no name, picture, member count or invite. The owner can turn it on in Server settings → Overview → Public page and pick what it shows: a description, the rules, a rounded count of members and of members online, and a Join button for one invite they choose (for members only; while invites are paused the page says so instead). The page has no scripts, loads nothing from anywhere but the server, encodes everything people wrote as text, asks search engines not to list it unless the owner allows that, and is rate-limited per address. Changes go in the audit log and the security log.

### GIFs
