The GIF picker uses KLIPY. An admin adds a KLIPY key and chooses how members' apps reach it:

- **Through the server** (the default): the server searches and fetches the GIFs, so your device never contacts KLIPY and KLIPY only sees the server. It only fetches from KLIPY's image hosts, only addresses it signed itself, and never stores the files.
- **Straight from KLIPY** (only if the owner picks it): your app searches KLIPY itself, so **KLIPY sees your IP address and what you search for**, under a per-member pseudonym rather than your account key. GIFs in messages don't load until you click them (you can turn on auto-load for your device), and they're shown in a sandboxed frame that can only load images from KLIPY's own image hosts.

Ads stay off, and anything that isn't a GIF from KLIPY's own hosts is left out.

### Feeds

The Feeds bot (off until an admin turns it on) makes the server fetch the RSS/Atom feeds, YouTube channel feeds and,
with the owner's own Twitch app, Twitch's API that admins pick. It reaches only public addresses (checked after DNS on
every connection, redirects included), only ports 80, 443 and 1024 and up, gives every unreachable or refused address
the same answer, cuts each request off after 20 seconds including its body, reads at most 2 MB, reads XML without DTDs
or external entities, and never fetches images. Text from feeds can't mention anyone. **The Twitch app's client secret
is stored in the server's database (`iskra.db`) as it is, like the KLIPY key**, so it's in the world folder and in
its backups: it's never sent to any app, and the owner can remove it (Server settings → Bots → Feeds → Twitch app) and
make a new one at dev.twitch.tv if a copy of the world folder or a backup gets out. Use a Twitch app made just for this
server; it can only read public data.

### Watch parties

A watch party only shares a clock: each app plays the video itself, from its source. **Whoever hosts the video sees your IP address**: YouTube for a YouTube video, the website for a link, your server for an upload. Before anything loads from YouTube or a website, the app says where it plays from and waits for you to press Watch (unless you ticked "Always load from <site>" on that device). YouTube plays in its privacy-enhanced (youtube-nocookie.com) player inside a sandboxed frame; no YouTube code runs inside the app itself, where it could reach your keys. The desktop app sends YouTube the web app's address as the referring page (YouTube requires one) and nothing else.

### Activities

Activities (games and mini-apps in a voice call) run in a sealed frame on a throwaway origin, like profile pages: no
network, no cookies or storage, no access to the app, your account or your keys. They talk only to Iskra, through a
small message bridge the app checks (size, type, rate) before anything reaches the server. They see players as an id
that only means something inside that activity, and a display name; never account keys.

- **Built-in activities** (Draw & guess, Quiz, Four in a row) are Iskra's own code, bundled with the app, so they run
  everywhere.
- **Activities an admin adds** are a zip the server checks file by file (no paths out of the bundle, a fixed list of file
  types, sizes counted while unpacking) and serves with the profile-page policy. They run only in the **desktop app**,
  in the same walled session as profile pages, where nothing can reach the network. Browsers and the phone apps list
  them but don't run them (a page script can always reach the internet through WebRTC in a child frame there).
- Listeners can watch an activity but send nothing to it. Activity messages have their own limits (per person, and a
  bandwidth budget per activity), so a busy activity can't slow your connection or flood the others; they aren't
  checked by AutoMod.
- What an activity sends goes through your server to the people playing and is never stored; only the latest snapshot,
  for people who join late, is kept in the server's memory while the activity runs. Because the server can read it,
  activities are off in end-to-end encrypted voice channels.
### Whiteboards

A board is a list of changes ("set these fields of this object") that the server puts in order and passes on, so everyone ends up with the same board. On a normal board the server checks every field (known fields only, numbers in range, colours as `#rrggbb`, text length, no control characters) and only accepts pictures that are images uploaded to that server by the person drawing (or already on that board); everything, text included, is drawn on a canvas, never turned into HTML. Drawing follows the channel's permissions, timeouts and server rules, and only moderators (or whoever opened a call's board) can clear one.

In an **encrypted channel** the board is end-to-end encrypted too: every change, snapshot and live cursor is sealed with the channel's current key and signed by the sender's device, under its own signing context (`iskra/wb/v1`), bound to the channel, the board and what it is (a change, a snapshot of the board up to a given change, or a cursor). The server only checks who sent it and for which board, and can't read, forge or move it. Whether a board is encrypted comes from its channel as your app knows it, never from the server's word about the board: if the two disagree nothing is sent, and on an encrypted board anything that arrives unencrypted (changes, a snapshot, a cursor) is ignored. It can't tidy up an encrypted board, so members' apps upload sealed snapshots, including a fresh one under the new key after someone joins, so new members can read the board. Apps drop changes they've already applied and changes signed long before the snapshot they started from, so an old change can't simply be replayed. Pictures aren't offered on encrypted boards (the server could read them). A member who can draw can also upload a snapshot that wipes the board, much as they could erase everything by hand.

### Activity status

"Playing X" is off until you turn it on in the desktop app. Games are recognised on your own computer by matching running program names against a list; only the game's name is sent, never the list of programs. It's kept in memory while you're online and hidden while you appear offline or invisible.

### Themes

A theme is a JSON file of colours, sizes and font choices. Every value is checked against a strict pattern and applied one setting at a time, so a theme can't inject CSS or code.

### Push notifications

- Notifications go from your server through your browser's push service (Google, Apple, Mozilla or Microsoft), encrypted so that service can't read them.
- **Direct message notifications never contain the message**, just "New message from X". Mentions and replies carry a short excerpt from the channel.
- Each server has its own push key, and a subscription belongs to one device. Your server only accepts addresses at known push services and doesn't notify a device you're actively using.
- The phone apps don't use push at all: they show notifications while the app is open, straight from your servers. No Iskra-run service sits between your server and your phone.

### Voice, video and captions on your device

AI noise removal, voice detection, evening out voices, cleaning up others' audio, camera background blur and replace, and live captions all run **on your own device**: no sound, picture or caption text is sent anywhere for processing, and captions are never stored or sent to the server. The models ship with the app, except the captions model, which the app downloads once from the server of the call you're in (the server fetched it once from Hugging Face; only members get a link to it). Both the server and the app check every part against SHA-256 hashes built into Iskra before using it, and the workers that run the models can't fetch anything. Details, models and licenses: [voice-processing.md](voice-processing.md).

**Clips** are recorded on the device of the person who saves one, from what their app already plays. Turning clips on is shown to everyone in the call and saving one posts a notice, but that's a courtesy between honest apps: nothing can stop a modified app from recording what it receives, in any call.

**Recording a voice channel** needs the "Record voice" permission (admins and the owner by default) and the desktop app, which saves one file per person (plus an optional mix) to a folder on that computer; nothing is uploaded, and the server never receives the audio. The server enforces who may start and stop, and shows a red "Recording" mark to everyone who can see the channel; people joining a recorded call join muted and are told first. Anyone can say "Don't record me" (stored for their account on that server, so it holds on every device), people whose app doesn't show the mark (older apps, bots) are never recorded, start and stop also leave a line in the channel's chat, and in encrypted voice channels recording only starts once everyone in the call agrees (people joining later are left out until they say yes). Leaving people out is done by the recorder's app, so it's the same courtesy between honest apps as clips, not a cryptographic guarantee. Starting and stopping go in the audit log (never any audio or file names).

### Hosting help and rented servers

- **What Iskra found out** about your connection comes from your own router's answers and your computer; no outside service is asked. The prompt for an AI assistant holds your local network details and the ports, never your public address, keys or invite links, and you see and can edit it before copying.
- **Rent a small server:** the app makes a one-time owner key and puts it in the setup text. The new server keeps it in a file only it can read and never logs it. Before trusting the server, the app asks it to prove it holds the key (HMAC over a fresh nonce), so a different machine at that address can't pose as yours; then it joins as owner and the key is deleted. Until then the app keeps the key in its encrypted store. The setup text downloads the server from GitHub and checks it against the published `SHA256SUMS.txt` before installing, and opens only the ports Iskra needs. Your provider can see what's on a server you rent from them.
- **Keep my server running / `install-autostart`** runs the server as you, never with administrator rights.

### Server updates

A standalone server can check GitHub for new versions and, on Linux with systemd, install them itself (the owner picks: off, tell me, or install automatically). A package is only used if its SHA-256 matches both `SHA256SUMS.txt` and the checksum GitHub lists for the file, its build-provenance attestation verifies on the server (Sigstore, signed by Iskra's release workflow on GitHub's runners for that file; on by default, the owner can turn it off with a warning), the archive holds nothing but plain files, and the new version starts on that machine. If it doesn't start, the previous version is put back. Every check, install, failure and rollback goes into the security log. `/health` reports only the version, uptime and whether voice is up: no names, addresses or member counts.

### Webhooks and bots

- A webhook URL contains a long random secret. The server only stores a hash of it and shows the URL once; an admin can replace it at any time. Treat it like a password, and use the `https://` address (a server without HTTPS can only take it in plain text): a server with HTTPS refuses webhooks sent to its plain `http://` address from other machines (with "use https"), rather than quietly forwarding them.
- **Calendar links** ("Add to my calendar") work the same way: the link a member gives their calendar app ends in 32 random bytes, the server keeps only a SHA-256 hash of them and shows the link once, and the member can replace it or turn it off at any time (the owner can turn links off for everyone, which ends them all). Whoever has the link can read the titles, times, places and descriptions of the events that member can see, until it's replaced or turned off: nothing else, never members' names, and nothing from encrypted channels. Fetches are rate limited per link and, for wrong links, per address, and the link is refused over plain HTTP from another machine. A server without a public `https://` address offers no link at all. In the phone app, events can instead go straight into the phone's own calendar: the app only changes events it added itself (each carries a marker), and remembers which is which on that device only.
- Webhook posts can't ping anyone unless an admin allows it for that webhook, and images from the payload are dropped, so a webhook message can't make viewers' apps contact a third-party address.
- Bots are marked with a **BOT** badge, can only join with a single-use bot invite from an admin, can't make or take calls, upload direct message files or create invites, and can't be made admin.
- **Invites that never expire** can only be made by admins and owners (checked by the server), are marked in the Invite dialog's Active invites list, and can be revoked there at any time.
- **Direct messages with bots** are end-to-end encrypted to the bot like any direct message, so the server can't read them, but whoever runs the bot can: the app says so in every direct message with a bot. A bot can only write first to members of a server it's on who allow direct messages from bots (My settings → Privacy & data, on by default), never to someone who blocked it, and never to another bot; it's rate limited per bot account.
- **What a bot reads is the admin's choice.** By default a bot gets only its commands, button clicks and forms, messages that mention it or reply to it, and its own messages; requests that read the rest (history, search, pins, threads, forums, docs) are refused. An admin can let a bot read all messages, when inviting it or later, and everyone can see which bots can. Bots that joined before this choice existed keep reading everything until an admin changes it.
- **Commands, buttons and forms** go to the bot through the server, which checks every one against what the bot declared and who may use it. Each interaction has a random token that works only for that bot, for 15 minutes. Answers marked private go only to the person who asked and are never stored.
- **Built-in bots** (Dice, Polls, Reminders) run inside the server: no outside program, no network connection. Their keys are made fresh and the private half is thrown away, so nobody can sign in as them. They read nothing but their own commands and never answer in encrypted channels.
- **Outgoing webhooks** send chosen events (messages and reactions in chosen channels, people joining or leaving, events starting) to an `https://` address an admin picks, never anything from encrypted channels, direct messages or group chats. Each request is signed with a secret for that webhook (HMAC-SHA-256 over the time, a delivery id and the body), so the receiver can check it came from your server. The server checks the address after every DNS lookup and never connects to private, loopback, link-local or cloud-metadata addresses, and never follows redirects; only the owner can allow addresses on the server's own network. A webhook that keeps failing turns itself off. Every member can see which sites their server sends to (**My settings → Privacy & data → Who Iskra talks to**).

## Limitations

We'd rather tell you than have you find out:

- **Server channels, voice channels and files are not end-to-end encrypted,** unless the channel was made an encrypted channel. Whoever runs the server can read them.
- **Encrypted channels:** the people who can see the channel decide who gets the key, so whoever controls the permissions (admins, and whoever runs the server, through the permissions) can add a reader; that reader's app is added by a member's app, signed and visible in the encryption panel, and only reads what is written from then on. A member who is removed keeps what they already read. A device's stored epoch keys let it read the channel's history, so a stolen unlocked device reads it too (as with direct messages kept on the device). Membership changes need a member's app online; until then, someone who just lost access can't receive anything (the server stops delivering at once), and someone who just gained it waits. Two members' apps that never compare notes could, in a rare race, see different (correctly signed) membership histories. A chain that was started over is only as trustworthy as the keys that signed it: Iskra shows who they are and asks you to compare safety numbers when you didn't know any of them, but it can't tell a friend who really restarted the channel from a server account using their name if you skip that check. We don't require the new chain to be signed by someone from the old one: by the server's rule nobody in the old chain could read the channel when it was restarted, so a legitimate restart is usually started by someone new, and a forger would simply leave the old members out.
- **Metadata.** Servers see who messages and calls whom, when, and for how long. Your push service sees when you get a notification.
- **Replacing a stolen account key is a race.** Whoever holds your old key can replace it too. On each server the first valid replacement wins; a second claim within 30 days makes the account disputed until an admin decides, and after 30 days the old key is dead. A thief who acts first on a server where you don't (or that has no other admin) keeps the account there until an admin steps in. Your friends see "safety number changed" either way: verify before trusting.
- **Keys on your device are only as safe as the device while Iskra is running.** Encryption at rest protects copies of the stored data, not a device someone can use as you. In the browser, without an app lock, anyone who can open your browser profile can open Iskra. Malware running as you can read keys from memory. Lock your devices, and use an app lock on shared computers.
- **Forward secrecy has limits:** it covers messages once their prekey is deleted (at most about five weeks after sending). A device that hasn't published a prekey (an older app version) gets messages wrapped to its long-term key instead: still end-to-end encrypted, without forward secrecy, and a server could hold back prekeys to force that.
- **Safety numbers are opt-in.** Until you compare them, you trust that the server showed you the right person the first time. [Key transparency](#key-transparency) catches a server that shows different people different keys, but not a fake person everyone is shown.
- **Calls use one key for the whole call**; in a group call the key changes only when the group does, so someone who leaves the call but stays in the group could still decrypt it (they could rejoin anyway).
- **Group chats:** the server can't add people or read messages, but it can hold back a change for a while, and two devices that never compare notes could, in a rare race, be shown different (correctly signed) versions of a group's history. There's no group-wide safety number: compare each person's.
- **Watch parties, link embeds and GIFs** load from their sources (YouTube, a website, KLIPY), which then see your IP address: only after you click (watch parties and embeds), or for GIFs only if the owner picked "Straight from KLIPY" (the default goes through the server). The full list is in [privacy-connections.md](privacy-connections.md).
- **Bot commands in encrypted channels** go to the server and the bot unencrypted: the command and its options (whatever you type after `/name`) are not end-to-end encrypted, though the channel's messages and keys never reach the bot. The app says so before you send, and the bot's answer is shown only to you.
- **Tying encrypted messages to their place has limits.** A replayed message, or an older version after an edit, is caught only on devices that already saw the newer one. Messages written before this protection (shown as "Older format") can still be moved by a server between a channel and its threads. And a removed member working together with the server can still backdate a message into the time they were a member, because both clocks would then lie in step; neither can make it look sent after the removal, or move it to another channel or thread.
- **Backup buddies:** your server keeps the recovery code (it needs it to encrypt every night), so someone who takes over your server or a copy of its folder can read the copies at your friends' servers too, though they could read the server itself anyway. They can also send junk copies that push out the newer good ones (at most 3 a day), but one older protected copy stays, and they can't make your friend delete anything early. Your friend's server sees your server's key and name, the size of each copy, when it arrives, and your server's IP address.
- **Outgoing webhook secrets are kept on the server** (it needs them to sign), so they're in the database, its daily backups and downloaded backups (encrypted with your passphrase). Anyone with a copy of the server's folder can sign requests as that webhook: regenerate the secret if a copy leaks. Incoming webhooks keep only a hash of their secret.
- **Profile pages:** in browsers and the phone apps, other people's pages show without scripts (see [Profile pages](#profile-pages)); only the desktop app runs them. If you paste someone else's HTML into your own page, its scripts run in your browser's preview, where a script can reach the network through WebRTC. A page may show images uploaded to its own server, and that server can see when they're loaded. Browser and WebView engines we can't test (WebKit on iPhones) are covered by the same rules but not by our tests.

## The desktop app

The desktop app is the same web app in a locked-down shell: sandboxed, no Node.js in the page, links open in your browser, and the page can only ask the app for push-to-talk, the screen picker, call alerts, updates, opening the system's privacy settings, hosting and restoring backups, its own settings, the taskbar badge, the keychain that protects your keys, passkey prompts for the app lock (in a separate window that can only show Iskra's own prompt page), profile page views and server-added activities (in their own walled session, see [Profile pages](#profile-pages)), and the game you're playing (when you turned that on).

- `iskra://` links only ever open an invite: anything else in them is ignored.
- **Embeds can't open things on their own.** Players in chat (YouTube, Twitch and the like) are frames in the app's window, so the app checks who asks: links open in your browser only right after you clicked or typed in the window, a few at a time, and pop-out windows only ever come from the app's own page.
- The page can only start or stop a hosted server by the id of one of the app's own server folders, never by a path. An installed app always runs its own copy of the web app (`ISKRA_DEV_URL` only works in a development build, on this computer).
- **Electron's RunAsNode fuse stays on.** The app relies on starting itself as plain Node (`ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1`):
  the [assistant's MCP bridge](assistant.md#use-iskras-tools-from-claude-desktop-or-claude-code-mcp) (`Iskra --mcp`) and
  the bot gallery's "Run this bot on this PC" do. The flip side: anyone who can already run programs as you can run
  the Iskra binary as Node, as they could run any Node or script interpreter. It gives them nothing they don't have;
  the keys stay protected by the OS keychain. If the fuse is ever turned off, both features need another way to start.

- **Windows:** every executable we ship is code-signed (Open Source Developer Viktor Lundgren, issued by Certum) and timestamped, so you can check it came from us and wasn't changed. The installer only installs updates signed with that same certificate.
- **macOS and Linux:** the macOS app is signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple; the Linux packages aren't signed. Every release has `SHA256SUMS.txt` and build-provenance attestations (`gh attestation verify <file> -R quikmn/iskra-voice`). Download only from the GitHub releases page.
- Servers you create in the app run on your computer and only open ports to the internet when you switch on **Let friends anywhere join**.
- **Bots on this computer** (My settings) run as separate programs with your rights, not inside the app's page: gallery bots ship with the app (so they update with it and nothing is downloaded at run time) and run with the app's own Node.js; a bot from a folder runs that folder's code, so the app asks you to confirm you trust it first. Bots only connect out to their server (nothing listens on a port); the page can only name a gallery bot or have you pick a folder in the app's own dialog, and bot invite links are kept in memory only until the bot has joined. A bot from a folder only runs after you confirm it in a native dialog (also before it may start with the app), and you're asked again when its entry file or `package.json` changed since (other files it loads aren't checked). Bots get only the parts of the app's environment programs need (the path, temporary and home folders, language, proxies), never anything else from the shell that started the app. Secret settings (like a Twitch app secret) never go back to the page and are encrypted with the OS keychain where there is one (on Linux without a keyring they're stored as-is, in a file only you can read); the bots' folder and files are readable only by you. Bots end when the app quits, and any left over after a crash are found by their recorded process and command line and ended before the app starts bots again.
- **Known trade-off:** running bots with the app's own Node.js needs Electron's `RunAsNode` fuse left on (`ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE`), so the app's executable can be used as a plain Node.js by anything already running as you. That gives nothing a local program doesn't already have; turning the fuse off would mean shipping or downloading a separate Node.js.

## Found a problem?

How this maps to SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001, the GDPR and OWASP ASVS, with the policies and evidence: [docs/compliance](compliance/README.md).

For a security problem, please [report it privately](https://github.com/quikmn/iskra-voice/security/advisories/new) or email spark@iskra.foo, not in a public issue. [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md) explains what's in scope and what to expect. For anything else, open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/quikmn/iskra-voice/issues).

Source: https://iskra.foo/docs/privacy-connections

# Who Iskra talks to

Iskra's rule: **your devices talk to your own servers, not to us or to third parties.** This page lists every
connection the apps (desktop, web, phone) and the server make to anyone other than the group's own Iskra server:
when it happens, what the other side learns, and how to turn it off. The apps show a short version in
**My settings → Privacy & data → Who Iskra talks to**; the privacy policy has the same list
([iskra.foo/privacy#third](https://iskra.foo/privacy#third)).

If you find a connection that isn't on this page, it's a bug: please report it (see [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md)).

## The apps

| Connection | Who contacts whom | When | What they learn | Default | How to turn it off |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Your servers** | Your device → each server you joined (HTTPS/WebSocket, voice through its LiveKit) | While you use it | Your IP address, everything you do on that server | On (it's the app) | Leave the server |
| **Link previews** | The **server** → the linked website | When a message with a link is shown | The server's IP; text only, no images are fetched | On | (server-side; your device never contacts the site) |
| **YouTube, Twitch, X, Reddit embeds** | Your device → `www.youtube-nocookie.com`, `player.twitch.tv`/`clips.twitch.tv`, `platform.twitter.com`, `embed.reddit.com` | Only after you press Play/Load on the placeholder ("Loads from YouTube…"), or for a site you ticked "Always load from <site>" on this device (then without autoplay) | Your IP address and what you play | Off: click-to-load | Don't click; forget the site in Privacy & data |
| **Watch parties from YouTube or a web link** | Your device → YouTube (privacy-enhanced player, and `i.ytimg.com` for the video's picture in the call) or the video link's site | After you press "Watch from <site>" (the host's own start counts; the start dialog says "Plays from <site>") | Your IP address | Off: asks first | Don't press Watch; you stay in the call |
| **Watch parties from an uploaded file** | Your device → your server | When you're in the party | — | — | — |
| **GIFs (KLIPY)** | The **server** → `api.klipy.com` and KLIPY's media hosts (proxied) | When someone searches or a GIF is shown, only if an admin added a KLIPY key | KLIPY sees the server's IP and searches under one pseudonymous id per server | Through the server | Admin removes the key |
| **GIFs, "Straight from KLIPY"** | Your device → `api.klipy.com`, `static*.klipy.com` | Only if the owner explicitly picked it (labelled "KLIPY sees members' addresses"); GIFs in chat still wait for a click unless you turn on auto-load | Your IP, your searches, a per-member pseudonymous id | Off | Owner switches back to "Through this server" |
| **Desktop update checks** | Desktop app → `github.com` / `api.github.com` (electron-updater, or the releases API for builds that can't update themselves) | 15 s after start, then every hour, and when the window gets focus again if the last check is 15+ minutes old; downloads from GitHub's release storage | Your IP and the app version | On (updates fix security problems) | My settings → Privacy & data → "Check for updates automatically" (the tray's "Check for updates" still works) |
| **Web Push** | Your server → your browser's push service (Google FCM, Mozilla, Microsoft WNS, Apple) → your device | Only if you turned notifications on for that device | That a notification was sent, and when (content is encrypted to your device) | Off until you turn it on | My settings → Notifications |
| **Alert words, follows and quiet hours** | none: your device → your own servers only | Your alert words, follows (people and roles you follow in a channel) and quiet hours stay on your devices and sync between them sealed (servers can't read them); the app matches words and follows itself, in encrypted channels and direct messages too. Only if you tick "Also when Iskra is closed" do your servers get a readable copy of the words and follows (words matched only in channels that aren't encrypted; a follow needs no text), and only servers your browser gets push from get your quiet hours schedule (days, times, time zone) | Your servers, as above; no third party | Words and follows: on your devices only. Schedule: only where push is on | My settings → Notifications (untick, or turn quiet hours off: the copies are deleted) |
| **Emoji and stickers from your other servers** | none: your device → the emoji's home server (a normal file download), then → the server you're posting on (a normal upload) | When you pick an emoji or sticker from another server in the picker | The server you post on gets the picture, its name and that you brought it (it keeps the same picture once, up to 300 emoji and 100 stickers); the home server sees only you downloading a file. Servers never contact each other | On for members (admins can turn it off per built-in role) | Pick emoji of the server you're on; admins: Server settings → Roles |
| **Search everywhere** | none: your device → each server you're on | When you switch the search panel to "Everywhere" (or Ctrl+K → "Search everywhere") | Each of your servers sees the search words and filters, as it does when you search it alone; nothing is stored. Your direct messages and groups are searched on the device | — | Search "This server" instead |
| **Streamer mode, "Turn on by itself"** | none: the desktop app looks at the programs running on your own computer for the ones you listed | While the switch is on | Nothing leaves the computer: the page only hears yes or no, and the mode's on/off syncs between your devices sealed like other settings | Off | My settings → Streamer mode |
| **The web app's files** | Browser → `app.iskra.foo` (Cloudflare Pages) | When you open the web app | Your IP (Cloudflare's short-lived logs); never your chats | Web app only | Use the desktop or phone app (they carry their own copy) |
| **DigitalOcean (Rent a server on DigitalOcean)** | Desktop app → `api.digitalocean.com` (HTTPS) with your OAuth key or token; your browser → `cloud.digitalocean.com` to sign in, then back to a one-time listener on `127.0.0.1` | Only while you rent a server there from the desktop app: listing sizes and regions, creating the droplet and its firewall, checking it, deleting them if setup fails | Your IP address and what the app creates in your account (DigitalOcean is your provider then). The app then asks `https://<ip>.sslip.io/health` on your new server, and the new server downloads Iskra from GitHub. The button that opens DigitalOcean uses Iskra's referral link (`m.do.co/c/...`): Iskra gets a small DigitalOcean credit; we never see your server or card | Off: only when you start it | Don't start it (the referral link only opens when you press the button); the key is forgotten after setup |
| **Bug reports** | Your device → `https://chat.iskra.foo/bug-reports` (Iskra's own server) | Only when you press Send in "Report a bug" (Help, the status menu, Ctrl+Shift+B) | What you wrote, your screenshots (stored without their metadata, like server icons), the email you gave (optional) and, unless you untick "Include logs", logs: app version and commit, OS and browser names, device kind, allowlisted settings (switches and choices, no ids or names), connection states per server (numbered, never named), failed request types and codes, voice state and stats, error names and bundle lines, update states. Never message text, file names, member or server names, keys, invite links, links or IP addresses (an allowlist, then a net for addresses, emails, links and key-shaped strings). The server sees your IP address for its rate limit and never stores it. Reports land in a private channel only the Iskra team reads and are deleted after a year at the latest | Off: only when you send one ("See what's included" shows exactly what goes) | Don't send one; "Save as a file" keeps it on your device |
| **HyperDHT (Connect without port forwarding)** | Desktop app (a server's owner, or a member joining such a server) → nodes of the public HyperDHT network: first the three bootstrap nodes Holepunch runs, then any node; then straight to the other computer (an encrypted tunnel) | Only if the owner turned on "Connect without port forwarding" (desktop-hosted servers), and for members only when the server's normal address can't be reached | Your IP address and the key you announce or look up, never what it is or what you say | Off until the owner turns it on | Owner: Server settings → Internet access; member: leave the server |
| **Captions model** | Your device → your server (`/models/...`) | Once, when you turn captions on | — | Off until you turn captions on | — |
| **Translation models** | Your device → your server (`/models/translate/...`) | Once per language and direction, when you translate from a language this device doesn't have and say yes to the download. The messages themselves are translated on the device and never sent | — | Off until an owner offers it and you agree to the download | — |
| **Voice ICE/STUN** | none from your device: the apps pass an empty ICE server list, so no STUN or TURN server is asked (a server's own LiveKit may ask Google STUN, see "A server") | — | — | No third party | — |
| **Spellcheck** | Windows/macOS: the system's own spellchecker (no network). Linux: off, because Chromium would download Hunspell dictionaries from Google | — | — | No third party | — |
| **Chromium background services** | Electron has no Safe Browsing, component updater, field trials or Google sign-in. The app also turns off Cast discovery (`MediaRouter`, `DialMediaRouteProvider`), the autofill server and `<a ping>` | — | — | Off | — |
| **Passkeys for the app lock** | Desktop: a local window on `https://app.iskra.foo` served from memory (no request leaves the computer); the OS handles the passkey. Choosing "use a phone" uses the OS's own hybrid transport | When you set up or use the app lock | — (OS-level for phone passkeys) | Off until you set it up | — |
| **Profile pages** | none: in the desktop app a page's scripts run in a walled-off session that can't reach the network (it shows only pictures uploaded to its own server); browsers and the phone apps show other people's pages without scripts | — | Nothing: a page can't load anything from elsewhere (images only from its own server) | — | — |
| **Your AI provider (the assistant)** | Your device → the AI provider you chose in My settings → Assistant (for example `api.anthropic.com`, `api.openai.com`, or a model on this computer at `localhost`); the desktop app sends it from its main process, the web and phone apps straight from the page. Never through Iskra or your servers | Only when you press Send in the assistant (and when a local MCP client you set up calls a tool) | The AI provider you choose sees what you send, only when you send: your question, the conversation so far, and what the assistant's tools read for it (names, channel lists, recent messages of a channel you can read). Never encrypted chats (unless you paste them), keys or invite links. Your key goes only to that provider | Off | My settings → Assistant (turn it off, remove the key) |
| **Local MCP clients (desktop app)** | An AI app on your computer (Claude Desktop, Claude Code) → `Iskra --mcp` → the running Iskra over a private local pipe or socket (no network port) | Only while "Allow local MCP clients" is on and that app calls a tool; every change waits for your OK in the Iskra window | That AI app sees the tool results it asks for (and sends them to its own provider) | Off | My settings → Assistant |
| **Calendar link ("Add to my calendar")** | Your calendar service (Google, Microsoft, Apple, or any app you give the link to) → your server, over HTTPS | Only after you press "Make my link" in Events → Add to my calendar and add the link to a calendar; the service then fetches it on its own schedule (Google up to once a day, Outlook every few hours, Apple about hourly) | Whoever has the link, so the calendar service you gave it to: the titles, times, places and descriptions of that server's events you can see, and the server's name and address. Never members' names, who is interested, or events in encrypted channels. The server sees the service's IP address | Off until you make a link (the owner can turn links off for the whole server) | Events → Add to my calendar → Turn off (or "Make a new link"): the old link stops working at once. Remove the calendar in your calendar app too |
| **Events in your phone's calendar** | none from Iskra: the phone app writes events into a calendar on the phone that you pick; the phone's own account sync (Google, Outlook/Exchange, iCloud) then copies that calendar to your account, as it does for every event on the phone | Only after you turn on "Put this server's events in my phone's calendar" for a server and allow calendar access; the app updates them while it's open | Your calendar account gets the titles, times, places and descriptions of that server's events you can see (never ones in encrypted channels). The app reads the list of calendars on the phone to let you pick one; it never reads your other events and only changes events it added | Off | Events → Add to my calendar → turn the switch off: the events Iskra added are removed. You can also take the calendar permission away in the phone's settings |
| **Links you click** | Your browser | When you click | What any website learns | — | — |
| **QR scanner** | none: the decoder (ZXing WebAssembly) ships with the app, never a CDN | — | — | — | — |
| **Fonts, icons, scripts, analytics, crash reports** | none: everything ships with the app; no analytics, ads or crash reporting | — | — | — | — |

The phone apps (Capacitor) run the same web app from the app bundle; Capacitor adds no telemetry, and the Android app
includes no Google Play services or Firebase. The phone's operating system has its own connections (app store,
OS updates), which Iskra doesn't control.

## A server

| Connection | Who contacts whom | When | What they learn | Default | How to turn it off |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Your router (UPnP / NAT-PMP)** | Server → the router on your own network | "Let friends anywhere join" | — (local network) | Off until the owner turns it on | Server settings → Internet access |
| **Let's Encrypt** | Server → `acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org`; Let's Encrypt → server (HTTP check) | Getting and renewing the HTTPS certificate | The server's domain name (public in Certificate Transparency logs) and IP | With "Let friends anywhere join" or `Https.Mode: acme` | Use your own certificate or none |
| **sslip.io** | Members' DNS resolvers → sslip.io's name servers | Resolving `1-2-3-4.sslip.io`, when there's no own domain | The lookups for that name (usually from members' ISPs' resolvers) | Only without a domain | Set your own domain |
| **Google STUN (via LiveKit)** | Server's LiveKit → a public STUN server (Google's by default) | Starting voice when open to the internet and the router didn't report the public IP | The server's IP only | Only in that case | Give the server a known address (router with UPnP/NAT-PMP) |
| **Hugging Face** | Server → `huggingface.co` (pinned commit, SHA-256-checked) | Once, the first time a member turns captions on | The server's IP | On demand | `server.json`: `"Captions": { "ModelDownload": false }`, or `ModelSource` for a local copy |
| **Mozilla (translation models)** | Server → `storage.googleapis.com` (Mozilla's Firefox Translations models, pinned paths, SHA-256-checked); members' devices then download them from the server | Once per model, the first time a member needs it | The server's IP | Off | Server settings → Translation |
| **HyperDHT** | Server's p2p sidecar → public HyperDHT nodes (see above) | While "Connect without port forwarding" is on | The server's IP and its public key | Off | Server settings → Internet access |
| **GitHub (rented servers)** | A server you rent from the desktop app → GitHub release storage | During setup (and later server updates) | The new server's IP | Only when you rent one | Don't rent |
| **GitHub (server updates)** | Server → `api.github.com`, GitHub release storage | 2 min after start, then every 6 h; standalone servers only (desktop-hosted servers update with the app) | The server's IP and version | Notify | Server settings → Server updates → Off |
| **Link previews** | Server → linked sites | See above | The server's IP | On | No switch yet (text only, no images) |
| **KLIPY** | Server → KLIPY | See above | The server's IP | Only with a key | Remove the key |
| **Push services** | Server → each subscribed device's push service | Notifications | Encrypted payload, timing | Only for subscribed devices | — |
| **Outgoing webhooks** | Server → the address an admin picked (HTTPS; plain HTTP only on the owner's own network) | When a chosen event happens: a new message or reaction in chosen channels, a member joining or leaving, an event starting | What the event contains (message text and author's name, member names); never encrypted channels, direct messages or group chats | None until an admin adds one; every member sees the hosts in My settings → Privacy & data → Who Iskra talks to | Server settings → Bots & webhooks → Outgoing (turn off or delete) |
| **Feeds bot** | Server → the feed addresses admins add (RSS/Atom sites), `www.youtube.com` (a channel's public feed, and its page once to look up a handle) and, only with the owner's own Twitch app, `id.twitch.tv` and `api.twitch.tv` | Only while an admin has turned the Feeds bot on: each feed every 5 minutes or more (Twitch every 2 or more) | The server's IP and that it follows that feed; never anything about members. Text only: images and thumbnails are never fetched (apps show link previews by their own rules). Only public addresses | Off | Server settings → Bots & webhooks → Bots → Feeds (remove feeds, or turn the bot off) |
| **Calendar links** | Members' calendar services → server (`GET /calendar/<token>.ics`, HTTPS) | When a member made a link and subscribed a calendar to it | That member's view of the server's events (titles, times, places, descriptions); nothing about members | Allowed; each member's link is off until they make one | Server settings → Overview → Calendar links (ends every link) |
| **Backup buddies** | Server → a friend's Iskra server the owner paired with (and back, only to answer it) | After each daily backup or *Back up now*, while backup buddies are on | That this server exists, its IP and server key, when backups happen and their size; never their contents (encrypted on this server first) | Off | Server settings → Backup & move → Backup buddies |

## The websites

- **iskra.foo**: on Cloudflare Pages; self-hosted fonts; nothing loads from other sites; no cookies. It counts page views as daily totals (page, referring site, country, device type, browser, operating system, download clicks) and stores nothing that identifies a visitor: see the [privacy policy](https://iskra.foo/privacy#sites).
- **app.iskra.foo**: the web app's files, on Cloudflare Pages. After it loads, it talks only to the servers you join.

## How this is checked

- `client/src/state/bugReport/diagnostics.test.ts`: bug report logs and payloads never contain seeded message text,
  names, keys, invite links, tokens, IP addresses or emails; `client/e2e/bug-report.spec.ts`: the preview of a real
  report shows nothing from the chat, the people or the server, and the report reaches the bug inbox channel.
- `client/src/state/siteConsent.test.ts`, `client/src/ui/chat/embeds.test.ts`: click-to-load and the per-site,
  per-device "Always load" list.
- `client/e2e/privacy.spec.ts`: a YouTube link makes no request to YouTube until clicked (the test watches every
  request), "Always load" survives a reload and can be forgotten, a YouTube watch party asks first, voice uses no
  STUN servers, and the "Who Iskra talks to" list renders. `client/e2e/gifs.spec.ts`: GIF search goes through the
  server by default and members' apps never contact KLIPY.
- `desktop`: `npm run test:network` starts Electron the way the app does, types into a spellchecked text box, and
  reads Chromium's own network log: nothing may ask for any host on the internet (runs in CI on Windows, macOS and
  Linux).

Source: https://iskra.foo/docs/voice-processing

# Voice processing

How Iskra cleans up your microphone and what you hear, blurs or replaces your camera's background, captions what
people say, and translates messages. **Everything runs on your own device**: the models and engines ship inside the app (and the web app, from
its own address), audio and video are processed in your browser or desktop app, and no sound, picture, transcript or
model input is sent anywhere for processing. Nothing about it is logged or stored, apart from your settings on this
device, the flags that remember when this device was too slow for AI noise removal or a background effect, and the
speech and translation models kept on the device so they're only downloaded once.

## Your microphone

| Setting (Settings → Voice & audio → Noise suppression) | What runs |
|---|---|
| **AI** | DeepFilterNet3, a neural network, as WebAssembly in a Web Worker fed by an AudioWorklet at 48 kHz |
| **Strong** (default) | RNNoise, as WebAssembly in an AudioWorklet at 48 kHz |
| **Standard** | The browser's own noise suppression |
| **Off** | Nothing |

- **Fallbacks.** AI needs AudioWorklet and WebAssembly with SIMD. If those are missing, the engine can't start, or it runs
  slower than real time for three seconds in a row (realtime factor above 0.6), or its worker is late for more than a
  quarter of each second three seconds in a row (a late frame now and then only costs a short crossfade), Iskra
  switches to RNNoise by itself and remembers it on that device. The developer console says why. Choosing AI again gives it another try. RNNoise falls back to the browser's suppression
  the same way. Settings always says which engine is active, why, and (in a call) how much CPU it takes.
- **AI noise removal strength** (Settings → Voice & audio, with AI on): **Gentle**, **Normal** (default) or **Max**:
  the most DeepFilterNet may turn anything down (18 dB, 30 dB, no limit). With a limit, what it takes out is mixed
  back in at that level, so noise stays far down and a wrong guess about the voice can only cost that much. Iskra
  runs DeepFilterNet with the local SNR thresholds its own command line tool uses (-15, 35, 35 dB: both stages on
  every frame); libDF's WebAssembly defaults (-10, 30, 20) skipped stages frame by frame and turned clean speech down
  by about 9 dB, choppily (see "How transparent it is" below). Changes apply right away, in a call too.
- **Automatic gain.** The browser's automatic gain control is off by default when Strong or AI runs (it pumps the
  level under the noise removal), and on with Standard or Off. My settings → Voice & audio lets you choose either way.
- **Voice activity.** With "Set automatically" on, Silero VAD (a small neural network, run in plain TypeScript in the
  same AudioWorklet) decides when you're speaking: the mic opens when it hears speech and stays open through pauses
  for 500 ms (hangover). It keeps the last 100 ms and sends them when it opens (pre-roll), so the start of a word
  isn't cut off. That makes you 100 ms late for as long as you keep talking; the gate never skips or squeezes audio
  to catch up (that sounds choppy and hurried). Silero notices a word 25–40 ms after its voiced part starts, so that
  always gets through; it notices the faintest lead-in (a breath or soft consonant 20–30 dB down) up to 145 ms
  after it starts, so that is now and then softened, by 15–30 ms typically and 45 ms at most on the test phrases
  (a longer pre-roll of 200 ms would keep all of it, at twice the delay). After a pause of
  more than the hangover it closes, and the next time starts over. In noise Silero is sure of a soft first sound later, so the gate already opens at a
  probability of 0.2 and closes again if Silero doesn't reach 0.5 within 200 ms (no added delay; noise alone hardly
  ever opens it). Turn "Set automatically" off for a manual volume
  threshold instead. Push-to-talk is never gated or delayed. Your own speaking ring follows the same detector.
- **Off the audio thread.** The audio worklet only moves samples: it cuts the mic into 10 ms frames for a worker that
  runs DeepFilterNet, and plays what comes back at a fixed delay, the way DeepFilterNet's own LADSPA plugin uses a
  processing thread. Frames travel in eight slots allocated once and reused (nothing is allocated per frame on the
  audio thread): buffers transferred back and forth over a MessagePort, or shared memory with Atomics when the page
  is cross-origin isolated (none of the apps are today: the web app, the desktop app's `app://` and the phone apps
  all use the port; the choice is made at run time). If a frame isn't back in time, the worklet crossfades (2.7 ms)
  to the mic as it is, lined up to the same delay, and back once frames arrive again: never silence, never a skip
  or a repeat. A frame that couldn't be sent at all also takes the next three with it (the network's look-ahead
  still held audio from before the gap).
- **Latency added.** DeepFilterNet: 24 ms of framing and queue (one frame, plus one device buffer of headroom for the
  worker: the delay follows the device's buffer size, 24 ms for the usual 10 ms) plus the model's own look-ahead
  (30 ms), 54 ms in all; running inside the audio worklet it was 10.7 + 30 ms, with no room for a slow frame. RNNoise:
  about 10 ms. Voice activity: 100 ms while you talk ("Set automatically" only; none with a manual threshold or
  push-to-talk).
- **Hi-fi.** In voice channels where an admin allowed it, turning on "Hi-fi audio" sends your mic in stereo at
  128 kbps with no noise suppression, echo cancellation or automatic gain. Use headphones.
- **Resilience.** The mic is published with Opus in-band FEC, RED (redundant audio: each packet also carries the
  previous ones, so a lost packet costs nothing) and DTX (next to nothing is sent while you're quiet). LiveKit's
  default codecs include `audio/red`, so every room negotiates it.

## What you hear

Where the app mixes call audio with Web Audio (Chrome, Edge, the desktop app; not Safari or Firefox), each incoming voice
goes through:

1. **Clean up others' audio** (off by default): DeepFilterNet3 when you use AI noise removal and up to four people
   are talking, RNNoise otherwise or when the device can't keep up. DeepFilterNet runs in a Web Worker, so starting it
   for someone who just joined never stalls the rest of the call; it uses the same queue as the mic (24 ms on top of the
   model's look-ahead, crossfading to the voice as it is when the worker falls behind).
   It runs at the Normal strength.
   Clips record the cleaned voices while this is on. Call recordings (desktop app) keep each person's voice as it
   arrives, without this clean-up, so they can be edited later; your own track is your mic after its processing.
2. **Even out voices** (on by default): a slow gain that brings each person towards the same loudness (only while they
   talk, at most ±12 dB, at most 3 dB per second, gliding sample by sample), then a gentle compressor (2:1 above
   -16 dBFS RMS, 10 ms attack, 200 ms release: only syllables well above the target) and a look-ahead limiter at
   -1 dBFS (it sees peaks 1.5 ms ahead and ramps down over that time, so it never clips or steps). Adds 1.5 ms.
3. Your per-person volume, on top.

## Your camera's background

My settings → Camera: **Off** (default), **Blur**, or **Replace** with a built-in picture (Aurora, Sunset: soft gradients
drawn by the app, nothing to download) or a solid colour. The preview there runs exactly what calls run.

- **What runs.** MediaPipe's Selfie Segmenter (a 256×256 person-segmentation network, run by MediaPipe Tasks in
  WebAssembly on the CPU) finds you in each frame, in a Web Worker. The mask is smoothed over time (quick to follow
  real movement, slow to flicker) and feathered at the edges, then WebGL2 in the same worker draws you over a blurred
  copy of the frame (you are left out of the blur, so you don't bleed into it), the picture or the colour.
- **Off the main thread.** In Chrome, Edge and the desktop app the camera's frames stream into the worker and back
  out (insertable streams), so the page never touches them and a hidden tab keeps going. Other browsers send frames
  to the worker as images.
- **Nothing of the room first.** In a call the effect is in place before the camera is published, and until the first
  mask is ready the whole frame counts as background.
- **Fallback.** Needs WebAssembly and WebGL2 in workers. If the effect can't start, or the device can't keep up
  (fewer than 10 frames a second, or more than 60 ms a frame, for three 2-second windows in a row), it turns itself
  off with a notice in the call ("your real background is showing") and remembers that on this device until you
  choose an effect again. In a call, Settings shows the frame rate and time per frame; the app logs them to the
  developer console every 10 seconds.
- **Library telemetry.** Newer MediaPipe Tasks releases (1.x) send usage statistics to Google; Iskra uses 0.10.35,
  which has none, and the workers that run on-device models can only fetch from the app's own address anyway.

## Live captions

Opt in per listener: the captions button in the call, or My settings → Voice & audio → Captions ("Show captions in
calls"). Off by default. Each speaker's last words show under their name above the call controls (read out by screen
readers as a polite live region); the × or the button turns them off again.

- **What runs.** Each incoming voice (and yours, with "Caption my own voice too") is tapped in an AudioContext of its
  own (the cleaned-up voice when "Clean up others' audio" is on), resampled to 16 kHz in an AudioWorklet and sent to
  a captions Web Worker. There Silero VAD (the same model as for your mic) cuts it into phrases (200 ms pre-roll,
  ends after 500 ms of quiet, at most 8 s, at least 300 ms of speech), so only speech is ever transcribed. Whisper
  base (OpenAI's model, 8-bit ONNX export) transcribes one phrase at a time with ONNX Runtime Web (WebAssembly, one
  thread): greedy decoding, no timestamps, Whisper's own "no speech" and confidence checks, and a stop for runaway
  repeats. The feature extraction and decoding loop are Iskra's own TypeScript (`client/src/state/captions/`).
- **Languages.** English and Swedish. "Automatic" lets Whisper pick between the two for each phrase; or fix one.
  Whisper base is good in English and usable but rough in Swedish.
- **Why Whisper base.** It's MIT licensed (code and weights), speaks Swedish, and is the smallest Whisper that's
  worth reading (tiny is about twice as fast but much worse, in Swedish especially). Moonshine is faster on short
  phrases but English-only under a permissive license. Whisper always looks at 30 s of audio, so each phrase costs
  about the same no matter how short; WebGPU and multi-threading (which needs cross-origin isolation the app can't
  have) would make it much faster and are left for later.
- **Keeping up.** One phrase at a time; at most 4 waiting and 3 people at once; a phrase that waited more than 8 s is
  skipped. Skipping 3 within 20 s, or one phrase taking more than 7 s, pauses captions for 20 s with "Captions paused:
  this device is too slow right now" and then tries again.
- **Privacy.** The text exists only in this page's memory: it's shown, kept for 8 seconds after the last words, and
  dropped. It is never sent to the server or to anyone, never stored, never logged, and not part of clips.
- **Where the model comes from: your own server.** Whisper base (78 MB: encoder, decoder and vocabulary) is not part
  of the app and not in git. The first time captions turn on in a call, the app says "Captions need a one-time 78 MB
  download from this server" and waits for **Download**; progress shows with a **Cancel** button. The parts come from
  the Iskra server the call runs on (`GET /models/whisper-base-1846881b/<part>`, on the web, in the desktop app and
  in the phone apps alike), with a short-lived link the app gets from the server first, so only members can
  download it ([PROTOCOL.md](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md#live-captions-model)). That server fetched the model once from Hugging Face, at the pinned commit, the first
  time anyone asked, and keeps it in its world folder (`models/`). So members' devices only ever talk to their own
  server; Hugging Face only sees the server's address, once. An owner can turn this off (`Captions.ModelDownload`
  in server.json, [hosting.md](hosting.md#live-captions)); the app then says "This server doesn't offer captions".
- **Hash check, twice.** The server checks every file and part against the SHA-256s pinned in
  `client/src/state/captions/model.json` (compiled into both the server and the app) before keeping anything, and the
  app checks every part again before it's used or kept, and when it's read back. A part that doesn't match is
  refused ("wasn't the right file"); a failed download says so with **Try again**. Either way the call goes on
  untouched.
- **Kept on the device** in Cache Storage (`iskra-models`), or IndexedDB where Cache Storage can't keep it (the
  desktop app's `app://`), under a key that doesn't depend on the server: one download per device, whichever server
  it came from. Files from an older version are removed.
- **Privacy.** Getting the model is an ordinary file request to your own server. No audio, text or anything about
  the call goes with it, and the workers that run the models can't fetch anything at all.

## Message translation

**Translate** in a message's menu (channels, threads, direct messages and group chats; press and hold on a phone) shows the message
in your language under the original: "Translated from Swedish · Show original". The translation button in a
conversation's header turns on **Auto-translate messages not in my language** there, and picks the language to
translate into (your app language unless you choose another; also in My settings → Language).

- **On your device, after decryption.** It runs in a Web Worker on the text your app already shows, so it works for
  end-to-end encrypted channels, direct messages and group chats too. No message text is sent anywhere: not to your server, not to any
  translation service. Translations live only in the page's memory and are gone when the app closes.
- **Which language.** [ELD](https://github.com/nitotm/efficient-language-detector-js) (n-grams, its smallest database,
  under 1 MB, bundled) tells the language on the device. Links, mentions, emoji, code and numbers don't count; a few
  letters ("lol", "ok") aren't enough, and auto-translate only acts when it's sure. On a close call between similar
  languages (Swedish, Danish, Norwegian) your own language wins, so your own messages stay untouched.
- **The engine.** [Bergamot](https://github.com/browsermt/bergamot-translator), the WebAssembly translation engine
  of Firefox Translations (5 MB, bundled; `client/vendor/bergamot`, made by `scripts/vendor-bergamot.mjs` from the npm
  release, checked by its SHA-512), runs Mozilla's [Firefox Translations models](https://mozilla.github.io/translations/firefox-models/)
  on the CPU: a chat message takes 10-150 ms. Plain text in and out, never HTML.
- **Languages.** English to and from Swedish, Danish, Norwegian (Bokmål), Finnish, German, French, Spanish, Italian,
  Dutch, Portuguese, Polish and Ukrainian (`client/src/state/translate/models.json`, written by
  `scripts/translate-pins.mjs` from Mozilla's model registry: released models only). Between two other languages it
  goes through English (Swedish → English → German) in one step.
- **Why Bergamot.** Its models are small because they're made for CPUs in browsers: 14-26 MB per direction as
  downloaded (17-32 MB unpacked), against about 110 MB for an Opus-MT model run with Transformers.js and ONNX Runtime,
  and they're faster. Mozilla keeps training and releasing them for Firefox. Code and models are MPL-2.0, so any
  server owner may pass them on.
- **Where the models come from: your own server.** They aren't part of the app and not in git. An owner offers them in
  Server settings → Translation (off by default; it shows what each language weighs). The first time you translate
  from a language this device doesn't have, the message says what it needs ("Translating from Swedish needs a one-time
  15 MB download from your server", with a word about mobile data on a phone) and waits for **Download**. The parts
  come from one of your servers that offers them (`GET /models/translate/<dir>/<part>`, with a short-lived
  members-only link; [PROTOCOL.md](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md#translation-models)). That server fetched that one model
  from Mozilla's storage the first time a member needed it, and keeps it in `models/translate/`: only languages
  members use are ever fetched, and Mozilla only sees the server's address. If none of your servers offers
  translation, **Translate** says so.
- **Hash checks.** The server checks every file and part against the SHA-256s pinned in `models.json` (compiled into
  both), the app checks every part again, unpacks it (gzip) and checks the unpacked file too. Anything that doesn't
  match is refused and never used or kept.
- **Kept on the device** in Cache Storage (`iskra-translate-models`), or IndexedDB where it can't (the desktop app),
  under a key that doesn't depend on the server: one download per language and direction per device. Models of an
  older version are removed.

## Voice message transcripts

**Show transcript** (the lines button on a voice message's player, in channels, encrypted channels, direct messages and group
chats) shows what was said under the player. My settings → Voice & audio → Speech → **Transcribe voice messages
automatically** (off by default) does it for every voice message you see.

- **The captions model, on your device.** It's the same Whisper base model and worker as [live captions](#live-captions),
  downloaded the same way (once, from your own server, after **Download**, SHA-256 checked, kept on the device). The
  app decodes the recording itself (the browser's own decoder, to 16 kHz mono), Silero VAD finds the speech, and the
  phrases are packed into as few 30-second Whisper windows as they fit. English and Swedish, as set for captions.
- **Never uploaded.** Neither the recording (which the app already has) nor the text leaves the device. Transcripts of
  channel voice messages are kept in IndexedDB (`iskra-transcripts`, at most 2000, the oldest dropped first) so they
  don't have to be made again; transcripts of end-to-end encrypted voice messages are kept in memory only and are gone
  when the app closes. Signing out deletes them.
- **Too slow.** If a transcript takes more than four times the recording's length (at least a minute), it stops with
  "This device took too long" and automatic transcripts stop on that device (asking still works; turning the setting
  off and on tries again). Browsers that can't run captions can't transcribe either and say so.

## Read aloud

**Read aloud** in a message's menu reads it with the device's own speech voices (`speechSynthesis`: Windows, macOS and
iOS voices; speech-dispatcher on Linux). A channel's menu has **Read new messages aloud** (for gaming: a speaker button
in the header shows it's on and turns it off). Messages sent with `/tts <text>` are read aloud for people who turned on
My settings → Voice & audio → Speech → **Play /tts messages** (off by default); sending them needs the `sendTts`
permission (admins have it; others get it from a role).

- **What's read.** The author's name and the message as plain words: mentions by name, custom emoji by name, links as
  their host names ("link to github.com"), code blocks named, not read ("code block, 3 lines"), spoilers never read,
  runs of the same emoji and stretched words shortened, at most 300 characters. Your own messages are never read.
- **When.** Only in the channel you have open, never while it's muted or set to "Nothing", in quiet hours, with do not
  disturb or in streamer mode. Switching channels stops it. At most five messages wait; older ones are dropped.
- **Nothing leaves the device.** The text goes to the operating system's speech engine only. Voice, speed and volume
  are settings on the device.
- **Screen readers.** A screen reader already reads new messages. A web page can't tell that one is running, so with
  one, leave "Read new messages aloud" off to avoid hearing everything twice.
- **Where it works.** The web app and desktop app (Windows, macOS; Linux with speech-dispatcher) and iOS. Android's
  web view has no speech synthesis, so the options aren't shown there.

## How transparent it is

`node scripts/audio-quality.mjs` in `client/` runs the e2e speech fixture (a real recording: a quiet room, noise
floor around -42 dBFS) through the same code the worklets run, block by block, and compares what comes out with what
went in (delay removed): clean, with fan and keyboard noise added (pink noise at -42 dBFS, clicks peaking at
-16 dBFS), and 20 dB quieter. `src/state/audio/quality.test.ts` holds the thresholds, plus a golden-file check
against DeepFilterNet's own command line tool (`deep-filter` 0.5.6: same output to within 16-bit rounding on clean
speech, within 0.5 dB of its quality on noisy speech) and three minutes through the simulated worklet (every sample
in order). Speech level is the median gain on speech, and its 5th percentile (the syllables turned down most);
gain motion is how much that gain changes from one 10 ms to the next.

| Input → stage | Before: SI-SDR / spectral distance dB | Before: speech level / dips dB | Before: gain motion RMS / max dB | After: SI-SDR / spectral distance dB | After: speech level / dips dB | After: gain motion RMS / max dB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Clean → AI noise removal | 3.2 / 5.8 | -9.5 / -4.0 | 2.47 / 9.9 | 20.6 / 5.0 | -0.5 / -1.3 | 0.31 / 2.1 |
| Noisy → AI noise removal | 6.1 / 9.6 | -0.8 / -11.2 | 2.53 / 9.7 | 19.7 / 9.0 | -0.6 / -1.2 | 0.39 / 2.5 |
| Clean → voice gate | -1.2 / 6.7 | 0.0 / -16.8 | 2.31 / 14.7 | > 99 / 0.2 | 0.0 / 0.0 | 0 / 0 |
| Clean → leveling | 10.4 / 2.3 | 1.4 / -4.3 | 0.59 / 4.1 | 12.7 / 1.7 | 4.2 / -3.7 | 0.23 / 1.5 |
| Clean → whole chain | -6.3 / 10.7 | -4.1 / -13.1 | 3.13 / 15.1 | 11.2 / 5.6 | 1.9 / -3.8 | 0.35 / 2.1 |
| Noisy → whole chain | -5.1 / 14.1 | -0.9 / -19.2 | 14.0 / > 99 | 11.5 / 9.3 | 1.7 / -4.1 | 0.41 / 2.4 |
| Quiet → whole chain | -5.9 / 13.2 | -5.7 / < -99 | 7.6 / > 99 | 7.9 / 8.3 | 4.0 / -7.0 | 0.51 / 3.0 |

- **Audio dropped while talking** (spread of the delay along the run): before 112 ms (clean) and 128 ms (noisy)
  through the gate; now 0. The gate's delay: before 250 ms, catching up by dropping audio; now 100 ms, steady.
- **Start of a word** (the fixture cut into 17 phrases, clean and noisy): the voiced start always gets through. The
  faint lead-in is softened by (median / p95) 27 / 45 ms clean and 15 / 45 ms noisy with the 100 ms pre-roll;
  measured alternatives: 60 ms 67 / 85, 80 ms 47 / 65, 120 ms 7 / 25, 200 ms none. No clipped samples anywhere, before or after; input volume 200% is limited instead of
  clipped. The gate opens once on the fixture and doesn't chatter, before and after.
- **Noise removed** (fan and keyboard, in the pauses, AI noise removal alone): 25 dB at Normal (30 dB limit), 17 dB
  at Gentle (18 dB), 32 dB at Max; before, everything (frames muted completely, speech too).
- The whole chain's SI-SDR is lower than its parts' because leveling changes the level slowly over the run (it
  should); the spectral distance and gain motion show what it does to the sound.
- What changed: DeepFilterNet's thresholds (the big one: clean speech was turned down by 9.5 dB, choppily, and some
  syllables muted), its strength limit, the gate (no more skipping), the leveler (RMS compressor, look-ahead limiter,
  gains that glide), and the gate's fade (it used to buzz faintly at half the sample rate while open).
- Not measured offline: Opus itself (48 kbps mono for voice, with FEC, RED and DTX) and the browser's own echo
  cancellation and automatic gain.

## CPU

Realtime factor = time spent / length of audio (0.05 = 5% of one CPU core). `node scripts/bench-audio.mjs` in
`client/` measures them on any machine. On a desktop PC (2026, x64, Node 24):

| | Realtime factor |
|---|---|
| DeepFilterNet3 (your mic, or one incoming voice) | ~0.07 (Chromium in the e2e tests: 0.05–0.12) |
| Silero VAD | ~0.025 |
| Leveling, per incoming voice | ~0.004 |
| Voice activity gate | < 0.001 |

What the audio thread pays (same script: time per 128-sample render call, which has 2.67 ms; the speech fixture
with noise):

| | Mean | p99 | Max |
|---|---|---|---|
| DeepFilterNet inside the render call (before) | 250 µs | 1.0–1.5 ms | 3.7–7.0 ms |
| DeepFilterNet in a worker, the worklet only queues (now) | 4 µs | 10 µs | 0.5–1.3 ms (first calls) |
| The worker, per 10 ms frame | 0.95–1.2 ms | 1.3–4.2 ms | 1.7–45 ms (the odd pause: garbage collection, the OS) |

In Chromium (the e2e tests) the worker takes 1.2–1.6 ms per frame on average and 2.0–2.6 ms at the slowest, with
no late frames, for your mic and incoming voices at once.

DeepFilterNet's start-up takes about half a second (model loading); the first use downloads about 12 MB (16 MB
WebAssembly and an 8 MB model, compressed). Phones are several times slower, which is what the automatic fallback is
for. The app logs the realtime factor to the developer console every 10 seconds while AI noise removal runs.

Live captions (`node scripts/bench-captions.mjs [file.wav]`, same machine): Whisper base takes about 2.0 s of encoder
plus 30–50 ms per word, so **2.3–2.9 s per phrase** whatever its length (Chromium: 2.4–2.7 s encoder); for the 8 s
test phrase that's a realtime factor of 0.35, for a 1–3 s phrase 1 or more. In other words: captions arrive 2–3 s
after someone finishes a phrase, and one desktop core keeps up with roughly one person talking continuously; with
more, phrases get skipped. Loading the model takes about 0.6 s (Node) to 1.5 s (Chromium, from the cache).

Background effects (Chromium in the e2e tests, 640×480 fake camera at 20 fps, software WebGL): 8–15 ms per frame
alone (segmentation about 10 ms, drawing 2–3 ms: roughly a third of a core at 30 fps), 25 ms per frame and 16 fps
while a whole call, AI noise removal and captions run on the same machine. A real GPU makes the drawing faster;
phones are slower, which is what the fallback is for.

| [ELD](https://github.com/nitotm/efficient-language-detector-js) (Efficient Language Detector, extra-small database) | npm `eld` 2.1.0 | bundled (in the translate worker) | Apache-2.0 |

DeepFilterNet's code was changed to build against tract 0.23 (`client/vendor/deepfilternet/tract-0.23.patch`; API
updates only, the model is unchanged) and to let the app set its local SNR thresholds (`wasm-thresholds.patch`).
`scripts/build-deepfilter.sh` rebuilds `deepfilter.wasm` bit for bit from the pinned sources,
`client/vendor/deepfilternet/Cargo.lock` and Rust 1.99.0 (on any machine: local paths are mapped out of the binary);
the "DeepFilterNet build check" workflow does that whenever any of it changes and fails if the bytes differ. The
golden files in `client/vendor/deepfilternet/golden/` are the official `deep-filter` 0.5.6 tool's output for
`node scripts/deepfilter-golden.mjs` (see that script). Silero VAD's network is reimplemented in
`client/src/state/audio/silero.ts` and reads the official model file; its output matches ONNX Runtime to within 1e-6.

`node scripts/get-models.mjs` (from the repo root) fetches Whisper at the pinned commit, checks its SHA-256 and
writes the parts into `client/.models/` (ignored by git). The e2e test servers serve the model from there
(`Captions.ModelSource`) instead of fetching it from Hugging Face, and CI caches it. Without it, the Whisper unit test
and the captions e2e test are skipped. `--blur` also re-checks the committed Selfie Segmenter. The
background pictures are drawn in code; there are no image assets.

### Voice bots (SDK)

The [bot SDK](bots.md#voice-bots) plays audio into voice channels with these packages. They're installed by
`npm install` in `bots/` (exact versions in `bots/package-lock.json`), loaded only when a bot uses voice, and never
part of the app or the server.

| Component | Version | Used for | License |
|---|---|---|---|
| [@livekit/rtc-node](https://github.com/livekit/node-sdks) with [@livekit/rtc-ffi-bindings](https://github.com/livekit/rust-sdks) (native, prebuilt for Windows x64, macOS x64/arm64, Linux x64/arm64; includes libwebrtc) | 1.1.0 / 0.12.73 | connecting to the server's LiveKit and publishing the audio track; resampling (`AudioResampler`) | Apache-2.0 (libwebrtc: BSD-3-Clause) |
| [mpg123-decoder](https://github.com/eshaz/wasm-audio-decoders) (mpg123 in WebAssembly) | 1.0.3 | MP3 | MIT; contains [mpg123](https://www.mpg123.de/), LGPL-2.1 |
| [ogg-opus-decoder](https://github.com/eshaz/wasm-audio-decoders) (libopus in WebAssembly) | 1.7.5 | Ogg Opus | MIT; contains libopus, BSD-3-Clause |
| [@wasm-audio-decoders/ogg-vorbis](https://github.com/eshaz/wasm-audio-decoders) (libvorbis in WebAssembly) | 0.1.20 | Ogg Vorbis | MIT; contains libvorbis and libogg, BSD-3-Clause |
| [@wasm-audio-decoders/flac](https://github.com/eshaz/wasm-audio-decoders) (libFLAC in WebAssembly) | 0.2.11 | FLAC | MIT; contains libFLAC, BSD-3-Clause |
| [codec-parser](https://github.com/eshaz/codec-parser) (used by the Ogg and FLAC decoders) | 2.5.0 | finding frames in Ogg and FLAC streams | LGPL-3.0-or-later |

WAV is read by the SDK itself (`bots/sdk/src/voice/audio.ts`). The LGPL parts are used unmodified, as the separate
npm packages they ship in.

### Rich text (code and math)

Code blocks and LaTeX math in messages, threads, forums and docs pages. Both are bundled with the app (no CDN), loaded
only when a message needs them, and their output is turned into React elements through an allowlist
(`client/src/ui/chat/safeTrees.ts`), never inserted as HTML.

| Component | Version | Used for | License |
|---|---|---|---|
| [lowlight](https://github.com/wooorm/lowlight) | 3.3.0 | syntax highlighting as a token tree | MIT |
| [highlight.js](https://github.com/highlightjs/highlight.js) (grammars, through lowlight) | 11.11.2 | the common languages, and guessing one for untagged blocks | BSD-3-Clause |
| [Temml](https://github.com/ronkok/Temml) (with its small `Temml.woff2` font and `Temml-Local.css`) | 0.13.5 | LaTeX to MathML | MIT |

### Fonts

The app's fonts (My settings → Appearance → Font) ship with it as variable woff2 files, Latin and Latin Extended
only, so nothing is fetched from a font service and they work offline in the browser, desktop and phone apps. The
licence texts are in the app at `/licenses/` (`client/public/licenses/`).

| Font | Version | Used for | License |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Inter](https://github.com/rsms/inter) | 4.001 (the same files as iskra.foo) | the default text font | SIL Open Font License 1.1 (`Inter-OFL.txt`) |
| [JetBrains Mono](https://github.com/JetBrains/JetBrainsMono) | 2.211 (the same files as iskra.foo) | code, and the Monospace font | SIL Open Font License 1.1 (`JetBrainsMono-OFL.txt`) |
| [Nunito](https://github.com/googlefonts/nunito) via [Fontsource](https://fontsource.org/fonts/nunito) | npm `@fontsource-variable/nunito` 5.3.0 | the Rounded font | SIL Open Font License 1.1 (`Nunito-OFL.txt`) |

System and Serif use the device's own fonts.

# Activities

Activities are small apps people use together in a voice channel: a game, a quiz, a shared toy. Someone in the call
opens **Together** in the call controls, presses **Start an activity**, picks one, and everyone else in the call sees "Alex started Four in a row —
Join". The activity opens in the call's big spot for everyone who joins.

Iskra comes with three: **Draw & guess**, **Quiz** and **Four in a row**. A server's admins can add their own in
**Server settings → Activities**. This page is about making one.

The wire protocol (what the server checks and relays) is in [PROTOCOL.md → Activities](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md#activities).

## How an activity runs

- **It's a web page in a sealed frame.** It has no network at all: no `fetch`, XHR, WebSocket, WebRTC, images or fonts
  from elsewhere, forms, pop-ups or navigation. It can use its own files, `data:` and `blob:` URLs, canvas, audio
  from its own files, and state in memory (it gets an opaque origin: no cookies, `localStorage` or IndexedDB).
- **It talks only to Iskra**, through the SDK below. Iskra sends what it says to everyone playing, through your server,
  in the same order for everyone (yourself included). Nothing it sends is stored, apart from one snapshot for people
  who join late, kept in the server's memory until the activity ends.
