- **Listeners watch.** People who may only listen in a voice channel can join an activity there and see everything, but
  what they send is refused.
- **No filters.** Activity messages aren't chat: AutoMod and word filters don't check them. Show other players' text
  with care (and never as HTML).
- **It never sees accounts.** Players are an id that is only valid inside this activity session, and a display name.
- **Where it runs:** activities added to a server run in the **Iskra desktop app**, which runs them in a wall where
  nothing can reach the network. Browsers can't be made that tight (a page script can always reach the internet
  through WebRTC in a child frame), so browsers and the phone apps list your activity but don't run it, and say it
  runs in the desktop app. The built-in activities run everywhere: they're part of Iskra.
- **Not in encrypted voice channels:** the server relays what activities send, so they're off there.

## Making one

A zip (up to 5 MB, 200 files, 10 MB unpacked) with at least these two files at the top (or inside one folder):

```
my-activity.zip
├── manifest.json
├── index.html
├── game.js
└── icon.png
```

`manifest.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "Snake duel",
  "description": "Two snakes, one screen.",
  "icon": "icon.png",
  "minPlayers": 2,
  "maxPlayers": 4,
  "version": "1.0",
  "sdk": 1
}
```

Only `name` (1–40 characters) is required. `description` is up to 200 characters, `version` up to 20, players 1–25.

Rules for the files:

- File names use `A–Z a–z 0–9 _ . -`, don't start with a dot, and sit at most 8 folders deep.
- Allowed types: `html htm js mjs css json txt svg png jpg jpeg gif webp ico avif woff woff2 ttf otf mp3 ogg oga wav m4a
  opus`. Text files must be UTF-8.
- **One page:** `index.html` is the activity. It can't navigate to another page.
- **Classic scripts:** use `<script src="game.js">` or inline `<script>`, not `type="module"` (module scripts need
  CORS, which a sealed frame's origin doesn't get). Bundle with any tool into one IIFE file.
- Only `.html` pages run scripts. Any other file (an SVG opened on its own, say) is served with scripts off.
- Iskra's server puts two scripts in front of your page: one that removes WebRTC, and the SDK, which defines
  `window.iskra`. You don't need to include anything.

Upload the zip in **Server settings → Activities → Add an activity**. The server checks every file; anything outside
the rules refuses the whole zip, with the reason.

## The SDK (version 1)

```js
const init = await iskra.ready()
// init.me       { id, name }              you, in this activity
// init.players  [{ id, name }, …]         everyone in it, longest-in first
// init.state    the snapshot, or null     what the activity looked like when you joined
// init.locale   'en', 'sv', …             the player's language
// init.theme    { scheme: 'dark' | 'light', colors: { bg, surface, surface2, border, text, muted, accent, green, red, amber } }

iskra.on('message', (data, from, seq) => { … })   // every message, yours too, in the same order for everyone
iskra.on('players', (players) => { … })           // someone joined or left
iskra.on('end', () => { … })                      // the activity is ending

iskra.send(data)       // any JSON, up to 8 KB, to everyone playing
iskra.setState(state)  // a snapshot (any JSON, up to 48 KB) for people who join later
iskra.end()            // ends it for everyone (if you may), else closes it for you

iskra.me               // { id, name }
iskra.players          // [{ id, name }]
iskra.host             // the id of whoever has been in longest
```

Call `iskra.ready()` first and register your `message` listener right after it resolves: messages that arrive before
anyone listens are held and handed over in order.

### Keeping everyone in step

The easy way to build a multiplayer activity on this SDK:

1. Keep all shared state in one object.
2. Write `apply(state, data, from)`: a pure function that returns the next state for a message (or the same state when
   the message isn't valid: out of turn, malformed, from someone who may not do that). Check everything: other
   players' apps send whatever they like.
3. To do anything, `iskra.send()` a message, and change the state only in your `message` listener. Every player
   applies the same messages in the same order, so everyone ends up in the same state, with no host needed.
4. Let `iskra.host` call `iskra.setState(state)` after changes (Iskra sends at most one snapshot every 1.5 s, the
   latest wins). Someone who joins gets that snapshot as `init.state`, then every message after it.

Things only one player's app should know (a word to draw, a quiz's answers) stay in that app until it reveals them in
a message. Never trust data as HTML: put text in with `textContent`.

### Limits

| | |
|---|---|
| A message | 8 KB of JSON; 10 a second (20 in a burst) per player; the whole session relays up to 256 KB a second, counted once per player it reaches |
| A snapshot | 48 KB of JSON; at most one every 1.5 s |
| Players | 25 at once, or your manifest's `maxPlayers` if fewer |
| Messages kept for late joiners | those since the last snapshot, up to 300 and 256 KB |

### The messages underneath

If you'd rather not use the helper: the SDK posts `{ iskra: 1, type: 'ready' | 'send' | 'state' | 'end', … }` to
`window.parent` (in the desktop app's wall, where there is no parent, it writes them as console lines starting with
`\u2063iskra-activity:`), and receives `{ iskra: 1, type: 'init' | 'players' | 'message' | 'ended', … }` as `message`
events. See `protocol/activity-sdk.js`; the app checks every message (`client/src/state/activityHost.ts`).

## A complete example

`index.html`:

```html
<!doctype html>
<html>
<body>
  <button id="go">Press me</button>
  <ol id="log"></ol>
  <script src="game.js"></script>
</body>
</html>
```

`game.js`:

```js
;(async () => {
  const init = await iskra.ready()
  let state = init.state ?? { presses: [] }
  const names = new Map(init.players.map((p) => [p.id, p.name]))
  iskra.on('players', (players) => players.forEach((p) => names.set(p.id, p.name)))

  const render = () => {
    const log = document.getElementById('log')
    log.replaceChildren(...state.presses.map((id) => Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { textContent: names.get(id) ?? 'Someone' })))
  }

  iskra.on('message', (data, from) => {
    if (data?.t !== 'press' || state.presses.length >= 50) return
    state = { presses: [...state.presses, from] }
    render()
    if (iskra.host === iskra.me.id) iskra.setState(state)
  })

  document.getElementById('go').onclick = () => iskra.send({ t: 'press' })
  render()
})()
```

Zip `index.html`, `game.js` and a `manifest.json` with a name, and add it to your server.

## The built-in ones

`client/src/activities/` holds the three built-ins, written against the same SDK: each is a reducer (`logic.ts`, unit
tested) and a small DOM view (`main.ts`). `client/activities.vite.ts` builds each into one self-contained HTML file.

---

Source: https://iskra.foo/docs/assistant

# The assistant (bring your own AI)

Iskra doesn't come with AI, and it never sees what you ask one. If you want help from an AI model, you bring your own:
a key from an AI provider, or a model running on your own computer. The app then talks to that provider straight from
your device, only when you press **Send**.

The assistant can:

- answer "how do I…" questions about Iskra, from Iskra's own docs (hosting, bots, this page, the wire protocol);
- help you write a bot, and set one up on your server;
- summarize or search channels you can read, when you ask;
- organize your server: create, rename and move channels and categories;
- make a colour theme from a description;
- if you turn them on: moderate (time out, warn, kick, ban, delete messages) and change server settings (roles, rules,
  deleting channels).

Every change shows you exactly what it will do and waits for your OK.

## Turning it on

1. Open **My settings → Assistant** and turn on the assistant. It's off until you do.
2. Pick a provider. **Anthropic (Claude)** is the default; the others are OpenAI, Mistral, Groq, OpenRouter, Google
   Gemini, any other OpenAI-compatible service, or a model on your own computer with **Ollama** or **LM Studio**.
3. Paste your API key and press **Save key**. Local models usually need no key.
4. Press **Test connection**. It lists the models your key can use (this costs nothing), so you can pick one under
   **Model**. For Anthropic the default model is `claude-opus-5-5`.
5. Open the assistant with the sparkle button in the server list (a sheet on phones).

The privacy line at the top of the panel always says where your messages go, for example "What you send goes to
api.anthropic.com. Iskra never sees it."

## Privacy

- **Nothing is sent until you press Send.** Then your message, the conversation so far and what the assistant's tools
  read for that question go to the provider you chose, under that provider's own terms. Iskra and your servers never
  see it.
- **Your key stays on your device**, encrypted with the device's other secrets (the same protection as your account
  keys), never in plain browser storage. It goes only to the address it was saved for: if you change the address to
  another site, the saved key is removed and you save it again.
- **Encrypted chats are never read for you.** The tools can't open direct messages, groups or end-to-end encrypted
  channels. If you want help with text from one, paste it yourself.
- **Reads are small.** Tools return names, ids and short message texts (at most 50 recent messages of one channel),
  never keys, recovery codes, tokens, invite links or passwords.
- The conversation is kept only in memory: it's gone when you press **New conversation** or close the app. The
  **Activity** tab lists what the assistant did (which tool, on which server, the outcome), on this device only.

## Providers

| Provider | Address (filled in for you) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Anthropic | `https://api.anthropic.com` | The web and phone apps send Anthropic's `anthropic-dangerous-direct-browser-access` header, which Anthropic requires for requests from a web page. The key is your own and stays on your device. |
| OpenAI | `https://api.openai.com/v1` | |
| Mistral | `https://api.mistral.ai/v1` | |
| Groq | `https://api.groq.com/openai/v1` | |
| OpenRouter | `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1` | |
| Google Gemini | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai` | Gemini's OpenAI-compatible API |
| Ollama | `http://localhost:11434/v1` | On this computer, no key |
| LM Studio | `http://localhost:1234/v1` | On this computer, no key |

Any other OpenAI-compatible service works too. Addresses must use `https`; plain `http` only works for `localhost`
(a model on the same computer). The model has to support tool calls for the assistant to act; without them it can still
answer questions.

**The desktop app** sends provider requests from its main process, so browser rules (CORS) don't get in the way. The
page tells the app the address you saved, and the app sends requests only to that address's provider endpoints
(`/v1/messages`, `/chat/completions`, `/models`), without following redirects, and stops reading an answer past 4 MB.

**The web app and the phone apps** send requests from the page, so the provider must allow that. Anthropic does (with
the header above). For a model on your own computer, allow Iskra's web address:

- **Ollama**: start it with `OLLAMA_ORIGINS` set to the app's address, for example
  `OLLAMA_ORIGINS=https://app.iskra.foo ollama serve` (PowerShell: `$env:OLLAMA_ORIGINS='https://app.iskra.foo'; ollama serve`).
- **LM Studio**: turn on **Enable CORS** in its server settings.

## Tools

The assistant acts through a fixed list of tools. Each one sends the same request as the app's own buttons, so your
server checks your rights for every one of them, exactly as when you click.

| Group | Tools | Asks you first |
|---|---|---|
| Search & read (always on) | help search, list servers, list channels, list members, list roles, search messages, read a channel's recent messages | No (what they read goes to your provider) |
| Organize (always on) | create, rename and move channels and categories; make a theme; set up a bot | Yes, every change. Only moving channels and categories and making a theme can be allowed **for this session** (per server, until you start a new conversation) |
| Moderation (off until you turn it on) | time out, end a timeout, warn, kick, ban, delete messages | Yes, every single time |
| Server admin (off until you turn it on) | change someone's role, create a role, set someone's roles, delete a channel, replace the rules | Yes, every single time |

- The approval card says what will happen in plain words, on which server, shows in full any text others will see
  (a channel name, a reason, the rules), and shows the exact request under **Exact request**. **Deny** is final for
  that action.
- **Set up a bot** creates a single-use bot invite (valid 7 days). The link is shown to you in the panel to copy; the
  model never sees it. Bot code reads it from the `ISKRA_INVITE` environment variable (see [Bots](bots.md)).
- There are no tools for keys, recovery codes, tokens, invite links, webhooks, passkeys, linking devices, backups or
  deleting your account, and none that send messages or direct messages for you.
- At most 30 tool calls a minute (10 changes), 40 changes in one conversation, and at most 12 steps for one question.
- Requests from an MCP client are never allowed "for this session": each change asks.
- Text from other people (messages, names, topics) reaches the model marked as data, with the rule that it is never an
  instruction. If a message tries to talk the model into something, the approval card is still there: nothing changes
  without your OK.

## Use Iskra's tools from Claude Desktop or Claude Code (MCP)

The desktop app can offer the same tools to an AI app on the same computer through the
[Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) (MCP), over stdio.

1. In **My settings → Assistant**, turn on the assistant and **Allow local MCP clients**. It's off by default.
2. Copy the command shown there. For **Claude Code**:

   ```sh
   claude mcp add iskra -- "C:\Program Files\Iskra\Iskra.exe" --mcp
   ```

   For **Claude Desktop**, add the snippet shown in settings to its config file (Settings → Developer → Edit config):

   ```json
   { "mcpServers": { "iskra": { "command": "C:\\Program Files\\Iskra\\Iskra.exe", "args": ["--mcp"] } } }
   ```

   (On macOS the command is `/Applications/Iskra.app/Contents/MacOS/Iskra`, on Linux your AppImage or `/opt/Iskra/iskra`.)
3. Keep Iskra open. Changes the other app asks for appear as approval cards in the Iskra window, marked "An app on this
   computer (MCP) wants to"; the same groups and limits apply.

How it works: `Iskra --mcp` starts a small bridge with no window. It connects to the running Iskra over a private local
channel (a named pipe with a random name on Windows, a socket file in Iskra's data folder on macOS and Linux), never a
network port. Both sides prove they know a random token kept in Iskra's data folder, so other users on the computer
can't use it. While **Allow local MCP clients** is off, Iskra doesn't listen at all and the bridge offers no tools;
turning it off also denies any of its changes still waiting for your OK. On Windows the bridge runs as a second copy
of the app in Node mode (Electron's `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE`), because the app's main process can't read the pipes an MCP
client starts it with. The other app sends what
it reads through the tools to its own AI provider, under that provider's terms.

## When it doesn't work

- **"The provider didn't accept the key"**: check the key in My settings → Assistant (replace it if needed).
- **"Couldn't reach the provider"**: check the address and your connection. In the web app, a model on this computer
  needs to allow Iskra's address (see above).
- **The model doesn't use tools**: pick a model that supports tool calls (function calling).
- **MCP: "Iskra's tools aren't available"**: open Iskra, turn on the assistant and Allow local MCP clients, and make sure
  the app isn't locked.

---

Source: https://iskra.foo/docs/testers

# Testing Iskra: a guide for testers

Thank you for testing Iskra! Iskra is a free app for voice and text chat with friends. This page tells you how to
install it, where to go, what to try, and how to tell us when something breaks.

You don't need to be an expert. Short and simple notes are perfect, in any language.

## 1. Install the app

**Android (Google Play):**

1. Open this link on your phone: https://play.google.com/apps/testing/foo.iskra.app
2. Tap **Become a tester**.
3. Tap **Download it on Google Play** (or open https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=foo.iskra.app) and install **Iskra**.

It can take a few minutes before Play shows the test version. Keep the app installed for the whole test.

**iPhone (TestFlight):**

1. Install **TestFlight** from the App Store.
2. Open this link on your iPhone: https://testflight.apple.com/join/r4tMgn3D
3. Tap **Accept**, then **Install**.

New test versions arrive by themselves. You don't need to do anything.

## 2. Join the test server

1. Open this invite link on your phone: https://app.iskra.foo/#/join/aHR0cHM6Ly9jb21tdW5pdHkuaXNrcmEuZm9v.7zA91nWmAVWFE8lCKapTTeE39UGJ2ogElKoV7eiC6X4.8zWYxRjbH9zeM43YyjZqfg
2. It opens in Iskra. (If it opens in your browser instead, tap **Open in the app**.) Agree to the terms and tap
   **I'm new to Iskra**.
3. Pick a name (your first name or a nickname) and tap **Join**.
4. Read the five server rules and tap **I agree**.

You land in **#welcome**. No email, phone number or password needed: your account is a key stored on your phone.

**Save your recovery key** when the app asks. It brings your account back if you reinstall the app.

## 3. The 10-minute tour

The **testing-guide** channel on the server has the same tour. Each channel also has a topic at the top saying what to
try there. Do the steps in any order. If something doesn't work, or you don't understand it, that's a useful report too.

- **Chat** (#general): send a message. Long-press it and **edit** it. Long-press someone else's message and choose
  **Reply**. React with an emoji. Type **@** to mention someone.
- **Voice** (Hangout): tap **Hangout** to join and allow the microphone. Try **mute** and **deafen**. Tap someone's
  name to change their volume. Lock your phone for a minute: you should stay in voice.
- **Whisper** (Lounge 1, 2 or 3): in **Settings → Voice & audio → Whisper**, put a friend on list 1. In voice, hold the
  **whisper** button in the call bar. Only your list hears you.
- **Teams and looking for group**: with two or more people in **Game night**, long-press the channel and choose
  **Split into teams…**, then bring everyone back. In **#gaming**, send **/lfg 3 Minecraft** and let others tap **Join**.
- **Disappearing messages**: write in **#disappearing**; it's gone after an hour. In a direct message, tap the
  **timer** at the top and choose **5 minutes**.
- **Translation** (#your-language): write in your own language. Long-press a message in another language and choose
  **Translate**. It runs on your phone; nothing goes to a translation service. It works between English and 12
  European languages so far.
- **Whiteboard**: open **#whiteboard** under Try things and draw something; others see it as you draw. In a voice
  channel, tap **More** in the call bar, then **Open a whiteboard**, and draw with someone.
- **Polls** (#polls): tap the poll button next to the message box, or send **/poll Pizza or tacos? | Pizza | Tacos**.
- **Threads** (#threads): long-press a message, choose **Start a thread**, and reply inside it.
- **Forums** (#feedback): make a post with a title and a tag. Tell us what you like or what confused you.
- **Events**: tap **Events** at the top of the channel list. Say you're interested, or plan one.
- **Stage** (town-hall): join and tap **Ask to speak**.
- **Watch together** (Watch party): tap **More** in the call bar, then **Watch together**, and paste a YouTube link.
- **Private and encrypted chats**: tap someone's name and choose **Message**. Direct messages are end-to-end
  encrypted: only the two of you can read them. A channel with a **lock** is encrypted too.

A good daily habit for the test: open Iskra, read what's new in **#announcements**, try one thing from the list, and
say hi in voice if someone is there.

## 4. Report a bug

Report bugs right in the app. It's quick, and it includes the details we need.

1. Tap **your name** at the bottom of the channel list. (Also in **Settings → About & legal**. On a computer: press
   **Ctrl+Shift+B**.)
2. Choose **Report a bug**.
3. Write **what happened** and what you expected. Add **steps** if you can.
4. Add a **screenshot**: take one on your phone, then tap **Add pictures**. Need to show the bug first? Tap **Keep
   using Iskra**: the report waits in a small chip, and tapping the chip brings it back with everything you wrote.
5. Tap **Send**. You get a report number.

On a computer the report opens in a window of its own, so you can keep using Iskra to show the bug. In the desktop
app it takes screenshots of Iskra's own windows (the main window or a popped-out one, never anything else on your
screen), right away or **in 5 seconds**, so you have time to open the menu that misbehaves.

**What gets sent:** your words and screenshots, the app version, your system and the app's language, and technical
logs from the last 30 minutes (settings, connection and voice status, errors). Your email only if you type it in.
Never your messages, names, servers, invite links or addresses. Tap **See what's included** to see it all before you
send. Reports go only to the Iskra team.

Ideas and questions are welcome too: post them in **#feedback** on the server.

## 5. Don't worry about

- **Updates**: they arrive by themselves through Google Play or TestFlight.
- **A short "Reconnecting…"**: it happens when your phone changes network or wakes up. Report it only if it stays.
- **Notifications while the app is closed**: the phone apps notify you while they're open. That's on purpose for now.
- **Screen sharing and starting your own server**: these are in the desktop app, not on phones.
- **Breaking things**: it's a test server. Messages and channels may be reset.
- **Your English**: write in any language you like.

## 6. Your privacy

Iskra has no ads, no tracking and no analytics; bug reports are only sent when you tap **Send**. Don't post private
things (address, phone number, passwords) on the test server. Details: https://iskra.foo/privacy

---

Source: https://iskra.foo/docs/bots

# Bots and webhooks

Iskra has two ways to bring other programs into your server:

| | What it is | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| **Webhook** | A secret URL that posts messages into one channel | Build results, alerts, game-server stats, anything that can send an HTTP request |
| **Bot** | A program that joins like a person: it answers `/commands`, buttons and forms, and posts | Dice, polls, reminders, games, role pickers |

Both show a **BOT** badge, so everyone can tell them apart from people. Admins manage both in **Server settings → Bots & webhooks**. No programming needed? Turn on a [built-in bot](#built-in-bots).

For server owners: [hosting.md → Bots and webhooks](hosting.md#bots-and-webhooks). How bots and webhooks are kept in check: [security.md → Webhooks and bots](security.md#webhooks-and-bots). Where your server sends things: [Who Iskra talks to](privacy-connections.md).

## Webhooks

### Make one

1. Open **Bots & webhooks** → **Webhooks**.
2. Give it a name (and optionally a picture), pick the channel it posts in, and click **Create webhook**.
3. Copy the URL. It's only shown once: the server keeps a hash of the secret, not the secret itself. Lost it? Click **New URL** (the old one stops working right away).

Treat the URL like a password: anyone who has it can post in that channel. Use the `https://` address when your server has one.

### Post a message

```sh
curl -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"content": "Build **passed** ✅"}' \
  https://chat.example.com/hooks/<id>/<secret>
```

The body uses the same fields as a Discord webhook, so tools that can post to Discord usually work by pasting the Iskra URL instead:

```jsonc
{
  "content": "Deploy finished",            // up to 4000 characters, formatting like chat
  "username": "Deploy bot",                // optional: a different name for this message
  "embeds": [{                             // optional: up to 10 cards
    "title": "v1.4.2 is live", "url": "https://example.com/changelog",
    "description": "3 fixes, 1 new map", "color": 5763719,
    "fields": [{ "name": "Region", "value": "EU", "inline": true }],
    "footer": { "text": "deploy #812" }, "timestamp": "2026-10-10T12:00:00Z"
  }],
  "allowed_mentions": { "parse": [] }      // optional: who may be pinged (see below)
}
```

- `?wait=true` answers with the posted message (JSON) instead of an empty `204`.
- Forms work too: `curl -d "content=hello" <url>`, or Discord's multipart `payload_json`.
- **Grafana** and other tools with a "Discord" notification type: paste the Iskra URL as the Discord webhook URL.

### GitHub, Gitea, GitLab and Slack

Add a suffix to the URL and Iskra reads that service's own format. Events it doesn't post about are answered `204`, so
nothing retries.

| Suffix | Where to paste it | What becomes a card |
|---|---|---|
| `<url>/github` | Repository *Settings → Webhooks* → Payload URL, content type `application/json` | Pushes, pull requests and issues (opened, closed, merged, reopened), comments, releases, finished workflow runs (failures, and successes of CI/Release/Deploy workflows), stars |
| `<url>/gitea` | Repository *Settings → Webhooks → Add webhook → Gitea* | The same as GitHub |
| `<url>/gitlab` | Project *Settings → Webhooks* → URL | Pushes, new tags, merge requests (opened, closed, merged, reopened), issues, comments, finished pipelines (failures, and successes that weren't scheduled). Confidential issues and comments are never posted. |
| `<url>/slack` | Any tool with a "Slack incoming webhook" option | `text` (Slack's `*bold*`, `<url\|label>` links), `blocks` (headers, sections, context) and old-style `attachments`. Answers `ok`, like Slack. |

**Signing secret.** Click **Signing secret** on the webhook, then **Generate** (or paste your own, 16–256 characters)
and **Save**, and paste the same secret into GitHub's or Gitea's *Secret* field or GitLab's *Secret token*. Iskra then
refuses `/github`, `/gitea` and `/gitlab` posts that aren't signed with it (`401`). A webhook with a signing secret is a
GitHub, Gitea or GitLab webhook: its plain URL and `/slack`, which can't be signed, are refused too, so a leaked URL alone
can't post anything. The secret is shown only while you set it. Webhooks without one keep working as before.

What's left out on purpose: images, thumbnails and avatar URLs from the payload. Showing them would make every viewer's app fetch a third-party address (revealing their IP). Give the webhook a picture in its settings instead.

### Limits and safety

| | |
|---|---|
| Message text | Same rules as chat (1–4000 characters, no invisible control characters) |
| Embeds | Up to 10 per message, 6000 characters in total; titles 256, descriptions 4096, up to 25 fields |
| Request size | 64 KB (1 MB for `/github`, `/gitea`, `/gitlab`, `/slack`) |
| Rate limit | Per webhook: 5 messages at once, then one every 2 seconds. Too fast gets `429` with `Retry-After`. |
| Mentions | Off by default: `@everyone`, `@here` and mentions of members are shown as plain text and ping nobody. Turn on **Can mention people** for a webhook you trust; the payload's `allowed_mentions` can then narrow it further. |
| Webhooks per channel | 15 |

Nobody can edit a webhook's message; admins can delete it like any other.

## Outgoing webhooks

The other way round: your server POSTs to a web address when something happens, for things that don't want to hold a
connection open (a Minecraft chat bridge, Home Assistant, IFTTT, a small script).

In **Server settings → Bots & webhooks → Outgoing**, pick a name, the `https://` address, the events and (for messages
and the other channel events) the channels. Events:

| Event | When |
|---|---|
| `message.created`, `message.updated`, `message.deleted` | A message is posted, edited or deleted in a chosen channel (deleted: only its id) |
| `reaction.added` | Someone reacts in a chosen channel |
| `thread.created` | A thread or forum post starts in a chosen channel |
| `voice.joined`, `voice.left` | Someone joins or leaves a chosen voice channel (who and where, nothing about audio) |
| `member.joined`, `member.left` | Someone joins or leaves the server |
| `member.updated` | A member's level, roles or server nickname change (never their profile) |
| `role.created`, `role.updated`, `role.deleted` | Roles change |
| `channel.created`, `channel.updated`, `channel.deleted` | Channels everyone can read (or that the webhook lists) change |
| `event.started` | A scheduled event starts |

Copy the **signing secret** shown once (**New secret** makes another). **Send a test** posts a `ping`, and **Log** shows
the last 50 attempts (status only, never what was sent). Every member can see the webhook's host under
**My settings → Privacy & data → Who Iskra talks to**.

Each request is JSON (the shape is in [PROTOCOL.md](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md#outgoing-webhooks)):

```json
{ "id": "3q2-7wAAAQ...", "type": "message.created", "timestamp": 1760000000000, "server": { "name": "Friends" },
  "data": { "message": { "id": 42, "channel": { "id": 1, "name": "general", "kind": "text", "parentId": null },
            "author": { "accountKey": "...", "name": "Alice", "bot": false }, "text": "hello", "createdAt": 1760000000000,
            "replyTo": null, "attachments": [] } } }
```

### Check the signature

Every request carries `Iskra-Webhook-Id`, `Iskra-Webhook-Timestamp` (Unix seconds) and
`Iskra-Webhook-Signature: v1=<hex>`, the HMAC-SHA256 of `iskra-webhook-v1\n<timestamp>\n<id>\n<raw body>` (`\n` is a newline) keyed with
the secret's UTF-8 bytes. Check it on the raw body (before parsing), compare in constant time, and refuse timestamps more than five
minutes off. Retries keep the same id, so you can skip ids you've already handled.

```js
// Node 18+
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto'

export function verify(secret, headers, rawBody) {
  const id = headers['iskra-webhook-id'], ts = headers['iskra-webhook-timestamp'], sig = headers['iskra-webhook-signature'] ?? ''
  if (!id || !ts || Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(ts)) > 300) return false
  const expected = 'v1=' + createHmac('sha256', secret).update(`iskra-webhook-v1\n${ts}\n${id}\n${rawBody}`).digest('hex')
  return sig.length === expected.length && timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(sig), Buffer.from(expected))
}
```

```python
# Python 3
import hashlib, hmac, time

def verify(secret: str, headers, raw_body: bytes) -> bool:
    msg_id, ts = headers.get("Iskra-Webhook-Id", ""), headers.get("Iskra-Webhook-Timestamp", "")
    if not msg_id or not ts.isdigit() or abs(time.time() - int(ts)) > 300:
        return False
    signed = f"iskra-webhook-v1\n{ts}\n{msg_id}\n".encode() + raw_body
    expected = "v1=" + hmac.new(secret.encode(), signed, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(headers.get("Iskra-Webhook-Signature", ""), expected)
```

Check: with the secret `whs_test`, timestamp `1760000000`, id `abc` and the body `{"type":"ping"}`, the signature is
`v1=61117e1080d5aed00a4e39e279580b31eabbedd00eda8331228b580fb2308c28` (the server tests check this vector).

### Delivery and safety

| | |
|---|---|
| Addresses | `https://` only, and only public addresses: the server checks the address after looking up the name, on every connection, and never follows redirects. Private, loopback, link-local and cloud metadata addresses are refused. |
| Your own network | For a receiver at home (Home Assistant on `192.168.x.x`, something on the same PC or on Tailscale), the **owner** can tick **Allow addresses on my own network** for that webhook; plain `http://` then works for those addresses only. Link-local and metadata addresses stay blocked. |
| Answer | Any `2xx` within 10 seconds. The body of your answer is ignored. |
| Retries | `408`, `429`, `5xx`, timeouts and network errors: again after 5 s, 30 s, 2 min and 10 min (with the same id). Other answers aren't retried. Order isn't guaranteed. |
| Turning off | After 10 deliveries in a row that failed (after their retries), the webhook turns itself off and admins are told. Turn it on again in its settings. |
| Rate | Per webhook: 30 events at once, then 5 a second, 100 waiting at most; more are skipped (and logged). |
| Never sent | Anything from end-to-end encrypted channels, direct messages and group chats (the server can't read them), and messages posted by incoming webhooks. |
| Per server | 10 outgoing webhooks |
| The secret | The server keeps each signing secret to sign with, so it's in the server's database and its backups. Keep backups private, and make a **New secret** if one may have leaked. |

## Built-in bots

Eleven small bots come with every server and run inside it, so there's nothing to install, host or keep running. An
admin turns each one on in **Server settings → Bots & webhooks → Bots**:

| Bot | Command | Does |
|---|---|---|
| **Dice** | `/roll 2d6+3`, `/roll d20` | Rolls dice (up to 100 dice and 10 terms; `/roll` alone is `1d6`). |
| **Polls** | `/poll Pizza or tacos? \| Pizza \| Tacos` | Starts a normal poll in a text channel (2–10 answers). |
| **Reminders** | `/remind me in 10m take the pizza out` | Reminds you about that message later (1 minute up to a year), like any reminder. |
| **Starboard** | (react with ⭐) | When a message gets enough stars (⭐ ×3 unless you pick another reaction or number; the author's own and bots' don't count), it gets a card in `#starboard` that links back to it. The card keeps its count and text up to date and goes when the message does. Messages from channels that are more private than the board never go there. |
| **Birthdays** | `/birthday set 14 March`, `/birthday list`, `/birthday remove` | Members who want to share their birthday (day and month, never the year; also in their profile for the server) get a greeting once a year, at the time and in the time zone you pick. |
| **Welcome** | | Greets people when they actually get in (after approval or agreeing to the rules, if you use those) with your own text (`{name}`, `{server}`, `{memberCount}`, markdown), optionally with a private welcome too. When lots of people join at once, they get one shared greeting. |
| **Feeds** | | Posts new posts from RSS or Atom feeds, new YouTube videos and, with the owner's own Twitch app, Twitch streams going live, each in the channel you pick, optionally mentioning a role. Only new things are posted (nothing old when you add a feed). The server fetches those sites itself (text only, never pictures), so it's off until you turn it on. |
| **Tags** | `/tag rules`, `/tag list` | Posts saved snippets (rules, links, answers to common questions; markdown, up to 2,000 characters). Admins and a role you pick add, change and remove them under its switch or with `/tag set rules Be kind.` and `/tag remove rules`; up to 200 per server. A tag can never ping anyone. |
| **Suggestions** | `/suggest Movie night on Fridays` | Turns an idea into a card in `#suggestions` (or the channel you pick) where everyone votes 👍 or 👎 (one vote each, changeable). Admins and a staff role mark it accepted, declined or implemented, with a reason if they like, and the author hears about it. A Suggest button card works too, and the `/suggest` message itself disappears. Optionally anonymous: cards don't show who wrote them, but staff can look it up (that's logged). Up to 3 suggestions per person every 10 minutes. |
| **Giveaways** | `/giveaway 1h 2w Steam key` | Staff (admins and a role you pick) start a giveaway with how long it runs and how many winners (add a role mention so only members with that role can enter). People press Enter; when the time is up the server draws the winners fairly and mentions them. `/giveaway end`, `cancel` and `reroll` (for a week after it ends). Bots and people who left never win, and a restart doesn't lose a giveaway. |
| **Counting** | (count in `#counting`) | Everyone counts up in one channel, one number each and never twice in a row (simple sums like 3+4 if you allow them). A mistake gets ❌ and the count starts over; the best streak shows on the bot's pinned card. Editing or deleting a number doesn't break the count. No points and no ranking of people. |

Turned on, each is a bot member like any other: give it a role or channel overrides to choose where it answers.
Starboard, Birthdays, Welcome, Feeds, Suggestions and Counting post in the channel you pick under their switch (they need to see it, not write in it); Tags and Giveaways answer where their command was typed. Each
reads only its own commands (Counting also reads the messages in its channel), answers mistakes privately to the person who typed them, and stays out of encrypted
channels. Turning it off removes it; turning it on again brings back the same member. Details:
[PROTOCOL.md → Built-in bots](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md#built-in-bots) and [Tags, Suggestions, Giveaways and Counting](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md#tags-suggestions-giveaways-and-counting).

## Bots

A bot is an ordinary Iskra identity (its own account and device keys) that connects with the same protocol as the app and says it's a bot. The server remembers that, and:

- shows it with a **BOT** badge,
- only lets it in with a **bot invite** (made by an admin; single use), and never lets a bot invite be used by a person,
- keeps it out of voice unless an admin allows it ([Voice bots](#voice-bots)), out of group chats and calls, and doesn't let it create invites, schedule messages or be made admin (guest, member or trusted only),
- lets it send and receive [direct messages](#direct-messages), end-to-end encrypted like everyone's, within limits people control,
- applies the same rate limits as everyone else (2 messages a second, bursts of 10).

**What a bot can read** is the admin's choice when making the bot invite (**Can read all messages**, off by default),
and can be changed later in **Bots & webhooks → Bots**; everyone can see it (`readsMessages` on the member). By default
a bot gets only:

- its commands, button clicks and forms ([interactions](#commands)),
- messages that mention it, reply to one of its messages, or start with one of its commands (`/roll …`),
- its own messages.

It doesn't get the rest of the chat, and requests that read it (history, search, pins, threads, forum posts, docs) are
refused with `bot_no_read`. Most bots never need more; turn it on for a bot that has to read along (a logger, a
translator). Bots that joined before this choice existed keep reading everything until an admin changes it.

A bot can be given [roles](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md#roles-and-permissions) like anyone else, so a moderation bot can get *Manage messages* or *Kick members*. As for people, it can only act on members ranked below it, and a bot is never ranked above trusted.

Bots and webhooks stay out of **end-to-end encrypted channels**: a bot holds no channel keys and never counts as a reader there, so it can't read or post in them (the SDK skips their messages), and webhooks can't post into them. Commands still work there, privately: see [Commands in encrypted channels](#commands-in-encrypted-channels). A bot can read and post in a voice channel's text chat like in any channel it can see.

### Your first bot in 5 minutes

You need [Node.js](https://nodejs.org) 22 or newer, [Git](https://git-scm.com), and a server where you're an admin. Any server works, including one you run on your own computer. Prefer Python? See [Python](#python); any other language works through [the bridge](#other-languages).

1. **Get the SDK.** It lives in the Iskra repository, next to the app code it reuses (it's also packaged for npm as
   [`iskra-bots`](#the-sdk-on-npm)):

   ```sh
   git clone https://github.com/quikmn/iskra-voice.git
   cd iskra-voice/bots
   npm install
   ```

2. **Make a bot invite.** In Iskra, open **Bots & webhooks** → **Bots**, choose **Member** as the bot's role (a guest usually can't post), leave **Can read all messages** off (this bot doesn't need it) and click **Create bot invite**. Copy the link. It works once, for 7 days.

3. **Write the bot.** Save this as `bots/my-bot.ts`:

   ```ts
   import { Bot } from './sdk/src/index'

   const bot = new Bot({ name: 'Greeter', invite: process.env.ISKRA_INVITE })

   bot.commands([
     { name: 'hello', description: 'Says hello', handler: ({ userName, reply }) => reply(`Hi ${userName}!`) },
     {
       name: 'score',
       description: 'Shows a score card',
       options: [{ name: 'team', description: 'Which team', type: 'string', required: true }],
       handler: ({ options, reply }) => reply({
         cards: [{ title: `Team ${options.team}`, color: 0x57f287, fields: [{ name: 'Points', value: '12', inline: true }] }],
         components: [{ type: 'row', items: [{ type: 'button', customId: 'cheer', label: 'Cheer 🎉' }] }],
       }),
     },
   ])

   // Someone clicked the button: answer only them.
   bot.onComponent('cheer', ({ userName, reply }) => reply(`${userName} cheers!`, { private: true }))

   // Messages that mention the bot (it doesn't read the rest of the chat).
   bot.on('message', (message) => {
     if (message.text.includes('pizza')) void message.react('🍕')
   })

   await bot.start()
   ```

4. **Start it** with the invite link:

   ```sh
   node build.mjs my-bot.ts
   ISKRA_INVITE='<the bot invite link>' node dist/my-bot.js
   ```

   In PowerShell: `$env:ISKRA_INVITE='<the bot invite link>'; node dist/my-bot.js`. It prints `[Greeter] Online in "<server>" as Greeter (member)`.

5. **Try it.** Type `/` in a channel: the app lists Greeter's commands. Pick `/hello`, or `/score` (it shows the
   `<team>` option as you type) and see the card; click **Cheer 🎉**. `/help` lists every command (only you see that
   answer). Mention `@Greeter` with the word pizza and it reacts.

The bot saves its keys and the server's address in `greeter.bot.json`, so from now on `node dist/my-bot.js` is enough (no invite). Keep that file private: it *is* the bot. Run `node build.mjs my-bot.ts` again after each change. The build bundles the SDK, which reuses the Iskra app's own crypto and connection code.

### The example bots

| | Run it | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| **Dice** ([`examples/dice.ts`](../bots/examples/dice.ts)) | `npm run dice` | `/roll 2d6` (answers with a card and a **Roll again** button; `/roll d20 yes` answers only you), `/coin`, `/pick pizza, tacos`, `/echo`; commands with options; a button handler; reacting to "good bot" when mentioned; welcoming new members; answering in DMs |
| **Music** ([`examples/music.ts`](../bots/examples/music.ts)) | `npm run music` | A [voice bot](#voice-bots) for the songs people upload: attach audio to a message that mentions @Music (or send it in a DM) and it joins your voice channel and plays it; `/play <link to a file on this server>`, a queue (`/queue`, `/remove`, `/clear`), `/pause`, `/resume`, `/skip`, `/stop`, `/volume`; a "Now playing" card with buttons; admins choose who controls it (`/music-control`) |
| **Jukebox** ([`gallery/jukebox`](../bots/gallery/jukebox)) | `npm run jukebox` | A [voice bot](#voice-bots): `/play [song]` joins your voice channel and plays the files in a folder (and radio streams you list), `/skip`, `/stop`, `/songs`; a "Now playing" card with **Pause**, **Skip** and **Stop** buttons that it keeps up to date |
| **Planner** ([`examples/planner.ts`](../bots/examples/planner.ts)) | `npm run planner` | `/poll Pizza or tacos? \| Pizza \| Tacos` (posts the result and a CSV file when it closes), `/remind 10m stretch`, `/event 2h Game night`, `/events` (a card); usage hints, edits, files, polls, events, an activity, and keeping state across restarts |
| **Dice in Python** ([`python/examples/dice.py`](../bots/python/examples/dice.py)) | `python examples/dice.py` (in `bots/python`) | The Dice bot with the [Python SDK](#python) |
| **Roll, any language** ([`roll.py`](../bots/examples/bridge/roll.py), [`Roll.cs`](../bots/examples/bridge/Roll.cs)) | `npm run bridge -- --name Roll -- python examples/bridge/roll.py` | A bot without any SDK, through [the bridge](#other-languages) |

Start either one the first time with `ISKRA_INVITE='<bot invite link>' npm run planner` (PowerShell: `$env:ISKRA_INVITE='<link>'; npm run planner`). Each needs its own bot invite.

### Gallery

The [bot gallery](../bots/gallery) has ready-made bots to run as they are or copy and change. Each is a small folder
with a README (what it does, its commands, settings and what it keeps), tests and its own `package.json`, so a copy
works on its own with the SDK from npm (`npm install`, then `npm start`; Node runs the TypeScript directly).

| Bot | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Trivia** ([`gallery/trivia`](../bots/gallery/trivia)) | `/trivia start`: questions with answer buttons (or answered by replying), points for the week and a results card every Monday. No levels, XP or all-time ranks. Your own question file works too. |
| **Feeds Plus** ([`gallery/feeds-advanced`](../bots/gallery/feeds-advanced)) | Adds to the built-in [Feeds](#built-in-bots) bot: RSS, Atom and YouTube feeds with include and exclude keywords, and Twitch "went live" alerts in a channel or as a DM to each person who `/twitch follow`s a streamer, with your own Twitch app. It only fetches addresses on the internet, never your own network. |
| **Server stats** ([`gallery/server-stats`](../bots/gallery/server-stats)) | A weekly card: members, new people, messages per channel. Counts only: never who wrote what. Needs **Can read all messages** for the full count. |
| **Jukebox** ([`gallery/jukebox`](../bots/gallery/jukebox)) | Your music folder and radio stations in a voice channel (see [Voice bots](#voice-bots)). |
| **Starter** ([`gallery/starter`](../bots/gallery/starter)) | A template for your own bot: commands, a card with a button, tests and a GitHub Actions workflow. Also [in Python](../bots/gallery/starter-python). |

From this repository, in `bots/`: `ISKRA_INVITE='<bot invite link>' npm run trivia` the first time, then `npm run trivia`
(likewise `feeds-advanced`, `server-stats`, `jukebox` and `starter`). Their tests run with `npm test`.

#### Bots on this computer (desktop app)

No Node.js needed: the desktop app runs gallery bots itself. In **My settings → Bots on this computer**, add one from the
list (Starter, Trivia, Feeds Plus and Server stats come with the app and update with it), press **Start**, and either
let the app make a bot invite on a server where you're an admin (with the rights that bot needs) or paste one. The app
starts it with its own built-in Node.js, shows whether it's online, its last log lines and its settings (like the
Twitch keys), and can start it with Iskra. Bots run while the app is open (also in the tray), connect out to their
server like the app does, and nothing listens on a port.

**Run a bot from a folder** runs your own bot or a copy from the gallery: a folder with a `package.json` "main", a
`bot.js`/`bot.ts`, or a `bot.py` (with the Python installed on your computer). Only run bots you trust: a bot runs
with your rights on your computer and can read and change your files. A bot's keys and data stay in the app's folder
for it (gallery bots) or in its own folder; the bot invite link is only used to join and never saved. Removing a
gallery bot deletes its keys there; it stays a member of the server until an admin removes it.

### The SDK

| API | What it does |
|---|---|
| `new Bot({ name, invite?, stateFile?, hearBots?, log? })` | `invite` is only needed the first time. `stateFile` defaults to `<name>.bot.json` (lowercase, spaces become dashes). Bots ignore other bots and webhooks unless `hearBots` is true, so two bots can't chat forever. |
| `bot.command(name, description, handler, { usage?, options?, role?, permission? }?)` | Answers `/name`. The handler gets `{ options, args, user, userName, channelId, dm, reply, defer, showModal, react, interaction, message?, command, bot }` (see [Commands](#commands)); `dm` is true for a command typed in a DM. `/help` is built in and lists the descriptions. |
| `bot.commands([{ name, description, usage?, options?, role?, permission?, handler }, ...])` | Several commands at once. Every command is registered with the server when the bot connects, so the app suggests it when people type `/` and sends it straight to the bot. |
| `reply(content, { private? })`, `defer()`, `showModal(modal)` | In command, button and form handlers: answer in public (a message that says who asked) or only to the asker; "thinking…" for slow work; show a [form](#buttons-menus-and-forms). Up to 5 answers per interaction, within 15 minutes. |
| `bot.onComponent(customId or /pattern/, ctx => ...)` | A click on one of the bot's buttons or select menus: `{ customId, values, user, userName, messageId?, reply, update, defer, showModal }`. `update(content)` replaces the message the button is on. |
| `bot.onModalSubmit(customId or /pattern/, ctx => ...)` | A form the bot showed, filled in: `{ customId, fields, user, userName, reply, defer }`. |
| `bot.on('message', m => ...)` | Messages the bot may read (not its own): by default those that mention it, reply to it or start with one of its commands; every message it can see if an admin let it [read all messages](#bots). `m.text`, `m.author`, `m.authorName`, `m.channel`, `m.attachments`, `m.reply(text)`, `m.react(emoji)`. |
| `bot.on('dm', dm => ...)` | A [direct message](#direct-messages) to the bot, decrypted: `dm.text`, `dm.from`, `dm.authorName`, `dm.files`, `dm.reply(text)`. Commands typed in a DM also reach their handlers, with `dm: true`. |
| `bot.sendDm(accountKey, text)` or `bot.sendDm(accountKey, { text?, cards? })`, `bot.downloadDmFile(file)` | Send a DM, end-to-end encrypted (cards become text); the bytes of a file someone attached to a DM (decrypted and checked). |
| `bot.on('messageEdited' \| 'messageDeleted' \| 'reactions' \| 'pollUpdated', ...)` | A message was edited or deleted; a message's reactions changed (the whole new list); someone voted or a poll closed. |
| `bot.on('ready' \| 'memberJoined' \| 'event' \| 'status', ...)` | Connected (again); someone joined; any raw server event; connection state. |
| `bot.send(channelId, text, { replyTo?, attachments?, cards?, components? })` or `bot.send(channelId, { text?, cards?, components?, attachments?, replyTo? })` | Posts a message (up to 4000 characters; waits and retries if rate-limited), optionally with [cards](#cards) and [buttons or a menu](#buttons-menus-and-forms). A thread's id works as a channel id. `reply(...)` takes the same. |
| `bot.edit(messageId, text)` or `bot.edit(messageId, { text?, cards?, components? })`, `bot.delete(messageId)` | Edit the bot's own message (cards and components replace the old ones, `[]` removes them); delete its own (or others', with *Manage messages* and a higher rank). |
| `bot.react(messageId, emoji, on?)` | Add a reaction (`on = false` takes it away). Server emoji as `<:name:id>` (ids from `emoji.list`). |
| `bot.sendFile(channelId, { name, data }, { text?, replyTo? })`, `bot.upload({ name, data })` | Send a file (`data` is a string or bytes), or upload one to attach later with `send(..., { attachments: [file.id] })`. |
| `bot.poll(channelId, question, answers, { multi?, durationMs? })` | Start a poll; votes arrive as `pollUpdated`. |
| `bot.thread(messageId, name)` | Start a thread from a message. |
| `bot.setActivity(text \| null)` | Show an activity under the bot's name. |
| `bot.mention(accountKey)` | A mention token that shows as @Name and notifies them. |
| `bot.channels`, `bot.members`, `bot.me`, `bot.channelByName(name)` | What the bot can see right now (kept up to date). |
| `bot.joinVoice(channelId)`, `bot.voice`, `bot.voiceChannelOf(accountKey)` | Join a voice channel to play audio (see [Voice bots](#voice-bots)); the connection the bot has now, or null; the voice channel someone is in. |
| `bot.fileUrl(file)` | The full address of a file on the server (an attachment), e.g. to play it. |
| `bot.request(type, body)` | Any request in [PROTOCOL.md](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md), typed: events (`event.create`), pins (`chat.pin`), roles (`member.roles.set`), search and so on. Errors are `RequestError`s with a `code` (`forbidden`, `not_found`, `rate_limited`, …). |
| `bot.stop()` | Disconnects. The bot reconnects by itself after network trouble or a server restart until you stop it. |

### Commands

A bot describes its commands; the SDK does it each time the bot connects (`bot.commands.set` in
[PROTOCOL.md](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md#bot-interactions)). When someone types `/` at the start of a message, the app
lists the commands of the bots that can answer in that channel: the bot, the command and its description. Arrow keys
move, Tab or Enter complete, Esc closes. After the name it shows the options as hints (`/roll <dice> [times]`) and an
option's choices to pick from.

**Sending a command doesn't post it.** The app checks the options and sends the command straight to the bot as an
*interaction*; the server checks them again, and who may use the command where. The channel only shows the bot's
answer, with "Viktor used /roll" above it. The rest of the channel never sees the command, and the bot doesn't need to
read the chat to get it.

```ts
bot.commands([{
  name: 'roll',
  description: 'Rolls dice',                    // one line, up to 100 characters in the app (/help shows it all)
  options: [                                    // up to 25; required ones first
    { name: 'dice', description: 'Like 2d6', type: 'string', required: true },
    { name: 'times', description: 'How often', type: 'integer' },
    { name: 'secret', description: 'Only you see it', type: 'boolean' },
  ],
  role: 'member',                               // optional: the lowest level that may use it
  handler: async ({ options, userName, reply }) => {
    // options: { dice: '2d6', times: 3, secret: true }, checked by the server
    await reply(`${userName} asked for ${options.dice}`, { private: options.secret === true })
  },
}])
```

- **Options** are typed: `string` (1–1000 characters, one line), `integer`, `number`, `boolean` (yes/no), `user` (an
  account key), `channel` (a channel id) and `role` (a role id). People type them in order, one word each; the last
  text option takes the rest of the line (`/say #general hello there`). With `choices` (up to 25) only those values are
  accepted, so leave choices out when any value should work and put examples in the description. `args` holds the
  text as typed, for bots that parse it themselves (or give a `usage` line instead of options:
  `usage: 'Pizza or tacos? | Pizza | Tacos'`).
- **Who may use it**: `role` (`member`, `trusted` or `admin`) and `permission` (like `manageMessages`) are enforced by
  the server, and the app doesn't list commands someone can't use. Which channels a bot answers in follows its own
  roles: it must be able to post there, so admins limit a bot with roles and channel permissions like anyone else.
- **Answers**: `reply(...)` posts a message, or with `{ private: true }` shows it only to the person who asked (never
  stored; they can dismiss it). Answer within about 3 seconds, or call `defer()` first: the app shows "Dice is
  thinking…" until you reply. An interaction takes up to 5 answers within 15 minutes; its token works only for this
  bot and this one interaction.
- An offline bot can't be asked (the app says so). A handler that throws is logged on the bot's console (with the error
  code) and doesn't stop the bot.

Typing a command as plain text still works, for bots that don't take interactions and from older apps: a message
`/name args` (or `/name@BotName args` to pick one bot) reaches the bot as a message, and the handler gets the same
context with `message` set and empty `options`. Bots ignore commands they don't know, so several bots can share a
channel. Limits: 50 commands per bot, names of 1–32 characters (`a–z`, `0–9`, `_`, `-`), 16 KB for the whole list.

#### Commands in encrypted channels

In an [end-to-end encrypted channel](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md#end-to-end-encrypted-channels) the server can't read the
messages and bots aren't in the channel's chain. Commands still work there, without leaking anything:

- The app lists commands of bots that take interactions and can read the channel by their roles, and says before you
  send: "Commands go to the bot unencrypted, not through this channel. Only you will see the answer." The command and
  its options go to the bot like any request; the channel's messages and keys never do.
- Every answer is private: shown only to you, never stored, so nothing unencrypted lands in the channel.

### Direct messages

People can message a bot, and a bot can message people, as [end-to-end encrypted DMs](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md#bot-dms).
The bot has its own keys (in its `.bot.json`, with prekeys it rotates weekly like an app), so the server only passes the
messages along, and whoever runs the bot reads them. The app says so at the top of a DM with a bot.

```ts
bot.on('dm', async (dm) => {
  if (dm.text === 'hi') await dm.reply(`Hi ${dm.authorName}!`)
  for (const file of dm.files) console.log(file.name, (await bot.downloadDmFile(file)).length, 'bytes')
})

await bot.sendDm(accountKey, 'Your turn in the game 🎲')   // e.g. bot.members, or the `user` of a command
```

- **Commands work in DMs.** People type `/roll 2d6` in a DM with the bot (the app suggests its commands there too); it
  stays end-to-end encrypted and reaches the same handler, with `dm: true` and the options read from the text. Answers
  are DMs: `private` makes no difference there, cards become text, and buttons, menus and forms are left out (they need a
  channel message). The bot checks a command's `role` itself, from the member list; commands that need a `permission`
  answer that they only work in a channel.
- **Who a bot can write to:** members of its server who haven't blocked it. People choose in **My settings → Privacy &
  data → Direct messages from bots** (on by default). With it off, a bot can only answer someone who wrote to it first. A bot's
  DM also follows the person's **Who can message me**: it can arrive as a message request, or be refused (`dm_closed`)
  for people who only take DMs from people they've talked to. Writing to the bot counts; so does using one of its
  commands or buttons, for 15 minutes (enough to answer by DM).
- **Limits:** on top of the usual 2 messages a second, a bot sends at most 1 DM a second over all its connections (bursts
  of 30), and starts at most 20 new conversations at once, then 20 an hour. Bots never message other bots, and
  [built-in bots](#built-in-bots) don't take DMs (they run inside the server and have no keys).
- People block a bot like anyone (its card → **Block**): then neither side can write to the other.

### Buttons, menus and forms

Bot messages (and private answers) can carry up to 5 rows of **components**: up to 5 buttons per row, or one select
menu. A click goes to the bot as an interaction; the bot answers like a command, or `update`s the message.

```ts
await reply({
  text: 'Game night: who is in?',
  components: [
    { type: 'row', items: [
      { type: 'button', customId: 'rsvp:yes', label: "I'm in", style: 'success' },
      { type: 'button', customId: 'rsvp:no', label: "Can't", style: 'danger' },
      { type: 'button', label: 'Rules', style: 'link', url: 'https://example.com/rules' },
    ] },
    { type: 'row', items: [{ type: 'select', customId: 'game', placeholder: 'Pick a game', maxValues: 2, options: [
      { label: 'Catan', value: 'catan' }, { label: 'Codenames', value: 'codenames' }, { label: 'Uno', value: 'uno' },
    ] }] },
  ],
})

bot.onComponent(/^rsvp:/, ({ customId, userName, update }) => update(`${userName} said ${customId.slice(5)}`))
bot.onComponent('game', ({ values, reply }) => reply(`You picked ${values.join(' and ')}`, { private: true }))

// A form, shown to the person who used the command (or clicked).
bot.command('plan', 'Plans a game night', ({ showModal }) => showModal({
  customId: 'plan', title: 'Plan a game night',
  fields: [{ customId: 'title', label: 'Title', maxLength: 60 }, { customId: 'notes', label: 'Notes', style: 'paragraph', required: false }],
}))
bot.onModalSubmit('plan', ({ fields, reply }) => reply(`📅 ${fields.title} is planned`))
```

| | Limits |
|---|---|
| Rows | Up to 5; a row has 1–5 buttons or one select menu |
| `customId` | 1–100 printable ASCII characters, unique in the message |
| Buttons | `label` 1–80 characters; `style` `primary`, `secondary` (default), `success`, `danger` or `link`. A link button has a `url` (http/https) instead of a `customId`: the app shows the address and opens it only when clicked, and the bot never hears of it |
| Select menus | 1–25 options (`label`, `value`, `description?`, `default?`); `minValues` 0–25 and `maxValues` 1–25 (default 1) |
| Forms | A `title` (up to 45 characters) and 1–5 fields (`short`: one line, up to 1000 characters, default 200; `paragraph`: up to 4000); each form can be sent once |
| All components | 8 KB per message |

Only bots can add components, and only to their own messages. The server checks every click before the bot hears of
it: the button must really be on the message and enabled, and picked values must be the menu's own.

### Cards

Bots can attach cards to their messages, in the same format and with the same limits as [webhook embeds](#post-a-message):
a title (with a link), a description, fields, a colour, an author, a footer and a time.

```ts
await message.reply({
  text: 'Your roll',                            // optional when there are cards
  cards: [{
    title: '🎲 2d6', description: '**7**', color: 0x695bff,
    fields: [{ name: 'Dice', value: '3, 4', inline: true }],
    thumbnail: { url: picture.url },            // a file the bot uploaded: const picture = await bot.upload({ name, data })
    footer: { text: 'Good luck' },
  }],
})
```

Unlike webhooks, cards can have a `thumbnail` and an `image`, but only from the server itself: a file the bot uploaded
(`bot.upload`, then use its `url`) or a small `data:image/png|jpeg|gif|webp;base64,...` URL (up to 16 KB). Addresses on
other sites are refused, so nobody's app ever loads something from a third party. Only bots can send cards.

### Voice bots

A bot can join a voice channel and play audio into it: music from files, sounds, or a radio stream. An admin decides:
tick **Can join voice channels** when making the bot invite, or turn **Voice** on for a bot in **Bots & webhooks →
Bots** (off by default; everyone can see it, `joinsVoice` on the member). Then:

```ts
const voice = await bot.joinVoice(channelId)          // e.g. bot.voiceChannelOf(user): where the person who asked is
voice.on('trackEnd', ({ track, reason, error }) => console.log(track.title, reason))  // finished, stopped, replaced, error, left
await voice.play('music/song.mp3')                     // resolves when it ends
voice.play('https://radio.example.org/stream.mp3', { title: 'Lo-fi radio' })
voice.play(bot.fileUrl(message.attachments[0]))       // a file someone uploaded to the server
voice.pause(); voice.resume(); voice.setVolume(0.5)    // 0 to 2
voice.stop()                                           // stays in the channel
voice.on('kicked', () => console.log('a moderator disconnected me'))  // it doesn't rejoin by itself
await voice.leave()
```

| | |
|---|---|
| What it plays | A file path, an `http(s)://` address the bot fetches itself (a file or an internet radio stream), a server file (`/files/…` or `bot.fileUrl(file)`), bytes, or any stream of bytes. Formats: **MP3, Ogg Opus, Ogg Vorbis, FLAC and WAV**, recognized from their first bytes. AAC/M4A isn't supported (most internet radios also offer MP3). `encodeWav(channels, rate)` makes WAV bytes from samples the bot made itself. |
| How it sounds | 48 kHz stereo, 96 kbps (128 kbps in [hi-fi channels](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md#hi-fi-voice-channels)), with redundancy against packet loss. Other sample rates are resampled. |
| Where | Voice channels it can post in (it needs that to be heard). Never stages, never end-to-end encrypted voice channels (it holds no keys). User limits, timeouts and server mutes apply as for people. |
| What it can't do | Hear anyone: its voice token can't subscribe to other people's audio, and it can publish one audio track, no camera, screen or data. |
| For people | The bot shows in the channel with the **BOT** badge. Anyone can mute it for themselves (right-click it → volume → **Mute for me**). Moderators can server-mute it and **Disconnect from voice** it (*Move members*), as for people. |

**Music** ([`examples/music.ts`](../bots/examples/music.ts)) is the ready-made one: people attach songs to a message
that mentions @Music, send them in a DM, or `/play` a link to a file already on the server; it joins their voice channel
and plays them in turn. `/queue`, `/remove 2`, `/clear`, `/pause`, `/resume`, `/skip`, `/stop`, `/volume 80` (0–200 %) and
the card's buttons control it. By default everyone listening may; an admin picks who with `/music-control` (everyone,
trusted and up, admins, or a role such as DJ), and people may always skip or remove their own songs. Its settings are
kept in `music.settings.json` next to the bot. It also plays the operator's own files and streams from `MUSIC_DIR`,
like Jukebox.

**No YouTube, Spotify or other streaming services, by design.** The SDK has no extractors for them and never will:
taking audio out of those services breaks their terms of service and usually copyright, and it's what got popular
Discord music bots shut down. Play files you have the right to play, and streams whose operators let you (many internet
radios do). Only let people pick from what the bot's operator chose, or from files on the server: Music plays only
uploads and links to this server's own files, Jukebox the files in its folder and the
stations in its `stations.json`, never an address someone types (a bot that fetched any address it's given could be
pointed at other computers on its owner's network).

Voice needs the packages in `bots/` (`npm install`): `@livekit/rtc-node` (LiveKit's SDK for Node, native, prebuilt for
Windows x64, macOS and Linux x64/arm64) and the WebAssembly decoders; see the [third-party notices](voice-processing.md#voice-bots-sdk).
The audio goes from the bot's computer straight to the server's voice service, like an app's.

### What bots can't do (yet)

- **Group chats and calls:** bots can't be in group chats, call or be called.
- **Files in DMs:** bots can read files people attach to a DM, but can't attach files to their own DMs yet.
- **Encrypted channels:** bots can't read or post there; commands work, with private answers (see above).

### When it won't start

| The bot says | What to do |
|---|---|
| `That doesn't look like an Iskra invite link.` | Copy the whole link from **Bots & webhooks → Bots**; it contains `#/join/`. |
| `No server yet: start the bot once with a bot invite link …` | First start: set `ISKRA_INVITE`. Already ran it? You're in another folder, so it can't find its `<name>.bot.json`. |
| `The server didn't accept this invite. A bot needs a bot invite …` | You used an invite for people, or a bot invite that was already used or expired. Make a new **bot** invite. |
| `This bot is no longer a member of the server …` | An admin removed it. Make a new bot invite and start it with that (it keeps its keys). |
| `forbidden` errors in the log | The bot's role can't do that there: check the channel's write level, or give the bot a role. |
| `The server didn't take the command list (bad_request): …` | A command, option or choice breaks a [limit](#commands); the message says which. Commands still work as text. |
| Its commands don't show up when typing `/` | The bot must be able to read **and** post in that channel (in an encrypted channel: read it). Commands with a `role` or `permission` show only for people who have it. |
| `forbidden` with `bot_no_read` | The bot was invited without **Can read all messages**, so it gets its commands and mentions only. An admin can change that in **Bots & webhooks → Bots**. |
| `Nothing answers the button "…"` in the log | Add a `bot.onComponent(...)` for that `customId` (or a pattern that matches it). |
| `forbidden` with `bot_no_voice` | An admin hasn't let the bot join voice: **Bots & webhooks → Bots → Voice**. |
| `Voice needs @livekit/rtc-node: run "npm install" …` | As it says: voice uses packages the rest of the SDK doesn't (with the npm package they're optional dependencies; install them in your bot's folder). |
| `forbidden` with `bot_dms_off` from `sendDm` | That person turned off DMs from bots; the bot can answer once they write to it. |
| `forbidden` with `dm_closed` from `sendDm` | That person only takes DMs from people they've talked to. The bot can answer once they write to it, or within 15 minutes of them using one of its commands. |
| `rate_limited` with `bot_dm_new_limit` | The bot started 20 new conversations in a short time; it can start more later (answering people who wrote to it still works). |
| `Couldn't read a DM from …` in the log | That message wasn't encrypted for this bot's keys (for example it was sent before the bot's `.bot.json` was replaced). New messages are. |
| `Can't play AAC …` / `… is a web page, not an audio file or stream` | Use MP3, Ogg, FLAC or WAV; for a radio, use its direct stream address (often ending in `.mp3`), not its web page. |
| `rate_limited` | The SDK already waits and retries sends; slow down loops that call `bot.request` directly. |

### The SDK on npm

The SDK is on npm as [`iskra-bots`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/iskra-bots) (one ES module with the app's core bundled in, and its TypeScript types),
for bots that live outside the repository:

```sh
npm install iskra-bots
```

```js
import { Bot } from 'iskra-bots'
```

Everything above works the same; the voice packages are optional dependencies. Each release is built and published by
GitHub Actions with a provenance statement, so `npm audit signatures` can check it came from this repository.
Maintainers build it with `npm run build:sdk` in `bots/` (`npm run pack:sdk` lists what would be
published); [docs/ci-cd.md](ci-cd.md#npm-bot-sdk) has the release steps.

### Python

The Python SDK (package `iskra-bots`, `import iskra`, in [`bots/python`](../bots/python)) does what the Node SDK does,
except voice: commands with `/help`, buttons, menus, forms and cards, files, polls, threads, end-to-end encrypted DMs,
reconnecting, and the same `<name>.bot.json`, so a bot can move between Node and Python and keep its identity. It's
asyncio, typed, and needs only [PyNaCl](https://pypi.org/project/PyNaCl/) (libsodium) and
[websockets](https://pypi.org/project/websockets/). Python 3.11 or newer.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/quikmn/iskra-voice.git
pip install ./iskra-voice/bots/python
```

```python
import os
from iskra import Bot

bot = Bot("Greeter", invite=os.environ.get("ISKRA_INVITE"))

@bot.command("hello", "Says hello")
async def hello(ctx):
    await ctx.reply(f"Hi {ctx.user_name}!")

@bot.command("score", "Shows a score card", options=[{"name": "team", "description": "Which team", "type": "string", "required": True}])
async def score(ctx):
    await ctx.reply({
        "cards": [{"title": f"Team {ctx.options['team']}", "color": 0x57F287, "fields": [{"name": "Points", "value": "12", "inline": True}]}],
        "components": [{"type": "row", "items": [{"type": "button", "customId": "cheer", "label": "Cheer 🎉"}]}],
    })

@bot.on_component("cheer")
async def cheer(ctx):
    await ctx.reply(f"{ctx.user_name} cheers!", private=True)

@bot.on("message")                                # messages that mention the bot
async def pizza(message):
    if "pizza" in message.text:
        await message.react("🍕")

@bot.on("dm")                                     # end-to-end encrypted DMs; commands work there too
async def dm(dm):
    if not dm.text.startswith("/"):
        await dm.reply("Hi! Try /hello")

bot.run()                                         # until Ctrl+C; or: await bot.start() in your own asyncio code
```

Start it once with the invite (`ISKRA_INVITE='<bot invite link>' python greeter.py`; PowerShell:
`$env:ISKRA_INVITE='<link>'; python greeter.py`); after that it finds the server in `greeter.bot.json`. The example
Dice bot is [`bots/python/examples/dice.py`](../bots/python/examples/dice.py).

| Node | Python |
|---|---|
| `new Bot({ name, invite, stateFile, hearBots, log })` | `Bot(name, invite=None, *, state_file=None, hear_bots=False, log=None)` |
| `bot.command(name, description, handler, details)`, `bot.commands([...])` | the same, or `@bot.command(name, description, options=..., usage=..., role=..., permission=...)` |
| `bot.onComponent(id or /re/, ...)`, `bot.onModalSubmit(...)` | `@bot.on_component("id" or re.compile(...))`, `@bot.on_modal_submit(...)` |
| `bot.on('message' \| 'dm' \| 'memberJoined' \| 'messageEdited' \| ...)` | `@bot.on("message" \| "dm" \| "member_joined" \| "message_edited" \| ...)` (the camelCase names work too) |
| Context: `userName`, `channelId`, `options`, `args`, `reply`, `defer`, `showModal`, `update`, `customId`, `values`, `fields` | `ctx.user_name`, `ctx.channel_id`, `ctx.options`, `ctx.args`, `await ctx.reply(content, private=True)`, `ctx.defer()`, `ctx.show_modal(modal)`, `ctx.update(...)`, `ctx.custom_id`, `ctx.values`, `ctx.fields` |
| `m.text`, `m.authorName`, `m.reply()`, `m.react()`; `dm.from`, `dm.reply()` | `m.text`, `m.author_name`, `m.data` (the whole message), `await m.reply()`, `await m.react()`; `dm.author`, `await dm.reply()` |
| `send`, `edit`, `delete`, `react`, `upload`, `sendFile`, `poll`, `thread`, `setActivity`, `sendDm`, `downloadDmFile`, `request` | `send(channel_id, content, reply_to=, attachments=, cards=, components=)`, `edit`, `delete`, `react`, `upload(name, data)`, `send_file(channel_id, name, data, text=)`, `poll(channel_id, question, answers, multi=, duration_ms=)`, `thread`, `set_activity`, `send_dm`, `download_dm_file`, `request(type, body)` (all `async`) |
| `bot.channels`, `bot.members`, `bot.me`, `channelByName`, `mention`, `fileUrl` | `bot.channels`, `bot.members` (a dict), `bot.me`, `channel_by_name`, `mention`, `file_url` |

Content is a string or a dict with the protocol's own field names (`text`, `cards`, `components`, `attachments`,
`replyTo`); messages, members and channels arrive as plain dicts (typed `TypedDict`s). Failed requests raise
`RequestError` with a `code`; a refused start raises `Rejected` (with the same explanations as in
[When it won't start](#when-it-wont-start)). Handlers may be plain or `async`; one that raises is logged and the bot
carries on.

The crypto is libsodium through PyNaCl, nothing hand-rolled, and its tests check it against the protocol's test vectors
([`protocol/vectors.json`](../protocol/vectors.json)) and against DMs the app's own code encrypted. Voice bots are
Node only for now.

### Other languages

Any language can run a bot through the **bridge**: a small program in the npm package that logs in as the bot with the
Node SDK (the normal signed handshake, keys in `<name>.bot.json`) and talks to your program in JSON, one object per
line, over your program's **stdin and stdout**. There's no HTTP API and nothing listens on a port: your program only
reads and writes lines.

```sh
# Starts your program and connects its stdin/stdout to the bot. The invite is only needed the first time.
npx iskra-bots bridge --name Roll --invite '<bot invite link>' -- python roll.py
npx iskra-bots bridge --name Roll -- dotnet run Roll.cs
```

Without a program after `--`, the bridge uses its own stdin and stdout instead, for a program that starts the bridge
itself. Options: `--name` (or `ISKRA_BOT_NAME`), `--invite` (or `ISKRA_INVITE`), `--state <file>` (or
`ISKRA_BOT_STATE`), `--hear-bots`, `--raw`. In the repository: `npm run bridge -- --name Roll -- python roll.py` in
`bots/`. The program is started without a shell, so on Windows name its `.exe` (`python`, `node`, `dotnet`). The
bridge's own messages go to stderr, and so does your program's stderr.

Two complete examples, each about 30 lines: [`roll.py`](../bots/examples/bridge/roll.py) (Python without the SDK) and
[`Roll.cs`](../bots/examples/bridge/Roll.cs) (one C# file).

#### The line protocol (version 1)

**From the bridge** (your stdin), events:

```jsonc
{"event":"hello","body":{"v":1,"bridge":"iskra-bots 0.2.1","name":"Roll"}}       // always the first line
{"event":"ready","body":{"me":Member,"channels":[Channel],"commands":[Command]}}  // online (again, after a reconnect)
{"event":"command","ref":"r1","body":{"command":"roll","args":"2d6","options":{"dice":"2d6"},
  "user":"<accountKey>","userName":"Viktor","channelId":1,"dm":false,"private":false,"messageId"?:42}}
{"event":"component","ref":"r2","body":{"customId":"again","values":[],"user":"...","userName":"...","channelId":1,"messageId"?:43,"responseId"?:"...","private":false}}
{"event":"modal","ref":"r3","body":{"customId":"plan","fields":{"title":"Game night"},"user":"...","userName":"...","channelId":1}}
{"event":"message","ref":"r4","body":{"message":Message,"authorName":"Viktor"}}  // messages the bot may read
{"event":"dm","ref":"r5","body":{"id":"...","from":"<accountKey>","authorName":"Viktor","text":"hi","sentAt":0,"files":[DmFile]}}
{"event":"memberJoined","body":{"member":Member}}
{"event":"messageEdited","body":{"message":Message}}   // also messageDeleted, reactions, pollUpdated (the server's bodies)
{"event":"status","body":{"state":"offline","retryInMs":2000}}                  // connecting, online, offline, restarting, rejected
{"event":"server","type":"chat.typing","body":{...}}   // every server event, only with --raw
{"event":"stopped","body":{"reason":"..."}}            // the bot couldn't start or was turned away; the bridge ends
```

Objects (`Member`, `Message`, ...) are the protocol's ([PROTOCOL.md](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md#objects)). A `ref`
answers what it came with for 15 minutes (the last 1000 are kept).

**To the bridge** (your stdout), requests, each with your own `id` (a string of 1–64 characters, or an integer):

```jsonc
{"id":1,"type":"bridge.commands","body":{"commands":[{"name":"roll","description":"Rolls dice","options":[...]}]}}
{"id":2,"type":"bridge.reply","body":{"ref":"r1","text":"Rolled 7","cards"?:[...],"components"?:[...],"private"?:true}}
{"id":3,"type":"chat.history","body":{"channelId":1}}     // any request in PROTOCOL.md, sent as the bot
```

and the answer to each, on one line:

```jsonc
{"id":2,"ok":true,"body":{"message":Message}}
{"id":3,"ok":false,"error":{"code":"forbidden","message":"...","key"?:"bot_no_read","args"?:{}}}
```

| Request | Body | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| `bridge.commands` | `commands`: the command list, as [above](#commands) (`name`, `description`, `usage?`, `options?`, `role?`, `permission?`). Replaces the list set before; `/help` is built in. Works before the bot is online. | `{ commands: [names] }` |
| `bridge.reply` | `ref` (a command, click, form, message or DM), and `text?`, `cards?`, `components?`, `private?` | `{ message }` (null for private answers and DMs) |
| `bridge.defer` | `ref` (a command, click or form): "thinking…" | |
| `bridge.update` | `ref` (a click), and the new `text?`, `cards?`, `components?` of the message it was on | |
| `bridge.modal` | `ref` (a command or click), `modal` ([a form](#buttons-menus-and-forms)) | |
| `bridge.react` | `ref` (a message, or a command typed as text), `emoji` | |
| `bridge.send` | `channelId`, `text?`, `cards?`, `components?`, `replyTo?`, `attachments?` (retries when rate limited; text over 4000 characters is cut) | `{ message }` |
| `bridge.dm` | `accountKey`, `text?`, `cards?`: an end-to-end encrypted DM | |
| `bridge.upload` | `name`, `data` (base64) | `{ file }`, for `attachments` |
| `bridge.dmFile` | `file` (from a `dm` event's `files`) | `{ data }` (base64, decrypted and checked) |
| `bridge.info` | | `{ me, channels, members, commands }` |
| anything else | the protocol request's body | its result |

| | |
|---|---|
| Line length | Up to 1 MiB per line from your program (longer lines are refused whole: `too_large`). Lines from the bridge have no limit of their own; they're as big as the server's events. |
| Encoding | UTF-8, one JSON object per line, `\n` (or `\r\n`) at the end. Read stdin as UTF-8. |
| Waiting answers | At most 64 requests at once (more: `busy`). Answers can come in any order: match them by `id`. |
| Before it's online | Requests wait until the bot is online (`bridge.commands` and `bridge.info` don't). |
| Errors | `code` is the server's ([PROTOCOL.md → Errors](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md#errors-and-close-codes)) or the bridge's: `bad_request` (a malformed line or body; `id` is `null` when the line had no usable id), `unknown_ref`, `unknown_type`, `too_large`, `busy`, `disconnected`, `failed`. |
| Other output | A line that doesn't start with `{` (a stray `print`) is passed to the bridge's log, not treated as a request. |
| Ending | When your program exits, the bridge stops the bot and exits with your program's exit code; without `--`, it stops when its stdin closes. |
| Versions | `hello` carries the protocol version (`v: 1`). New events, fields and request types can be added in version 1, so ignore what you don't know; anything incompatible would be version 2. |

What the bridge doesn't change: the bot is still a bot (the same [limits](#bots), read scope and badge), and the
program it runs can do anything the bot can, so run programs you trust, and keep `<name>.bot.json` private.

Writing a client from scratch is possible too: a bot is any client that follows [PROTOCOL.md](../protocol/PROTOCOL.md):
make an Ed25519 account key and device key, certify the device, connect to `wss://<server>/ws`, and send `auth` with
`profile: { name, bot: true }` and the bot invite code (the last part of the invite link). The Python SDK is a complete
example of that.
